docs.title: KasugaLibNext Documentation
docs.text: This site is the development documentation for KasugaLibNext and its downstream mods, aimed at mod authors who want to integrate rendering, modelling, and data-driven capabilities.

docs.title: Site Structure
docs.text: Section Intended reader Content getting-started/ First-time integration Setting up a project from scratch and getting the first example running guides/ Arriving with a concrete task Getting-started tutorials, example recipes, and verification steps reference/ Looking up signatures APIs, configuration schema, commands, and failure behavior explanation/ Wanting to understand the mechanics Module boundaries, data flow, algorithms, and resource ownership meta/ Project and versions Compatibility matrix, migration guides, licenses, contributor documentation, and verification records

docs.title: Documentation Maintenance
docs.text:
When adding a callable API, complete its package name, signature, units, default values, error conditions, and lifecycle in reference/, and link to the corresponding explanation; when changing an API, update the call examples and configuration tables in step; when migrating or renaming, update the index, the root README, relative links, and anchors. Explanation docs use type names, mathematical expressions, and diagrams to explain the mechanics; method references, configuration tables, and operating steps belong in reference/.

The full conventions are in the "Documentation Maintenance" section of reference/README.md.

docs.title: Explanations and Design
docs.text:
This directory explains algorithms, data flow, module boundaries, timing, and resource ownership. Concrete APIs, parameters, schemas, integration code, and commands are collected in API reference.

Topic Explanation Format Readers and common subsystems, pose composition, and outfit cache boundaries Model Subsystems Shared skeleton definitions, Caliko reverse mapping, and diamond closure Skeleton Dynamics Fixed step, native solving, animation targets, and physics writeback Physics Author physics, body profile, secondary motion, and large coordinates MMD/glTF Camera component tracks, optical zoom, and shared clock Camera Animation Layered states, actions, and pose blending FSM Shared variant definitions and per-instance selection state Multiplexer Descriptor/execution separation, shader preparation, effects, and post-processing graphs Custom Rendering Layer responsibilities, mount publishing, and in-flight GPU reads UML Framework Core, graphics API, and host adaptation boundaries Rendering Backends Vanilla visibility, per-view marks, and sampling deduplication Render Scheduling Screen unprojection, world UI, and input ownership World UI Input Final blit, read-only borrow, and shared capture Frame Output Same-process camera view isolation, world subscription, and GPU synchronization Multi-Camera and Offscreen Translucent passes, WBOIT, and depth compositing Alpha Rendering Stylized textures, material variants, and generation-based caching PBR Weather density layers, ray marching, and shadowing Volumetric Clouds Content tree, property conversion, factories, and registration dispatch Data-Driven Registration

docs.title: How cameras and the shared animation timeline work
docs.text: For the control interfaces, track fields, and clip examples see the API reference.

docs.title: Pose sources and component tracks
docs.text:
A camera first takes position, orientation, FOV, and output size from a pose provider, and animation only overrides the components it defines. Position uses world coordinates and rotation follows the host camera's angle convention; unwrapped angles interpolate directly, so continuous multi-turn rotation can be expressed. Direct control starts from the current pose, replaces the provider, and ends the original animation, so the next frame is not overwritten by the old tracks.

Track keyframes are sorted and copied at construction, adjacent keyframes interpolate by the easing function, and outside the first and last the endpoint is held. Components with no track keep coming from the provider. Optical zoom changes the projection; it does not scale the world or the output texture. The relationship is:

tan(newFov / 2) = tan(baseFov / 2) / zoom

Zoom is evaluated against the base FOV of the current provider and is not multiplied across successive frames. Invalid zoom caused by interpolation is guarded by a positive-value bound.

docs.title: Clock ownership
docs.text:
A standalone player owns its own clock; the game tick advances time and render frames only sample by partial tick. Sampling must not advance the clock again. A shared timeline is driven by one host, and models and cameras only follow, which prevents one scene from being advanced repeatedly by multiple targets.

During shared playback, pause, seek, and speed control act on the common clock; closing one camera or detaching one target does not stop the others. Pausing the frame output of one camera and pausing the whole timeline are different operations. After playback finishes the end pose can be kept; clip looping is decided uniformly by the timeline period, and shorter targets hold their own endpoint within the shared period.

docs.title: Model and camera channels
docs.text:
Model poses and camera poses share the timing/sampling kernel, but their output targets handle bone, morph, material, and named camera track channels separately. The logical camera name is independent of the output view ID, and one camera track can be bound to multiple actual camera views. A model reload only swaps the output target and does not reset the external shared clock. The layer weights and state transitions of a layered state machine are still managed by the state machine itself.

The control thread delivers the clock through an immutable snapshot and the render thread samples it. A closed or failed camera no longer accepts control, which keeps old controller references from driving resources that have already been released. The output size of a window camera view is still determined by the framebuffer/DPI and is not frozen by animation tracks.

docs.title: How data-driven registration works
docs.text: For file structure, fields, factories, and property extensions see the API reference.

docs.title: From content descriptions to the registration tree
docs.text:
Data packs describe blocks, items, and block entities; the parsing layer builds only the raw content tree. Property parsers turn a description into property transforms, factories turn a type description into registration nodes that already exist, and finally the virtual registry group is attached to the mod's main registration tree. Data content reuses the existing registration event dispatch, and no second parallel registration system is maintained.

flowchart TD
    Resources[Mod content descriptions] --> Parse[Parse into a raw content tree]
    Parse --> Properties[Block and item property transforms]
    Properties --> Factory[Type factories]
    Factory --> Tree[Virtual registry group]
    Tree --> Dispatch[Existing registration event chain]

Parsing, property extension, and object construction are kept apart, so custom content can reuse the default property handling and Java registration can coexist with data registration. Creative tabs are still injected through the existing modifier path. Complex behavior stays on the code side; content only selects a behavior factory and its parameters.

docs.title: Initialization order
docs.text:
The content tree is built lazily at the first registration dispatch, not during some arbitrary resource scan. That way factory types and custom property parsers can finish initializing with their context class first, so parsing does not fail from a missing factory because static registration has not happened yet.

A group's hierarchy organizes and shares properties, but group inheritance does not mean that all item properties are already fully merged. Certain types, circular dependency detection, DataFixer types, and more complex item components remain implementation boundaries; the mere existence of a description file is not proof that they are supported.

docs.title: Discovery, reload, and source ownership
docs.text:
The index separates registration-phase content from reloadable content. Both phases share path validation, index parsing, and content shape handling, which are handed to registration dispatch and reload orchestration respectively; each reload type is declared by a host extension, not hardcoded by the orchestrator. Content candidates are merged in a deterministic order, the same effective identity adopts last-wins, and pack overrides are processed in pack stack order too.

A reload cycle first clears the definitions contributed by resource sources, then collects, decodes, and registers candidates, and finally re-checks dependencies across definitions. State machines and clips registered from code are held by the code side, survive resource reloads, and take precedence over resource definitions of the same name. Diagnostics are stored by source and phase ownership, and error boundaries are limited to the corresponding file or handler so that other content can still be processed.

Interfaces, schema, content authoring, and extension guides all live under the data-driven API topic.

docs.title: How custom render pipelines work
docs.text: For the interfaces, Shader DSL, and integration examples see the API reference.

docs.title: Descriptor and execution separation
docs.text:
A pipeline keeps its draw state, execution stage, and ordering information in an immutable descriptor; the registry activates, replaces, and releases it. A configuration that describes the same content can be reused, while the execution object that holds GPU resources and host state belongs to one registration. After a registration is replaced, an old handle still refers to the old object, so unloading an old module does not delete a new object by mistake.

World drawing is organized by host stage. Within a stage, entries are ordered by priority and then by resource identity. The registry caches an execution snapshot per stage and invalidates it on change, so the draw traversal does not depend directly on the mutable registration list. A failure in one callback does not stop the other pipelines in the same stage. Pose stacks are isolated per callback, and a buffer batch must complete within that draw.

docs.title: Ownership and generation-based resources
docs.text:
A static registration belongs to the client lifecycle, while dynamic content belongs to a scope that can be closed. A parent scope owns its child scopes, and resources are released in reverse registration order. Draw state and the texture-variant cache belong to the registration object itself, and replacing a name yields an independent cache.

A shader handle stays stable across a resource reload, while the compiled instance inside it is replaced per generation. The generation advances only when a new instance is installed successfully. Editable parameters are stored independently of the compiled instance, so a resource reload does not lose user parameters. Different registrations cannot share a lifecycle just because they use the same ID.

docs.title: Shader preparation and the render thread
docs.text:
Converting generated IR into GLSL and resource descriptors is CPU work and runs on a bounded background executor; OpenGL compilation and linking must return to the render thread. Concurrent requests for the same program share one conversion, whose result goes into a bounded cache. A full preparation queue fails explicitly rather than falling back to a synchronous conversion on the calling thread.

Each frame the compilation queue bounds how many jobs start and the budget spent before starting, and schedules across owners. A driver compilation that has already started cannot be cut off midway, so the budget is not a strict cap on frame time. Closing and replacing cancel preparation tasks that have not started yet. The failure policy decides whether to disable the current pipeline or abort the reload in progress; a late preload has no reload context to abort.

docs.title: Execution model of the Java DSL
docs.text: A Java builder builds typed shader IR immediately; it does not parse a Java AST or decompile lambdas. Java conditions and loops only control how the IR is built, and runtime GPU control flow has to be represented explicitly in the IR. Reusing an expression object is not the same as creating a GLSL local variable. The graphics program checks, at build time, the names and types of vertex outputs and fragment inputs, plus the consistency of uniform and sampler declarations across stages. The current backend converts IR into GLSL 150 and Minecraft core-shader resources.

docs.title: Effect instances and post-processing graphs
docs.text:
Effects of the same kind share a renderer and pipeline state, and each instance holds position, lifetime, and interpolation data. The client tick advances effects; the draw stage culls by interpolated bounding volume and sorts by distance to the camera when needed. A level switch clears instances and the post-processing target pool.

Post-processing builds a directed acyclic graph from declarative read/write relations and explicit dependencies. Every intermediate target has one clear producer; cycles, multiple writers, and undeclared targets are rejected at build time. A single pass does not read and write the same target, which avoids framebuffer feedback. A target's physical identity includes the graph ID, so identically named logical targets in several graphs do not collide. Targets are reused by descriptor and actual size, and the last graph registration releases the targets it manages.

The pre-execution preparation can cancel the frame without allocating unused targets. Within a frame the preparation and the passes share temporary data containers, and target access is bounded by the declarations. The host's main target is restored when post-processing ends or throws. Touching low-level GPU objects directly bypasses these constraints, and state restoration is then the caller's responsibility.

docs.title: How final frame output works
docs.text: For registration, consumers, lifecycle, and readback see the API reference.

docs.title: Capture point
docs.text: The capture sits at the host's final screen blit, after the world, post-processing, HUD, GUI, and loading screen have finished. The output reuses the shader and scaling of the native final blit; it does not replace the main render target, and it does not render the world again for the final frame. A world camera view product and the final main frame that includes the full interface are different layers; see Multi-Camera and Offscreen for details.

docs.title: One capture shared per view
docs.text:
The router uses the view as the resource-ownership boundary. A frame of one view is captured once, and synchronous consumers borrow the same completed frame and color texture. The target is allocated lazily on the first valid output and released when the last consumer leaves. With no subscribers, the native screen blit runs directly.

An exclusive output cancels only this frame's screen blit; it does not stop window events, the game loop, or the display swap. When consumption or capture fails and no exclusive output succeeded, the screen presentation is kept, so an export failure does not swallow the picture for good.

docs.title: Borrowing, synchronization, and release
docs.text:
The output is a synchronous read-only borrow on the render thread; a consumer may not resize it or delete the texture. The next frame overwrites the storage, and a size change replaces the target. Keeping the picture beyond the callback requires copying into your own GPU/CPU storage and handling synchronization. A GPU texture number is only a handle: it is not a CPU pointer, and it cannot be handed to a thread that has no current GL context.

An exception in one consumer removes only that consumer, while an exception during target creation or drawing closes the whole view. When a subscription is closed or replaced during delivery, the actual release is deferred to the end of that delivery, so other callbacks can still read the borrowed frame.

The output color is RGBA8 with opaque alpha and no depth attachment; the origin follows the OpenGL bottom-left convention. The target is sized to the actual framebuffer pixel size. The capture restores the read/draw FBO, the viewport, and any GPU state it changed temporarily; a consumer still has to restore its own extra changes, and on host shutdown the output resources are released together before the main context is destroyed.

docs.title: How the layered animation state machine works
docs.text: For the data schema, action / guard references, and binding see the API reference.

docs.title: Definitions and instances
docs.text: A state machine definition describes variables, parallel layers, states, and transitions, and is loaded into the definition registry during a resource reload. A running instance holds the current state, the state duration, variable values, and blend progress, and none of that state may be written back into the shared definition. The file identity is independent of the machine's logical identity, and the host binds an instance by the logical identity.

docs.title: State advancement and actions
docs.text: Each layer has its own state graph; a tick selects a transition based on guards, triggers, and completion conditions, and runs the entry, exit, update, and transition actions at the corresponding stages. Content references function ids registered on the code side, which avoids executing arbitrary code at data-load time. Ephemeral triggers are cleared at the end of the tick cycle, while ordinary variables stay in the instance.

docs.title: Pose blending
docs.text:
Multiple layers composite the pose in a deterministic order. The base layer provides the baseline, additive layers stack local motion on top, and override layers replace the specified range according to the bone mask. During a transition the pose is blended over time between the poses of the previous and next states; render frames sample smoothly with the partial tick rather than advancing the logical state any further. The result contains bone local transforms, morph weights, and material frames, and then enters the unified bone, IK, and physics flow.

The state machine owns action timing; the selection from a simple context to a model variant can be handled by Multiplexer. The two can be combined: the model variant decides which instance is used, and the state machine decides how that instance moves.

docs.title: How MMD and glTF Ragdoll Adaptation Works
docs.text: For profile, manifest, runtime deployment, and commands see the API reference. For the generic data and the Caliko structures see Skeleton Dynamics.

docs.title: Reading Layer and Generic Runtime
docs.text: The MMD Reader converts the author's rigid bodies, joints, and IK into generic skeleton definitions, and keeps the raw tables available for format access. glTF provides no standard rigid body/IK tables, so the Reader only keeps physics candidates arranged by node; the human topology has to be described explicitly. Both enter the same skeleton runtime; bone references, writeback strategy, and scale information travel with the definitions, so the model format is not re-decided during the physics step.

docs.title: Author Physics and the Body Profile
docs.text:
Using the author's rigid bodies directly suits secondary motion such as skirts, hair, and accessories. The body profile generates capsules, semantic masses, and joints from the actual bone segments, and replaces author shapes that are not meant for human collision with body colliders. Equal-length bone segments pick their direction by a stable bone order, so the object allocation order does not change the collider orientation.

Unregistered secondary-motion chains can keep their original shape, damping, and filtering relationships. An attachment point on the main body drives the secondary-motion chains one-way through a kinematic proxy that moves with the main body, with the filter layer isolated from the main body, which keeps a large number of skirt/hair rigid bodies from dragging the main body backward. Under hybrid mode, secondary-motion bones keep the animated translation and write back only the physics rotation, so a change of reference frame does not stretch the bone segments.

docs.title: Scale and Large Coordinates
docs.text:
Vertices, bones, rigid body shapes, and joint positions must use a consistent import scale; gravity always stays in world units and must not shrink with the model scale, otherwise a small character falls in the wrong slow motion. A glTF affine bone hierarchy also keeps scale/shear, so writing back the physics TR requires computing the local pose within the full parent transform, to avoid applying the parent scale twice.

World translation is stored in a separate double anchor. Bones and native physics use float coordinates near the origin; at render time the difference between the world anchor and the camera is computed in double first, and only then written into the float matrix. This way short bone segments and small colliders are not quantized at large coordinates.

docs.title: Native Joints and Environment Boundaries
docs.text: Box3D handles integration, contact, CCD, sleeping, drag, and joint solving. Author spheres/boxes/capsules map to native shapes, and the Minecraft environment is connected through incremental static colliders. An infinite plane is approximated by a large thin box placed along its normal. PMX six-axis joints are currently approximated as spherical cone/twist, and the three-axis translation is tightened to a fixed anchor; the various author joint types are not fully distinguished. Per-vertex soft bodies and fluid buoyancy are not integrated. A dimension change, leaving the world, and deployment teardown all need to release the environment, the drag, and the native resources.

docs.title: How Model subsystem format boundaries work
docs.text:
For the interface reference see Generic model posing and animation and Skeleton Dynamics.

A Model describes only the common geometry, materials, skeleton, morph, and named animation. The format of a model file decides how that content is read; it does not decide which capabilities are available at runtime. Original file records may be kept in metadata, and the runtime subsystem evaluates through the converted common definitions instead of selecting model capabilities by the concrete class of the metadata.

flowchart TD
    A[PMX / PMD Reader] --> D[Common Model and Skeleton definitions]
    B[glTF Reader] --> D
    C[MC / Blockbench / External Reader] --> D
    D --> E[Instance Pose / animation / FSM]
    E --> F[Inheritance and fixed axis → IK → physics]
    F --> G[Common skinning and render data]

Bone transform inheritance and fixed axes are generic skeleton capabilities. Indexes and flags in the file are converted at read time into direct bone references and constraint data. Evaluation resolves the referenced local pose first, so a value from the previous frame is not read just because another branch has not been traversed yet. Inheritance loops have no well-defined order and are rejected at build time; the positional closure of a diamond IK is a separate solve constraint. Cross-branch inheritance affects vertices outside the source bone's subtree, and updates must cover those dependencies.

Animation keeps each source's sampling algorithm and only requires that the output be a common Pose. A named clip library combines samplers and source data, the player handles time, and PoseSink writes into the model instance. A static pose is a clip sampled at a constant value and uses the same channel ownership and reset rules. VPD/VMD do not require the target skeleton to carry PMX metadata; matching bone names and channel identities are enough for a write. Topological retargeting between different skeletons remains the integrator's responsibility.

The IK switch is also a common channel in the Pose, so animation and state machines can both use the same write path. A shared Model holds the capability definitions, while each instance holds playback position, bone transforms, IK state, and physics simulation state. An ordinary MC model can reuse these capabilities directly without faking MMD/glTF metadata.

A build check in the render core forbids the common structures, the dynamic runtime, math, and the framework from depending on a concrete format package, limiting format access to the Reader/Converter/Sampler boundary.

docs.title: Outfit assembly and cache boundaries
docs.text:
The assembly capability of a common Model maps clothing bones onto the body skeleton and remaps vertex bindings, morph, materials, animation, and dynamics, producing a reusable shared model definition. Named body regions are supplied by the resource integrator; hiding one removes faces and vertices that are no longer used. For the interface reference see the Model assembly and outfit cache API.

The cache key covers the source objects and their revisions, part order, bone mapping, final hidden regions, and integration settings. A rebuild happens only on a cache miss; multiple instances of the same outfit share the assembly result and each holds its own pose state. Eviction follows most-recently-used order, and the entry count and vertex count together bound how much is retained, so outfit combinations do not grow without limit. Modifying a resource in place requires a revision bump or an explicit invalidate; hashing the content of a whole model does not belong on every query path.

What is cached is bind pose geometry; animation is still evaluated on the instance skeleton. Merged geometry cuts submissions and repeated skeleton processing, but different materials and alpha states still have to be rendered separately. Only removing hidden body and inner clothing regions reduces the vertex and pixel cost of those areas. Only parts that share motion semantics can share a skeleton directly; a garment's own bones, morph, and secondary motion must be preserved at assembly time and their dependencies remapped. Shared bones must also have compatible bind matrices, and a matching name is not a substitute for matching coordinates.

Assembly clones the mutable structures, material and frame definitions are isolated per part, and texture resources continue to be held by the original resource system. The cache itself holds only CPU model definitions; ownership of GPU buffers and per-instance state stays with the existing backend. Cache eviction does not destroy a model that is still rendering, whereas a resource reload requires the host to end the old instance before releasing its borrowed resources.

A resource-level definition holds only the host key, bone mapping, and visible regions, not the Model object of any one load. The Minecraft adapter waits until all sources are published, then resolves the definition into a complete assembly request. When a source is replaced or deleted, the publish notification first withdraws the derived instances and their cache references, and keeps the definitions so that the next generation can resolve them again. Several definitions may share one cached model, but instances are isolated by resource key, and replacing one definition does not reclaim another definition's instances.

An outfit swap prepares first and switches after. While a source is missing the previous outfit stays in use; on success the base pose and logical drivers are migrated before the old instance is reclaimed. A resource reload has to withdraw the objects that borrowed the old textures first; the handle keeps the state to restore and mounts again once the next generation is ready. Model geometry revision and the per-character logical clock are independent, and refreshing the sampling sources of a named animation does not replace a timeline that other targets follow.

docs.title: Anchors and deformable attachments
docs.text:
An Anchor describes a display coordinate frame on a bone and is evaluated after animation, IK, and physics. Its bind-space transform works like a vertex: the inverse bind is applied first, then the current bone pose, so rotation and non-uniform scaling stay consistent with skinning. A local attachment offset is converted to author coordinates at bind time and only follows the bone at runtime; during rendering the camera origin is subtracted in double precision, so large coordinates are not converted to float early and small offsets are not lost.

Equipment, tools, and weapons that move as a unit are placed through Anchors, and the host renderer decides how they are displayed. Garment vertices may be controlled by several bones at once, and shared-skeleton assembly preserves that deformation semantics. An outfit slot can organize both kinds of attachment at once, but a single rigid-body attachment frame cannot provide per-vertex skinning for a garment and does not replace bind-space adaptation. For the interfaces and the Minecraft item integration see the Anchor API.

docs.title: How model variant selection works
docs.text: For the Java DSL, Builder, and runtime methods see the API reference.

docs.title: Shared definition and instance state
docs.text: Multiplexer describes the choice from context to appearance with variant nodes and guarded transition edges. The definition itself holds no runtime state; the same content type shares a definition, and each host instance keeps its own current variant, target variant, and cross-fade progress. The context delivers information such as block properties and redstone state as a snapshot, and the selector does not depend on specific Minecraft objects.

docs.title: Selection and advancing
docs.text: Read-only selection evaluates the available variants against the current context; advancing updates both the instance's transition progress and the selected state. A guard hit starts a transition; during the cross-fade the current output corresponds to the target variant, and the instance information the blending process needs is kept. Each host advances independently, so the same definition can select different appearances in different scenes.

docs.title: Division of responsibility with the state machine
docs.text: Context-driven switches, gears, and model variants suit the variant selector; behavior that depends on duration, actions, parallel layers, and animation sequences suits the layered state machine. Variant selection decides which model to use, and the state machine keeps driving the pose and action timing of the selected model.

docs.title: How offscreen rendering, multi-camera, and shared output work
docs.text: For examples of creating cameras, multiple windows, headless startup, FBO consumption, and recording see the API reference.

docs.title: One client and several world views
docs.text:
Cameras come in three types: Player, Free, and Fixed. Player uses the player's native view and the final main frame; Free has a world pose that can be controlled directly or driven by animation; Fixed binds a follow target, samples its position/orientation during rendering, and combines an offset with an independent projection. The type is independent of the resource lifecycle of pause, failure, and close. A follow target at the core layer describes only world coordinates and angles, and the host supplies the entity adaptation. The projection and follow binding of a Fixed camera are stored separately, so zooming does not replace the target. When the entity is temporarily unavailable the camera is kept and output and chunk subscription for that view stop; they resume once the host provider supplies the target again.

Target sampling happens before the camera view's private level is installed. A callback that reads the target also uses the same native source level, so a native entity is not mistaken for one in the wrong dimension. Render configuration changes are deferred until the current scope and callbacks end, and the camera view session is replaced on the next frame so that resource ownership stays consistent.

Camera views render sequentially in the same client process and the main OpenGL context. Each camera view has its own level caches, camera, terrain renderer, projection, and color/depth targets, while the main view keeps the native path. An auxiliary window only presents the completed texture and does not create a new player connection or game tick. The full main frame also includes HUD and GUI, whereas an additional camera view produces only the world image.

A hidden desktop context and a Linux EGL pbuffer both run a full client and still need an OpenGL driver. Headless is not fixed-timestep video export and does not automatically include an encoder. An auxiliary window has its own read FBO and bidirectional fence; the main context waits for the read to finish before it overwrites the texture, but it does not block the whole frame with a CPU glFinish.

docs.title: Same-process isolation and render ordering
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Host frame / shared animation token] --> B[Camera view A world / resource / Iris scope]
    B --> C[A world and Iris final compositing]
    C --> D[A consumers]
    D --> E[Camera view B separate scope and output]
    E --> F[Restore main view and render]
    F --> G[Main post-processing / HUD / GUI]
    G --> H[Final main frame output]
Configuration or resource Isolation mechanism Position, orientation, FOV, size Per-camera-view Camera, projection, and color/depth FBO Chunks and lighting Per-camera-view ClientLevel, ClientChunkCache, light engine Terrain and entity drawing Per-camera-view LevelRenderer, RenderBuffers, mutable entity/block-entity dispatchers Render distance Per-camera-view 2..32 chunks, with independent server subscription and client render distance Iris shader pack Per-camera-view ShaderPack, PipelineManager, material settings, uniform time, capture, and shadow state Materials and models Per-pack-stack resource manager, TextureManager, ModelManager, atlas Quality Per-camera-view Fast/Fancy, leaf type, AO, mipmap Fog and clouds Per-camera-view fog history; Iris/Sodium cloud format flags are stored per CloudRenderer instance

Camera views on the same pack stack and mipmap share loaded models and atlases, released by reference count, while mutable renderers and dispatchers are held individually. Resource packs stack in list order, with later packs taking precedence. The base resources keep vanilla and mod resources and do not inherit the user or server packs selected by the main view; packs that are needed are written into resourcePacks explicitly. Both directories and zips are supported. The player skin, cape, and elytra downloaded on connect, plus the shared light texture, font glyphs, particle atlas, and mod-generated textures with no file resource, are borrowed resources and are not deleted with the camera view. The camera view's own atlas takes precedence and is not replaced by the main view's atlas.

The Iris entry points route to their own instances inside the scope, and some static state is isolated by switching and restoring it. A chunk-build task captures the camera view's resources, materials, and quality when it is created and restores that context when the worker runs it. A vanilla rebuild task also holds a resource lease and returns it only after cancellation or after CPU building ends, so closing a camera view does not release a model or material that an asynchronous task still reads. The vanilla ViewArea is positioned from the actual camera view coordinates. This requires sequential rendering in one context and does not support drawing camera views on several threads at once.

The host tick and RenderFrameEvent.Pre/Post still run once per frame, model animation is deduplicated by a shared frame token, and visibility marks are cleared before each camera view draws. Inside a scope the MC level, renderer, buffers, targets, camera, and resource getters point at the current camera view, and the world stage receives the camera view's frustum and matrices. Custom time history can be partitioned by WorldRenderPipelineContext.viewId().

Leaving the scope restores the main state as well as the GL read/draw FBO, viewport, projection, and draw/fog state. A close inside a callback is deferred to the end of that delivery. A level switch destroys the old session and rebuilds it for the current level next time; shutting down Minecraft releases everything. A vanilla builder pack still in flight is released when it returns, and Sodium releases native buffers, sky VBOs, pipelines, and FBOs after its terrain workers stop.

docs.title: Distant chunks and entities
docs.text:
The server also needs KasugaLib installed with this feature; an integrated server in single player uses the same protocol. A server that does not support the channel makes the camera view fail explicitly instead of pretending that a distant world was loaded.

The server manages subscriptions by camera UUID, epoch, dimension, and center, requests FULL and non-ticking chunk tickets in batches, and does not block the main thread waiting for generation. Per subscription and per tick it requests at most 8 tickets and sends 4 snapshots that are already complete and light-ready; a block or lighting change triggers a resend. The client feeds chunks, heightmaps, lighting, and block entities into their own ClientLevel. Movement discards out-of-range caches and stale-epoch data and clears the light and Sodium trackers. Pause, close, logout, a dimension change, and a heartbeat timeout all revoke the server-side tickets.

Entities sync spawn, position, head rotation, full metadata, equipment, attributes, passengers, and any existing leash to the camera view's level every 5 ticks; the copy interpolates on its own, does not consume the vanilla packDirty, and keeps the main player's entity tracking. This subscription is not a new player connection: distant areas can be loaded and filmed, but non-ticking tickets do not extend the server-side simulation range for AI or redstone.

docs.title: Output contract and boundaries
docs.text:
OutputFrame<FrameTexture> exposes the view ID, the frame number per view, the size, and the color texture. The color is RGBA8 with opaque alpha, OpenGL bottom-left origin, and no depth attachment. The router owns a color target per view; all subscriptions of one frame receive the same OutputFrame and resource objects, borrow them for reading only, and may not write, resize, or delete them. The next frame overwrites them, and a resize or the close of the last subscription deletes the old objects; an unsubscribe inside a callback defers the release to the end of that delivery. Keeping the picture beyond the callback requires copying it into your own GPU/CPU storage on the spot, and the DEBUG preview also copies before compositing. Consumers run on the render thread and should not wait on encoding or network work; they may implement their own PBO/fence readback and bounded worker queue, but a bare texture ID cannot be handed to an asynchronous thread that has no current GL context.

The resources in the table above are isolated, but this is not a copy of the whole client:

  • An additional camera view outputs world stages and the Iris final compositing, and does not include HUD/GUI, the hand, the glowing outline, or the main view's GameRenderer.postEffect. The full main frame goes through the final output entry.
  • Quality supports Fast/Fancy, AO, and mipmap but not all options (Fabulous, particle presets, the separate cloud toggle, and so on). The main light texture, fonts, particle engine, and the vanilla core shader loader are shared; a pack that changes fonts, particles, or core shaders cannot be assumed to be fully isolated, and a distant camera view has no separate server-side particle event stream.
  • It does not fully reproduce resource-pack overlays metadata, third-party reload listeners, mod entity pairing payload/attachment, or the effects and audio protocols.
  • Third-party code that reads static state directly, caches the main level, or advances logic in a world stage still needs adaptation; an effect with time history should be managed by view ID.
  • Multi-camera with a long render distance adds generation, network, CPU/GPU, and VRAM load. On a public server the permissions, subscription count, and resource budget are bounded by higher-level policy.

docs.title: Read-only consumers share the completed frame
docs.text:
The output router now captures and holds storage per view. All subscriptions of one frame receive the same OutputFrame<FrameTexture>, and the shared target is released only after the last subscription closes; closing or replacing a subscription inside a callback does not delete the borrowed texture early. The first registration selects the target factory, and GPU storage is allocated only on the first valid output. Different views still own their own output targets.

N synchronous read-only subscriptions to one view Before After Output color texture / FBO N copies 1 copy Final capture per frame N times 1 time Alpha initialization operations per capture 2N clears 2 clears Consumer calls N calls N calls

The nominal size of RGBA8 color storage is 4 × width × height bytes; about 7.91 MiB at 1080p and about 31.64 MiB at 4K. The table above does not count driver metadata, world render targets, window presentation, or a consumer's own copy/encoding storage. A MIRROR main frame still needs the normal screen blit, and every auxiliary window still needs to present; the shared capture does not remove that work from those consumers.

This change does not add CPU zero-copy or asynchronous readback. A GPU texture ID is not a CPU address, and RgbaReadback.copy still performs a synchronous GPU readback, a Java array copy, and a Y flip. A read-only GPU consumer can just borrow the handle; cross-frame or asynchronous consumption needs its own storage and synchronization mechanism.

docs.title: How PMX stylized PBR baking works
docs.text: For configuration, rule registration, context, and diagnostic commands see the API reference.

docs.title: 1. How it works
docs.text:
PMX source materials mainly provide a base texture, a diffuse color, a specular color, and a specular strength, and do not directly contain full PBR textures. KasugaLib performs one pre-bake during client resource loading:

  1. Read the numeric properties of the PMX material and derive automatic conversion parameters.
  2. Apply the Java registration rules and then the player JSON rules.
  3. Generate a normal texture from the luminance gradient of the base texture.
  4. Generate a specular texture that fits the current LabPBR/Iris path.
  5. Splice base color, normal, and specular into their three corresponding atlases.
  6. Write the result to the disk cache, so later resource reloads reuse it first.

docs.title: Automatic parameters
docs.text:
• smoothness: mapped from the PMX shininess.
  • f0_code: derived from the average of the PMX specular color, with the automatic value clamped to 4–90; it never guesses metal automatically.
  • subsurface: defaults to 0.
  • normal_strength: defaults to 0.08.
  • emission: defaults to 0.

docs.title: Output channels
docs.text:
Normal texture:

Channel Content R Encoded tangent-space X G Encoded tangent-space Y B AO, currently 255 A Height, currently 255, which means parallax height is disabled

Specular texture:

Channel Content R Perceptual smoothness G Dielectric F0 or the LabPBR metal code B Porosity/SSS; a non-zero SSS maps to 65–255 A Emission

Normal sampling uses repeat/wrap at texture edges, matching PMX's repeatable UV behavior.

docs.title: Separate material variants
docs.text:
The atlas identity is decided by the source texture plus the final PBR parameters together:

  • Same source texture, same parameters: reuse one variant.
  • Same source texture, different parameters: generate a separate variant with its own normal and specular sprites.
  • If the same atlas identity is bound again to a different source image or parameters: throw a conflict error immediately instead of silently averaging.

docs.title: GPU, CPU, and cache
docs.text:
• The preferred path generates the normal and specular outputs together on the render thread through an offscreen framebuffer and MRT.
  • When the GPU shader is unavailable, the session switches automatically to the deterministic CPU reference baker.
  • The GLSL of the GPU baker lives in assets/kasuga_lib/shaders/pbr/stylized_bake.vsh and stylized_bake.fsh.
  • The GPU baker explicitly saves, zeroes, and restores GL_PIXEL_PACK_BUFFER, GL_PIXEL_UNPACK_BUFFER, and the pack/unpack row-length and skip state.

docs.title: Loading performance
docs.text:
• The linear indexOf lookup in PMX vertex deduplication was fixed, turning the near-O(n²) path for large models into a hash index.
  • Unused copies of the base texture are no longer added to the PBR atlas repeatedly.
  • The PBR disk cache prefetches in parallel on resource loading threads, and only misses go back to the render thread for GPU baking.
  • The content hash of the same source image and profile is reused within one load.
  • BufferedImage is converted to NativeImage directly, without first encoding to an in-memory PNG and decoding it again.
  • The CPU fallback runs at most two bakes at once, so it does not occupy every resource loading thread.
  • An in-world resource reload uses generation-based publishing: the new model is built in the background first, and the atlas and sprite mappings are swapped atomically on the game thread once they are all ready; Kasuga model drawing is suspended during the reload, and the old backend instance of a replaced model is cleaned up.

Baking happens during loading and reloading, not every frame. The actual visual effect of the channels depends on the host and the shader pack; many parameter variants increase atlas area. A change to the algorithm or the channel semantics must invalidate the old cache.

docs.title: How Native Physics and the Pose Pipeline Work
docs.text: For generic rigid bodies, scenes, controllers, the tick loop, and the Minecraft integration see the API reference.

docs.title: Data Flow and Evaluation Ownership
docs.text:
Model animation writes the local pose first, procedural modules and IK produce the current animation targets, native physics advances the dynamic rigid bodies, and finally the physics results are written back to the bones and the display anchors are computed. An anchor must follow the final pose, not an intermediate result from the animation stage.

flowchart LR
    A[Animation sampling] --> B[Local pose and external targets]
    B --> C[Hierarchy evaluation and Caliko IK]
    C --> D[Animation targets and active control forces]
    D --> E[Box3D fixed step]
    E --> F[Bone physics writeback]
    F --> G[Final hierarchy and display anchors]
    G --> H[Render upload]

When physics owns the pose, animation target evaluation takes on the IK work for this frame. After the physics writeback only the hierarchy is rebuilt; IK must not be solved again, and the original animation must not be re-applied over the physics results. Targets can be reused by the epoch of bone input changes; while the input stays unchanged during one physics step there is no need to rebuild the whole animation hierarchy for every fixed substep. The final pose revision is reused by the later upload.

docs.title: Fixed Step and Native Capabilities
docs.text:
Box3D handles integration, broad phase, narrow phase, contacts, joints, CCD, and sleeping; the Java layer only does object mapping, fixed-timestep accumulation, lifecycle, and state synchronization. A single update caps the number of catch-up passes, and accumulated time beyond that is dropped, so a stutter does not trigger unbounded catch-up. The physics pose used for drawing is interpolated between completed states.

The native library is an optional capability; a distribution that ships no platform library can still run models, animation, and IK, but cannot advance native physics. This differs from a Java fallback solver: when the library is missing, the code does not quietly switch to a different set of physics behaviors.

docs.title: Rigid Bodies and Joints
docs.text:
A rigid body can be a compound collider made of several body-local child shapes. The world owns the native objects, and closing the world releases the whole object set; modifying a dynamic object requires waking the corresponding native rigid body. Forces are integrated within a timestep, and an impulse changes momentum directly. A kinematic body is driven by the animation, a dynamic body is written back to the bones in reverse; a rotation-only writeback keeps the animated translation.

The constraints of ball, weld, distance, revolute, and prismatic joints are all enforced by the native engine. An author's six-axis limits may be approximated as cone/twist after adaptation; a fixed anchor does not mean the author's translation range is fully supported. The softness and limit error the native engine allows also differ from a mathematically rigid constraint.

docs.title: World Anchors and the Collision Environment
docs.text:
The double world anchor is kept apart from the local float physics coordinates; environment collision, rays, and drag convert into the same simulation coordinate frame first. Moving the world or migrating a scene requires relocating the bone targets, the rigid bodies, and the environment together, otherwise it introduces wrong impulses or position jumps.

Minecraft block physics builds compounds from the real VoxelShape, and the environment mesh incrementally maintains the local collision region. Block updates drive invalidation, with a periodic refresh as a fallback; the player takes part in local interaction through a kinematic proxy. This client-side local simulation provides no server-authoritative entities, saving, or complete synchronization, and it does not extend the server's level simulation range.

docs.title: Active Ragdoll and Boundaries
docs.text: The active controller turns the same-frame animation/IK targets into bounded PD spring forces and torques, and Box3D still handles contacts and joints. The controller changes targets and applies forces; it cannot directly override the native integration. Physics must not freeze because of render frustum culling. A world keeps only one drag constraint; fluid buoyancy and per-vertex PMX soft bodies are still not integrated.

docs.title: How model material alpha rendering works
docs.text:
Model materials are now split into three classes by the glTF/generic material alpha contract:

Class GPU state Fragment behavior Order OPAQUE No blending, depth write Ignores the sampled alpha and outputs 1 AFTER_ENTITIES priority 0 MASK No blending, depth write Fragments below the material alphaCutoff are discarded, the rest output 1 AFTER_ENTITIES priority 1 BLEND OIT accumulation/revealage, no depth write Discards only the near-invisible alpha <= 1/255 and keeps the actual alpha AFTER_TRANSLUCENT_BLOCKS, WBOIT needs no sorting

BackendInstance creates a separate FlatModelData and vertex buffer for each non-empty pass, so a model with several materials does not draw incompatible geometry repeatedly into the wrong RenderType. OPAQUE and MASK can still go into the global batch, but the batch key includes the alpha pass; BLEND does not go into the global batch, which keeps the two OIT geometry submissions apart from ordinary batching state.

The glTF alphaMode and alphaCutoff reach the backend through GltfMaterialData. An older loader with no alpha contract defaults to OPAQUE; the PMX loader infers OPAQUE, MASK, or BLEND from the diffuse alpha and the texture alpha.

The non-Iris path for BLEND is weighted-blended OIT (WBOIT) with two geometry sub-passes: the first adds color * alpha * weight and alpha * weight into an RGBA16F accumulation, and the second multiplies 1 - alpha into an R16F revealage. Both passes use the scene depth copied from the main framebuffer and test depth without writing it; a final fullscreen resolve computes color = accumulation.rgb / accumulation.a and alpha = 1 - revealage, then composites back into the main target with straight-alpha source-over. KasugaLib's BLEND geometry therefore does not depend on far-to-near submission order on this path.

With an Iris shader pack enabled the same accumulation/revealage/resolve targets are used, but Iris's entities_translucent shader is kept to produce the straight-alpha color after materials, PBR, lighting, and fog. Since Kasuga's depth weights cannot be injected into its fragment shader without changing the shader pack, the Iris path uses constant-weight WBOIT with a weight of 1: RGB accumulates with SRC_ALPHA, ONE, A accumulates with ONE, ONE, and revealage stays ZERO, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA. The translucent entity shader of Iris 1.8.12 brings its own 0.1 alpha test, below the 0.5 cutoff MASK usually uses.

Iris binds the shader pack gbuffer in every ShaderInstance.apply() and may override blend state, so Kasuga rebinds the OIT attachment after apply and before draw, and explicitly restores the blend equation, blend factors, and color/depth masks. The scene depth is copied from Iris's after-translucent default framebuffer, and the resolve writes back into the same framebuffer; only the dedicated OIT composite shader may bypass the Iris unknown-shader guard, and the compatibility policy for other mod shaders is not loosened.

WBOIT is an approximation, not exact arbitrary-layer source-over, and it does not fold vanilla water or shader pack translucent fragments into the same OIT equation; the stage is still AFTER_TRANSLUCENT_BLOCKS, so its scope is "the KasugaLib BLEND layer on top of an already finished scene". When a floating-point target is unavailable, the Iris pipeline has no bindable world framebuffer, or a runtime framebuffer operation fails, it falls back safely to the old far-to-near sorting path. Iris OIT resolves only the main color, so a shader pack that expresses translucent materials through custom extra gbuffer channels may still need pack-specific integration.

The material alphaCutoff of MASK and the near-zero 1/255 working cutoff of BLEND are two separate concepts: the first decides whether depth is written, and the second only removes nearly invisible OIT work items.

For debug commands, keybinds, and the acceptance entry see the API reference.

docs.title: How model visibility and render scheduling work
docs.text: For model handles, scheduling methods, and Entity/BlockEntity integration examples see the API reference.

docs.title: Division between logic and drawing
docs.text: The state machine and the pose driver decide how a model moves, while the host render entry decides where it is placed and whether it is visible. Both act on the same model instance; they must not create separate instances to manage animation and drawing apart. A resource mount belongs only to the render-resource lifecycle.

docs.title: Visibility strategies and orthogonal gates
docs.text:
Continuous drawing, explicit host control, and vanilla renderer marks are the three strategies. Distance and frustum are extra gates that do not disappear when the mode changes. A vanilla renderer emits a visibility mark only after entity tracking/frustum or block-entity view distance/section culling; the global model pipeline consumes that mark.

Instances are distinguished by object identity. A culled instance skips animation sampling and upload for the frame, while an independent runtime keeps advancing its physics. Static block geometry suits section-mesh batching; a skinned model that changes its vertices every frame has to be managed by a dynamic host or an explicit strategy, and cannot rely on a static chunk dispatcher to give per-block dynamic callbacks.

docs.title: Frame and view boundaries
docs.text:
The host renderer writes the visibility mark, the first model material stage freezes it, and later stages reuse it. The double-buffered marks are swapped at the frame boundary, and an instance that was not marked again expires. Models with mixed materials share pose sampling, so the passes do not advance the animation repeatedly.

Each camera view clears the visibility marks on its own but shares the frame's animation token. An instance visible only in a later view is still sampled once, and an instance already sampled in an earlier view is not advanced again. The scheduling state is cleaned up when the last mount is removed, so unmounted instances do not linger.

The world stage submits opaque and mask materials first, then submits blend models after translucent terrain. For the alpha algorithm and depth behavior see Alpha Rendering, and for multi-camera state isolation see Multi-Camera and Offscreen.

docs.title: How the boundary between rendering modules and the graphics API works
Module dependencies
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Host[modelling: Minecraft host adapter] --> GL[render-opengl: OpenGL / LWJGL]
    Host --> Core[render-core: UML and rendering contracts]
    GL --> Core
    Future[Future Vulkan / Metal backend] -. implements the same contracts .-> Core

render-core is an ordinary Java library: it does not apply the ModDev plugin and does not depend on Minecraft, NeoForge, LWJGL, or a concrete graphics API. checkGraphicsApiIsolation runs before compileJava and inspects source imports plus compile and runtime dependencies, so those dependencies cannot re-enter the core. DataFixerUpper is used for the existing data codecs; it is not Blaze3D or the Minecraft renderer. Dependencies on formula and utils have transitive resolution disabled, so only the existing Java expressions and data structures are reused.

render-opengl does not apply ModDev either. It depends on the core and on LWJGL, and manages GL buffers, textures, shaders, VAO, fences, FBOs, readback, and the preview window. The host that runs it must supply the current GL context, the correct thread, and the LWJGL natives for the platform.

modelling keeps the Minecraft world render events, RenderType, VertexFormat, texture atlas, lighting, Iris/Sodium compatibility, and multi-camera world rendering. These classes are host adapters for the current Minecraft + OpenGL combination and cannot serve as a generic interface for another graphics API.

docs.title: UML and resource lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant P as ModelPipeLine / ModelInstance
    participant B as RenderBackend
    participant C as RenderContext
    participant D as Concrete graphics API
    H->>P: load model, create instance, bind PoseDriver
    H->>B: add(key, adapter, instance)
    B->>C: create context and apply()
    C->>D: create backend resources
    loop every view, every render stage
        H->>B: renderAllObjects(hostContext)
        B->>P: schedule, sample pose per frame
        B->>C: beforeRender(hostContext)
        B->>D: upload data, submit draws
    end
    H->>B: remove(key) / close()
    B->>C: close()
    C->>D: release or defer reclamation of resources

The core contains model loading, model structure, skeleton, morph, animation, FSM, pose sampling, and scheduling, plus the RenderBackend, RenderContext, ModelGeometryAdapter, RenderableFactory, RenderBuffer, and TypedBuffer contracts and the output routing. Its resource type, host frame context, and transform metadata are all generic and do not require GL objects or Minecraft classes.

Backend / BackendContext provide the default mount and release behavior, and a concrete backend implements context creation, data packing, and drawing. A failed mount does not publish a half-finished context; removing an instance releases only that mount's backend resources, while the model instance itself is managed by the model pipeline.

The core still contains the existing Java/JNI physics adaptation for Box3D. Physics is not part of a graphics API; when used standalone, a host that enables Box3D has to provide the native library for its platform as well.

docs.title: Upload and output
docs.text:
UploadRing handles only slot rotation, dirty-element merging, version tracking, and resource lifecycle, and performs allocation, writes, and completion status queries through UploadDevice. GpuUploadRing in the production path is now its OpenGL adapter and keeps the original constructors, statistics types, and FloatBuffer entry points. The macOS TBO orphan policy is still provided by MacTboUploadDevice in the OpenGL module.

The integer buffer token and long completion token of UploadDevice are opaque handles internal to a backend, not native resource numbers shared across APIs. A new backend can map them onto its own resource table. A device must guarantee that reads already submitted stay valid after the storage is replaced, and a completion query must not block. A device that cannot meet this contract should use its own upload implementation and reuse the higher-level UploadBuffer / RenderBuffer.

FrameOutputRouter<T>, FrameOutputTarget<T>, OutputFrame<T>, and camera state belong to the core. T is defined by the backend. FrameTexture is the OpenGL framebuffer/texture carrier and belongs to the OpenGL module; other APIs should provide their own output carrier and target.

docs.title: Adaptation boundary
docs.text:
A new backend implements its own resource representation, shaders, synchronization, and submission; windows, host events, and interop stay in the host adaptation layer. For the extension steps see the API reference.

The existing public class names are kept for call-site and serialized-name compatibility. Some GL classes therefore still use the historical uml.backend.gpu package name, and the pure-math Direction keeps its historical models.mc.util package name. Whether something belongs to the core follows the Gradle module dependencies; the core cannot import the OpenGL module.

This split did not implement a Vulkan/Metal backend, and it does not let Minecraft's Blaze3D switch APIs at runtime. The Minecraft effect pipeline descriptor still uses its own draw state for now; replacing the whole renderer of that host would also require the corresponding host adaptation and shader generation path.

docs.title: How generic skeleton physics, IK, and closure constraints work
docs.text: See API reference for constructors, fields, validation, the Reader/Builder, and runtime interfaces.

docs.title: Format reading and shared definitions
docs.text:
Physics rigid bodies, joints, bone inheritance, fixed axes, IK chains, and diamond closure definitions belong to the Skeleton's shared data. A format Reader converts authored data into generic bone references and solver settings only at model construction time; at runtime there is no need to wrap glTF as PMX data. Raw format metadata may still be retained for full format access, with ownership kept separate from the generic runtime definitions.

Shared definitions copy collections and vectors, but the bone objects themselves remain shared structural references. Targets, enable toggles, IK corrections, and physics state belong to individual model instances, and multiple instances do not exchange solver state through shared definitions. The bone-to-chain reverse mapping is built ahead of time, avoiding a scan of all chains on every bone evaluation. Definition extension should be completed before instance creation.

docs.title: Pose and position solving
docs.text:
The bone hierarchy first composites the bind pose, morph, and animation local transforms, then hands the driver bone and endpoint positions to Caliko's FABRIK. Bone inheritance first resolves the source's current local pose, and the fixed axis then extracts the twist about that axis; these constraints apply to skeletons from any source. The library handles position solving; the adaptation layer reverse-maps the solved bone-segment directions into local rotations, and re-evaluates the affected bone subtrees.

current world direction → current bone inverse matrix → local direction
solved world direction → current bone inverse matrix → local target direction
minimal rotation between the two local directions → add IK correction → recompute hierarchy

The coordinate inverse transform avoids treating a world rotation directly as a bone local rotation. Cones and hinges are handled by Caliko; PMX multi-axis Euler box limits are projected onto the local correction and re-solved, and complex box limits are not guaranteed to find all feasible solutions. Non-uniform scaling, shear, and translation animation also change the effective segment lengths, so the result is judged by the endpoint residual after writeback to the real hierarchy.

Inputs are built from the current pose each time, preventing the library from reusing a stale animation solution based only on an unchanged target/base. Chains that already satisfy the target keep their original pose and do not choose another bend solution. MMD chains may take over the authored local pose, avoiding double rotation from VMD directly driving the chain bones and IK; single-bone toe direction targets instead ignore the controller's pure translation, preserving the toe orientation semantics.

docs.title: Representing the diamond closure
docs.text:
The Skeleton is still a single-parent tree. The closure is represented by two independent branches: the two bases share a pivot at the bind position, and the two endpoints represent the same closure point. A typical quadrilateral has two segments per branch, with lengths determined by the bound bones; the topological closure itself does not require four equal sides.

flowchart TD
    P[shared pivot: two independent bases] --> L[left intermediate joint]
    P --> R[right intermediate joint]
    L --> A[left endpoint]
    R --> B[right endpoint]
    A -. position closure .- B

The midpoint of the controller targets is used as the shared target first, handing the two branches to Caliko separately. When limits or unreachability cause non-coincidence, the midpoint of the two solutions is taken and projection continues for a limited number of iterations. Branches sharing driver bones or mutually nested hierarchies would let one writeback overwrite the other branch, so these structures are rejected at construction.

The closure residual counts both the endpoint spacing and the base spacing. Stopping iteration does not mean convergence, so diagnostics need to retain residual and satisfied. This closure only constrains positions; it does not lock endpoint poses and does not apply a mechanical feedback joint to the physics world.

docs.title: Physics writeback and stable initial conditions
docs.text:
Animation and IK first provide physics targets; after the dynamic rigid bodies finish integrating, they replace the corresponding local poses. After writeback only the final hierarchy is rebuilt; IK is not solved again, avoiding correction of physics results. Equal-length child bones for the body capsule are chosen in stable bone order, preventing hash traversal from changing the pelvis orientation and the landing initial conditions.

Six-axis author joints are still approximated to Box3D spherical cone/twist, and per-vertex soft bodies are still not simulated. For native integration, floating origin, and affine hierarchy writeback, see Physics principles and format adaptation principles.
