docs.title: How the UML render framework and resource ownership work
docs.text: For the public interfaces, generics, lifecycle contracts, and buffer integration see the API reference.

docs.title: Layer responsibilities
docs.text:
The core defines the model, skeleton, pose, scheduling, resource context, buffer, and output contracts and does not depend on Minecraft or a concrete graphics API. The host owns the frame and view entry points, the backend owns resources and drawing, the geometry adapter converts model representations, and the resource factory creates the resources of one instance. These responsibilities compose, but geometry conversion must not also manage the shared executor, frame marks, and the draw pipeline.

flowchart TD
    Host[Host frame and model pipeline] --> Scheduler[Scheduling]
    Host --> Backend[Draw backend]
    Backend --> Context[Mounted resource context]
    Context --> Factory[Per-instance resource factory]
    Factory --> Geometry[Geometry adapter]
    Context --> Buffers[CPU and GPU buffers]

Mounted resources, the host frame context, and pre-render metadata are different objects. The backend offers its services to the factory explicitly, so an adapter does not have to look the backend up by string. The context caches the resources the factory creates but does not own model instances, shared adapters, or executors.

docs.title: Prepare-then-publish
docs.text: A new mount must be prepared successfully before it is published. If a replacement fails, the unpublished new context is closed and the old mount is kept; on success the new mount is published before the old resources are released. Removal first unregisters from the registry and then closes the context; closing the whole backend tries to release every mount and aggregates the exceptions. Closing is idempotent, and a closed context cannot allocate resources again. A shared view is read-only, and changes have to go through the lifecycle entry points.

docs.title: Scheduling and sampling are separate
docs.text: Scheduling decides only strategy visibility, and the backend applies the distance and frustum gates in order. Different views have their own visibility marks and share the pose sampling cache within a frame. Physics advancement is independent of draw visibility. For the concrete frame ordering see Render Scheduling.

docs.title: Buffers and in-flight reads
docs.text:
CPU buffer indices count elements, while capacity and stride are in bytes, and the two must not be mixed up. A short update covers only the prefix and keeps the tail and the capacity; a slice borrows the original memory and must not outlive the close.

A GPU upload receives a complete snapshot, and the dirty ranges describe the changed elements. Ring slots track version and historical modifications separately and fill in the accumulated differences when the slot is used again. Storage must not be overwritten while a GPU read is in flight; a device may replace the storage and decide reclamation with a non-blocking completion query. Every draw and translucent replay records consumption, and a completion mark must not be missed even when the frame's data did not change.

The device layer owns graphics API operations and state restoration, and the ring owns the buffer/fence lifecycle. The macOS TBO orphan policy belongs to the OpenGL device implementation and has no place in the platform-independent model and scheduling layers. For the module boundaries see Rendering Backends.

docs.title: How multi-layer volumetric cloud rendering works
docs.text: For cloud field configuration, instance control, preview, and the verification entry see the API reference.

docs.title: Weather and density layers
docs.text: The sky is made of independent low, middle, and high density layers, and a weather window controls the cloud clumps, gaps, and thickness variation. The continuous density can connect and overlap across weather grid boundaries, which avoids a discrete arrangement of one cloud per cell. The low layer keeps cumulonimbus envelopes, the middle layer spreads out, and the high layer uses stretched, anisotropic shapes; a cloud tower can also span several height layers. Scene height and coverage presets are art configuration, not meteorological measurements.

docs.title: Rendering and cost
docs.text:
A cloud field is drawn with one sky-covering ray march and one compositing draw, and no fullscreen pass is created per cloud. It first intersects the ray with each layer's height interval, sorts and merges the overlapping intervals, and skips the gaps between layers outright. The sampling budget is allotted by the square root of the interval length, so a thin high cloud is not starved of budget by the lower layers and does not disappear; the densities of several cloud layers at one point are added. The total number of samples per ray is bounded by the budget, and the march ends early when transmission is very low. Weather windows and GPU textures use a cache of at most 8 entries, so travelling does not grow memory without limit.

A shared shape texture keeps the cumulonimbus tower and anvil envelopes; periodic Perlin-Worley/Worley noise generated in the background provides the body, billowing, and erosion of the continuous cloud layers. Each layer uses its own weather, noise phase, and shape scale, and thin clouds use a stretched, anisotropic shape. The cloud field samples nearby density along the sun direction to approximate self-shadowing and uses density scattering with highlight compression to keep the relief of the cloud body; a single cumulonimbus uses a cached lighting voxel atlas, usually updated every 0.25 seconds.

For the cloud field, FAST/BALANCED/HIGH use width and height resolutions of 1/3, 1/2, and 1 of the original viewport; the total budget per ray is 112/160/256 samples and the local lighting samples are 1/2/3; thin high clouds use simplified lighting. The corresponding resolutions for per-cloud quality are 1/3, 1/2, and 1, with at most 48/80/128 fine steps. A low-resolution result is upscaled with conservative depth and depth-aware interpolation. Both paths truncate at the opaque scene depth and write no depth; sky clouds are not limited by the terrain far plane, and the host GL state is restored.

Long-range views add atmospheric perspective and distance fade. There is currently no long-distance shadowing across clouds, no ground cloud shadow, no temporal reprojection, and no full weather simulation; translucent objects such as water are composited with the clouds by render stage. The extra gbuffer channels of an Iris shader pack are not verified yet, so acceptance with the shader pack disabled does not imply compatibility.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• User-provided volumetric cloudscape implementation from Horizon Zero Dawn
  • Guerrilla: Nubis, original material from 2017
  • SIGGRAPH 2015: The Real-time Volumetric Cloudscapes of Horizon: Zero Dawn
  • WMO: cumulus outline, billowing top, and flat base
  • WMO: the tower and anvil of cumulonimbus
  • WMO: low, middle, and high cloud layers and their distribution across layers
  • NOAA: the ten basic cloud types and the shapes of multi-layer clouds

This implementation uses continuous density layers, procedural weather regions, and a small number of cumulonimbus shape envelopes; it does not copy the spherical-shell cloud layer or the frame-split reprojection of the original system. The hardware timings in the cited material do not represent the performance of this repository's implementation.

docs.title: World UI Input Design
docs.text:
A transparent input Screen lets players move the system cursor freely in front of world-space UI. Crosshair and free-cursor modes share the same plane-intersection and event-routing stages. For API contracts, units, integration, and acceptance commands, see the reference. 中文.

flowchart LR
    C[Crosshair: viewport center] --> P[Screen unprojection]
    S[Transparent Screen: GUI cursor] --> P
    P --> R[Render-view ray]
    R --> H[Existing ray-plane intersection]
    H --> L[Inverse UI transform: local coordinates]
    L --> N[Nearest valid rectangle]
    N --> I[Hover / button capture / keyboard focus]
    I --> G[GuiEventListener and child widgets]

docs.title: Coordinate Spaces and Render Timing
docs.text:
For cursor coordinates (x,y) and logical viewport (W,H), normalized device coordinates are nx = 2x/W - 1 and ny = 1 - 2y/H. Apply the inverse of the actual rendered projection P to (nx,ny,-1) and (nx,ny,0), performing the perspective divide. The first point is the ray origin; the normalized difference is its direction. An interior depth point supports infinite far planes, and the same construction works for orthographic cameras.

The viewpoint, screen plane, and UI plane in the reference sketch lie along this ray. The projection already contains FOV, aspect ratio, optical zoom, and render bobbing, so no estimated eye-to-screen distance or fixed cursor-offset multiplier is needed. A screen point determines a ray; a target plane or another hit constraint is required to select a unique world point.

Let M be the complete local-to-view matrix used to draw a UI. Intersect the ray and plane in view space, then apply M^-1 to obtain UI-local pixel coordinates. M includes the host model-view, camera translation, panel placement/rotation/scale. This avoids mixing a world-space ray with a plane that has already had the camera position subtracted, or subtracting half the panel size twice.

Each frame, the backend copies the projection and each interactive panel's final transform, then finishes input updates. Between frames, events use the most recently presented geometry. Clicks recompute the pointer hit before dispatch rather than relying on an earlier hover. Frame completion also updates hover and capture coordinates when the cursor is stationary but the view or panel has moved. Offscreen cameras cannot replace the main player's input snapshot.

docs.title: Canvas and Depth
docs.text:
The world plane composites one texture. Widgets, glyphs, and shadows first render into an independent RGBA+depth canvas using the ordinary orthographic GUI projection. This preserves fine separations such as 0.03 GUI-Z. Compressing the full GUI depth range into 0.1 world blocks can quantize text and shadow to the same perspective depth, producing stripes, missing fragments, and unstable borders. One unit of padding beyond the GUI depth endpoints includes the MAX_GUI_Z + 0.03 shadow layer. Every composite vertex stays at local Z=0, keeping the panel position and picking plane identical regardless of internal GUI depth.

The canvas clears to transparent black, so normal GUI blending stores premultiplied RGB. World composition uses ONE / ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA to avoid multiplying alpha twice and darkening edges. The plane tests scene depth but does not write it. Draw scopes restore framebuffer bindings, viewport, projection, blending, depth, clipping, and texture state. Removal, world changes, and shutdown release canvases; resizing replaces attachments. Panel clipping uses canvas height rather than window height.

docs.title: Input Ownership
docs.text:
Hover tracks the nearest currently hit panel. Keyboard focus tracks the last clicked panel. Each mouse button separately captures the panel that accepted its press. These can differ: when dragging from A over B, B can be hovered while A continues to receive drag and release events. Drag deltas are differences between successive projected local coordinates, not screen-pixel deltas.

Capture continues outside the rectangle by intersecting the extended panel plane. If intersection is temporarily unavailable, the last valid local coordinates are retained. Closing, removal, or focus loss still sends release to the original target. Keyboard presses also retain their target, and a focus change balances held keys with releases. Duplicate move notifications do not dispatch zero-distance drags.

The input layer does not copy or redraw the panel as a second two-dimensional Screen. Minecraft's Screen lifecycle releases/regrabs the cursor and clears gameplay keys. The transparent Screen consumes input and forwards it to the router while world simulation continues. World rendering, plane intersection, and input capture remain separate, allowing an existing occlusion or alternative hit solver to consume the same ray source later.

Normal crosshair mode has temporary keyboard ownership when the last clicked panel's nested focus chain leads to an editable text widget. A client-only KeyboardHandler HEAD hook consumes events before vanilla updates KeyMapping or handles chat/debug shortcuts; a later key notification cannot prevent those effects. Entering/leaving clears gameplay keys without changing mouse ownership or the current Screen. Escape recursively clears child focus and balances held keys. Physical keys still held at exit retain suppressed repeat/release events so they cannot become movement. Since window focus loss may skip native releases, a fresh press clears its old record and resumes gameplay.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The current implementation accepts Screens and other GuiEventListeners with explicit rectangular bounds. It uses geometric plane picking and does not synchronize server state. Callbacks for server-controlled business behavior should send packets; the server must validate permissions, distance, and business state. Panel registration belongs to the caller. Closing the input layer only clears input state.
