docs.title: Offscreen Output and Multi-Camera Rendering
docs.text:
This page maintains the interface, startup and operation reference; for isolation, data flow and synchronization principles see the explanation page. The Player, Free and Fixed categories and their creation entry points are in the camera API. The configuration of the standalone-world camera views below applies to Free/Fixed; Player shares the vanilla final main frame and the player's current configuration. The performance and client acceptance sections below keep the historical records from that time; they do not mean this documentation migration re-ran the corresponding tests.

This page corresponds to Minecraft 1.21.1 / NeoForge 21.1.203; the compatibility path actually verified Sodium 0.6.13 and Iris 1.8.12. All camera views render in order inside one client process and the main OpenGL context; multi-window uses auxiliary contexts with a shared texture to display finished frames. Camera views each own world caches, a terrain renderer, camera, projection, color/depth targets and an Iris pipeline, while the main view still takes the vanilla rendering path.

Offscreen output delivers a GPU FBO and the game tick keeps running. The headless startup entry points support a hidden desktop context and an EGL pbuffer context on Linux without X11/Wayland. A full Minecraft client and an OpenGL driver are still required; there is currently no fixed-timestep offline video exporter and no built-in video encoder, so a caller can send frames to its own compositing, encoding and transport modules.

docs.title: Dual-Camera DEBUG Startup
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaDebugDualCamera=true

# Optional: enter an existing singleplayer world; omit it to enter normally from the menu.
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaDebugDualCamera=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

The equivalent JVM switch is -Dkasuga.debugDualCamera=true. It is off by default and creates no DEBUG camera view or preview target. On entering a world it creates debug:first-person and debug:third-person, with first person on the left and third person on the right, and the window title states the left-right order. The two have separate sessions, FOV follows the user setting, size follows the window, render distance 8 chunks, Fancy, shader pack off. Third person sits 4 blocks back along the view direction and checks for wall occlusion; first person hides the player's own entity.

The DEBUG preview is the world image and contains no first-person hand or HUD. Opening a menu/inventory pauses the side-by-side compositing and displays the original screen normally. Leaving the world releases the camera views and they are rebuilt automatically the next time you enter. The main view still runs, and DEBUG compositing happens before the final screen output; while it is active, subscribing to the main view also captures the side-by-side image.

The automated check is for an isolated world copy only:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaDebugDualCamera=true \
  -PkasugaDebugDualCameraCaptureFrames=180 \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

After previewing 180 frames it writes debug/dual-camera.png, prints DUAL_CAMERA_DEBUG_PASS and closes the client. The plain DEBUG switch keeps running and does not exit automatically.

docs.title: Multi-Window
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaDebugMultiWindow=true

After entering a world, first and third person each get their own window and the MC main window keeps displaying. It works with kasugaQuickPlayWorld / kasugaClientDirectory; for testing, -PkasugaDebugDualCameraCaptureFrames=120 prints MULTI_WINDOW_DEBUG_PASS and exits after both paths have presented 120 frames. Off by default. DEBUG temporarily disables pause-on-lost-focus and restores the previous setting afterwards; an ordinary API caller can set mc.options.pauseOnLostFocus itself.

import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.gl.FramePreviewWindow;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.mc.MinecraftFrameWindows;

// Owns both the camera and the window: closing either this view's native window releases the camera.
var windowCamera = MinecraftFrameWindows.createCamera("monitor:wide", () ->
        new WorldCameraView(100, 80, 100, 0, 20, 0, 70, 640, 360), settings,
        new FramePreviewWindow.Options("Wide camera", 640, 360));
windowCamera.pause();
windowCamera.resume();
windowCamera.resize(1280, 720);
windowCamera.close();

// Owns only the window and a subscription: closing this window does not close the existing camera.
var mirror = MinecraftFrameWindows.open("capture:wide",
        new FramePreviewWindow.Options("Existing camera", 640, 360));
var mainMonitor = MinecraftFrameWindows.open(MinecraftFrameOutputs.MAIN_VIEW,
        new FramePreviewWindow.Options("Final MC + GUI", 640, 360));
mirror.close();
mainMonitor.close();

All operations are called on the MC render thread. The camera size follows the window framebuffer/DPI; while minimized the last valid size is kept. Close events are handled every frame, and a paused camera view can also be closed. A window that only subscribed keeps the last frame after the source camera view stops publishing, and the caller is responsible for closing it. Exiting MC releases the windows together and only then releases the main context.

An auxiliary window uses a GL context with a shared texture, its own read FBO and a bidirectional GPU fence. Presenting only copies the finished frame and adds no world rendering; a camera view captures once per frame and multiple subscribers share the read-only output FBO. Each auxiliary window still has its own context-local read FBO, which is only the read entry point onto the shared texture and does not allocate a separate output color texture. The main context may overwrite the next frame only after the texture read completes; no CPU glFinish is used. Every present restores MC's current context / GL capabilities. Standalone windows can be stretched, and the image keeps its aspect ratio with black bars. GLFW initialization, the global error callback and termination are still managed by MC.

This is not multiple clients: player input, ticks and the main window event loop still belong to one MC. Linux Null/EGL mode provides no native window, and calling the multi-window API reports an explicit error.

docs.title: Headless MC Launcher
docs.text:
The repository provides scripts/run-headless-client.sh and the Gradle runClientHeadless entry point. By default it uses the standalone modules/modelling/run/headless-client directory and does not reuse the everyday client. A single-player Quick Play world must already exist under that directory's saves/; an existing directory can also be specified:

./scripts/run-headless-client.sh \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/headless-client \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaHeadlessFps=60

# Or connect straight to a server; the client session's authentication requirements still apply.
./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaHeadlessServer=localhost:25565

# Gradle direct entry point for a desktop machine.
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless -PkasugaHeadlessBackend=hidden \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

This is the startup entry point for this repository's NeoForge development client; it keeps the Gradle mod/classpath configuration and does not handle account login or video encoding. Without a world/server specified it starts into an offscreen menu for a caller's client extension to control; it does not create a new world automatically.

Mode GL context Display service hidden, default on macOS/Windows a GLFW window hidden from creation needs a desktop display environment egl, default on Linux GLFW Null platform + EGL pbuffer needs no X11/Wayland/Xvfb

Before startup, prepareHeadlessClient sets earlyWindowControl = false in the chosen client directory's config/fml.toml, so that NeoForge does not display a splash before the game mixins take effect. This setting is kept in that directory. MC does not go fullscreen, the context is not displayed, vsync is not enabled and pause-on-lost-focus is disabled; the render frame rate is controlled separately by kasugaHeadlessFps (default 60). The first-time accessibility introduction screen is skipped, while game ticks, world loading, resource packs and the regular loading screens still run.

Linux needs Java 21, a C compiler, CMake, patch, curl and an EGL driver that supports desktop OpenGL. For example, a Debian/Ubuntu Mesa environment can install libegl1, libgl1-mesa-dri, build-essential, cmake, patch, curl. On first launch the script automatically downloads the pinned GLFW 3.4 source, verifies its SHA-256, applies a small in-repository pbuffer patch and compiles a shared library with X11/Wayland disabled. The build output lands in modules/modelling/build/headless-glfw/cmake/src/libglfw.so and is reused on later launches.

# Linux: the script unsets DISPLAY / WAYLAND_DISPLAY and defaults EGL_PLATFORM=surfaceless.
./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

# Pre-build separately, or deploy a precompiled library for the same architecture.
./scripts/build-headless-glfw.sh
KASUGA_HEADLESS_GLFW_LIBRARY=/opt/kasuga/libglfw.so \
  ./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaHeadlessServer=localhost:25565

# Force software rendering; only for functional verification on a machine with no GPU.
LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 ALSOFT_DRIVERS=null \
  ./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

The upstream GLFW 3.4 plain EGL path only selects a window surface; the patch selects a pbuffer config and calls eglCreatePbufferSurface on the Null platform only. Substituting the upstream GLFW library for this one is not equivalent. If you start Gradle's egl mode directly, you must unset the display environment variables yourself, set EGL_PLATFORM=surfaceless and pass -PkasugaHeadlessGlfwLibrary=/absolute/libglfw.so. The JVM equivalents are -Dkasuga.headless=egl and -Dorg.lwjgl.glfw.libname=..., and NeoForge's early window configuration must still be turned off before startup.

No display service still means a GL driver is required. Hardware EGL depends on driver support and render node permissions; multi-camera shader packs and large resource packs still consume the corresponding CPU/GPU memory. A hidden window or a pbuffer does not eliminate world rendering cost, and software rendering does not stand for production hardware performance.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The real client uses a world copy and an isolated directory to check shader/shadow sessions, pixel content of different material atlases, chunks and entities beyond 1024 blocks, restoration of metadata defaults, main RGB consistency, fog and state restoration, resize, pause/resume, callback closure and failure release.

./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest :modules:modelling:renderGlTest
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaTestWorldViews=true -PkasugaTestCameraIris=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

# The path with Iris/Sodium not installed.
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaRendererMods=false -PkasugaTestWorldViews=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/vanilla-test-client

The client artifacts are debug/world-views/report.json and PNGs, with the success marker WORLD_VIEWS_SMOKE_PASS. The standalone GL regression covers final blit RGB/orientation/alpha, resize, abnormal state recovery and resource release, and needs no full MC launch.

docs.title: JFR Testing and Performance Optimization
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaTestCameraPerformance=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/performance-test-client
python3 scripts/analyze-camera-jfr.py \
  /path/to/cameras-4.jfr --output /path/to/analysis.json

The real MC runs 0, 1, 2 and 4 additional camera views in turn, then re-measures 0 at the end; each group warms up for 8 seconds and JFR profile records for 12 seconds. The additional camera views are 1280×720, 4 chunks, Fancy, no shader pack, and the main view uses the test shader pack, vsync is off and an empty consumer measures delivery. The test exits by itself; the results are the per-group JFR files and report.json in debug/camera-performance/; do not enable DEBUG or another benchmark at the same time. Each run overwrites that directory, so copy the records before comparing.

2026-10-02, Apple M3 Max, main window 1708×960, first round of comparison in the real client:

Metric for 4 additional camera views Before optimization After optimization Host frame mean CPU render 2.913 ms 2.953 ms Host frame P95 3.305 ms 3.278 ms Host frame P99 3.870 ms 3.500 ms Sum of mean camera pass durations 1.262 ms 0.945 ms Render thread allocation rate 207.31 MB/s 156.70 MB/s Cloud path allocation samples 131 12

Two optimizations were implemented from the JFR data:

  1. The Iris/Sodium hadShadersOn flag used to be global, so with the main view's shader pack on and the camera views' off it flipped back and forth, which repeatedly invalidated the cloud geometry cache. It is now kept per CloudRenderer instance and switched/restored during drawing; real-client tests covered the actual Mixin path.
  2. Gaussian sampling for fog/sky color produced a temporary Vec3 on every loop iteration. The camera views use the same kernel, sampling and addition order, accumulate in scalars and create the final Vec3 at the end. Comparing 200 fixed random positive/negative and fractional coordinates against vanilla, the double bits of all three components are identical, and the sampling order of 216 samples matches too. The main view keeps the vanilla path.

The observed allocation rate dropped by about 24% and the sum of mean camera pass durations by about 25%, while the whole-frame mean stayed flat, so there are no grounds for claiming an FPS increase. The first 0-camera-view mean was 2.900 ms and the closing re-measurement 1.601 ms, which shows clear warm-up/world activity/environment variance. The two rounds are not a statistical A/B with the world state locked, and they cover neither complex commercial shader packs, large entity scenes nor other GPUs.

Host frame timing uses RenderFrameEvent.Pre/Post and does not wait for the GPU to finish, so it does not represent full swap/present, encoding or end-to-end latency. kasuga.CameraRenderPass records world + Iris final composition and excludes the output blit/consumers; kasuga.CameraChunkSnapshot records server snapshot build/encoding. The allocation rate uses the jdk.ThreadAllocationStatistics delta divided by time; do not accumulate ObjectAllocationSample.weight, because the first sample may carry allocations from before recording started. The number of allocation samples is a pointer for locating hotspots, not an exact byte count.

The raw records are in ../modules/modelling/build/camera-performance-baseline and modules/modelling/build/camera-performance-optimized/, and are local build artifacts. The remaining hotspots are mostly biome/noise reads, terrain/entity frustum filtering and entity vertex building. Later work should re-measure in complex scenes; the full entity state sent every 5 ticks could be deduplicated further by value, but the sync semantics for returning to default values must be preserved.

docs.title: Player Motion Synchronization Fix
docs.text:
A camera view subscription sends entity state every 5 ticks, whereas the vanilla teleport handler interpolates over 3 ticks, which produces a two-tick stutter. Distant camera view entities were changed to interpolate over 5 ticks. For entities the main client already tracks, the camera view copies their position, previous-tick position, rotation and limb animation history into their own copy before each render; a player's client-side predicted movement no longer takes a round trip through the server subscription. The separate Entity/ClientLevel is kept, and FOV/render resource isolation is unaffected.

A real-client regression has the player move/turn/change walking animation continuously, and at partial tick 0, 0.25, 0.75 and 1 of 120 output frames checks that the copy's position interpolation, rotation history and animation phase agree:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaTestCameraMotion=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

This test deliberately modifies the player position inside the isolated world and restores it at the end. The success marker is CAMERA_MOTION_SMOKE_PASS, and the report is debug/camera-motion.json.

docs.title: Final Code Re-Measurement
docs.text:
After the player motion fix, vanilla distant terrain positioning and the RGBA readback interface were added, the same JFR scenario was run again (empty consumer, excluding the synchronous CPU readback cost):

Additional camera views Mean CPU render P95 P99 0, first 2.198 ms 4.053 ms 5.440 ms 1 2.033 ms 2.543 ms 2.852 ms 2 2.125 ms 2.534 ms 2.952 ms 4 2.846 ms 3.267 ms 3.878 ms 0, closing re-measurement 1.253 ms 1.479 ms 1.657 ms

With 4 camera views the render thread allocation rate is 138.14 MB/s, the sum of mean camera pass durations is 1.040 ms and the cloud path allocation samples are 14. Against the original 207.31 MB/s record, the observed allocation rate dropped by about 33%, while whole-frame time is still at a similar level; the warm-up and unlocked-world limitations above still apply. "1 camera view being faster than the first 0-camera-view run" must not be read as additional camera views speeding anything up. The records and analysis are kept in ../modules/modelling/build/camera-performance-final.

Verification summary: 625 JVM cases, 0 failures/errors, 1 skipped; 9 standalone GL check groups passed, including RGBA orientation, alpha and PBO/pack state restoration; the vanilla and Iris client multi-camera checks, the dual-camera DEBUG actual output, the 120-frame player motion regression and the final JFR test passed. The integrated server's chunk/entity subscription path was actually run; a standalone dedicated server and arbitrary third-party shader pack/resource pack combinations are outside this verification's coverage.

docs.title: Verification of Multi-Window and Headless Startup, and Additional Optimizations
docs.text:
After the new features were completed, renderingReleaseCheck passed; the JVM checks are 627 cases, 0 failures/errors, 1 skipped. The standalone GL regression is 10 groups, adding shared window texture presenting, bidirectional fences, current context/capabilities restoration, resize and independent window closing, plus Sodium-type RGBA native blit keeping RGB and forcing output alpha=1.

Actual check Result macOS MC + Iris/Sodium, multi-camera windows and mirroring an existing camera view passed; closing a paused camera view, DPI resize, other camera views continuing after one window closes Multi-window first/third person DEBUG startup MULTI_WINDOW_DEBUG_PASS macOS run-headless-client.sh hidden mode HEADLESS_CLIENT_SMOKE_PASS, main frame plus two camera view PNGs Debian 12 aarch64, no DISPLAY / WAYLAND_DISPLAY, GLFW Null + EGL HEADLESS_CLIENT_SMOKE_PASS, main frame plus two camera view PNGs

The Linux verification used Mesa 22.3.6's llvmpipe / OpenGL 4.5 and did not start Xvfb. It checked that the native window was never visible, that the context came back to its place, that there was no GL error, and that RGBA was non-empty with an opaque alpha. The main frame PNG includes the hand/HUD, and the camera view PNGs are their respective world views; JFR also recorded 80 render passes per camera view. What ran was the JVM / classpath exported from that NeoForge client configuration; the whole Gradle project was not rebuilt inside the VM. This proves that the client rendering path can run without a display service; it does not prove NVIDIA/AMD hardware EGL, Windows or all third-party shader pack combinations.

The test VM temporarily used 12 GiB of memory and a 6.5 GiB Java heap and loaded this machine's large test models, including three 16384×8192 atlases; this is not a minimum runtime memory requirement. The artifacts are kept in the ignored modules/modelling/build/headless-linux-smoke/debug and headless-linux-jfr.

Two startup/background performance issues were fixed as well:

  • GLFW Null's glfwWaitEventsTimeout is an empty function, so MC's frame limiting loop busy-waits. EGL mode was changed to LockSupport.parkNanos, and early wake-ups are still handled by the original frame deadline loop. For the same 60 FPS offscreen menu, 4 seconds of JFR each: before the optimization, 26 of 74 render thread execution samples were in limitDisplayFPS; after, 0 of 50. This is short-duration CPU sampling evidence and cannot be taken as a world rendering FPS gain or an exact CPU percentage.
  • The PBR cache key used to allocate a whole-image int[] and an equally large byte buffer for scratch, adding 8 × width × height bytes of scratch. It now chunks by 4096 pixels with 32 KiB of scratch, and the SHA-256 descriptor, size and big-endian ARGB order are unchanged. Tests cover chunk boundaries, different raster formats and subimages, and old on-disk caches stay valid. The actual memory demand of the source image, the bake result and the GPU atlas is still there.

The earlier 0/1/2/4 camera view JFR tables do not include the new window presenting cost or the synchronous CPU readback cost, so their durations cannot be applied directly to multi-window or software EGL deployments.

This is the hands-on page for the offscreen and multi-camera topic. For the output and camera contracts see multi-camera output contracts, and for the principles see offscreen output and multi-camera principles.

docs.title: Build and Verification Entries
docs.text: Run from the repository root. The tasks below are listed with the evidence they provide; this does not mean the current documentation pass re-ran client or GPU acceptance. Model selection, configuration and output paths for a specific topic are in the matching API reference.

docs.title: JVM And Release Checks
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest
./gradlew :modules:formula:test
./gradlew renderingReleaseCheck

modelUnitTest runs the modelling tests on a plain JVM/JUnit setup, avoiding the NeoForge dedicated-server launcher. When CMake is configured for the current platform, the Box3D native tests are included; without native build capability the matching tags are excluded. Local PMX/glTF asset tests also depend on a local fixture, so a skipped result for a missing optional asset cannot count as real-asset verification.

renderingReleaseCheck covers Gradle plugin tests, shader tests/assemble, render-core/render-opengl assemble, the modelling JVM tests, contentTesting compilation and the jar/source/javadoc artifacts, plus library assemble. That task is not the same as running a real Minecraft world or running every standalone GL regression.

docs.title: Standalone OpenGL Harness
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderGlTest
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderPreview
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderBench

These tasks start a standalone OpenGL context. Shaders, upload, framebuffer, GPU readback and timer queries run on the current platform; they do not by themselves prove the same results on Minecraft, Sodium/Iris or another platform. For cloud-field scene selection see Volumetric clouds API.

docs.title: Development Client
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaTestModel=mmd
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/isolated-client \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

A Quick Play save must already exist under saves/ in the isolated directory; use a dedicated test world or a copy. runClientHeadless is still a full client: hidden by default on desktop platforms, EGL by default on Linux; for driver requirements see headless API.

Content Reference MMD/glTF models, native ragdoll model runtime entry points, configuration/deployment Full GUI and pixel-by-pixel checks of the final output Frame Output Cameras, shared timeline and windows Camera Animation, multi-camera Alpha/OIT submit order and debug buffers Alpha/OIT World UI free cursor, text, scrolling, and dragging World UI Input Multi-layer sky and a single cloud Volumetric clouds

docs.title: Recording The Verification Scope
docs.text: A verification record should state the compile/JVM, native physics, standalone GL, real-client and platform/renderer combinations separately. Reports, screenshots and logs record the run date, hardware, configuration, task and success marker; historical records keep their original dates, and old JFR samples, a successful build or standalone-scene GPU time must not be read as the current game FPS or as an all-platform compatibility conclusion.

docs.title: Real-Asset Wardrobe Swap and MC Equipment Example
docs.text: Development example class: lib.kasuga.rendering.models.mc.api.WardrobeExample, in the contentTesting source set. It loads user-supplied assets through the production PMX Reader, then uses only the generic Model, the assembly cache, material instances, Skeleton Anchor and the MC equipment adapters. The example code does not ship in the release package.

docs.title: Local Asset Preparation
docs.text:
Using the already-extracted test directories pack_1 … pack_9, this example picks:

Component Asset Base body pack_7/TDA Morphable Base by Ayuchan513/TDA Base Edit by Ayuchan.pmx Texture-swappable clothing pack_4/RibbonDress/Dress_ShortSleeves.pmx Colorway the asset's original Dress_Sapphire.jpg / Dress_Rose.jpg Replaceable clothing model pack_4/RibbonDress/Dress_LongSleeves.pmx, original Mist colorway Matching-skeleton assembly comparison pack_3/#1 Dress by Ayuchan513/Dress by Ayuchan513.pmx Hair pack_8/VRoid Overall Hair Presets/13.pmx, included in every outfit Held item the vanilla MC Diamond Sword; can also switch to the Iron Pickaxe

Run from the repository root:

python3 scripts/prepare-wardrobe-example.py \
  --fixtures /absolute/path/to/extracted-fixtures \
  --output /tmp/kasuga-wardrobe-client/resourcepacks/kasuga-wardrobe-local \
  --enable

The script needs only the Python standard library; it keeps the original PMX and texture content and generates six .mmd.zip archives, the matching scale=0.1 configuration and model_proxy.json. The Rose archive only swaps the short-sleeve Sapphire texture for the original Rose texture, so that a second atlas sprite is preloaded; at runtime the two copies of the garment are never rendered at the same time. --enable appends that directory's resource pack to the test client's options.txt, keeping the other resource packs; without the flag, enable it by hand in the MC resource pack screen.

Assets, resource packs, saves and reports should live in a local test directory and are not committed to Git.

docs.title: Interactive Run
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/tmp/kasuga-wardrobe-client \
  -PkasugaWardrobeDemo=true

On entering the test world, the example opens a standalone preview window by itself; the camera looks at the real model 40 blocks above the player. Only one Wardrobe session is allowed per client. You can also pass no property and run /ksglib wardrobe start after entering the world.

Command Behavior /ksglib wardrobe start Recreates the example and the standalone window; reports an error when the source is not ready /ksglib wardrobe texture blue / rose Switches the material frame on the short model, keeping the same mesh and instance /ksglib wardrobe model short / long / ayuchan Replaces the clothing model, keeping the same body and handle /ksglib wardrobe item sword / pickaxe / none Changes the held item without modifying the real player's inventory /ksglib wardrobe capture Automatically captures six stages, written to debug/wardrobe-example/ /ksglib wardrobe status Shows the current model, texture, item and assembly cache counters /ksglib wardrobe stop Releases the window, camera, equipment bindings, instance, assembly and source references

A resource reload or leaving the current world closes the session; a fresh start picks up newly published assets. Material frames do not migrate to another clothing model automatically, so this example explicitly selects blue when switching back to short.

docs.title: Automated Screenshot Acceptance
docs.text:
First create a test save in the test directory above, or copy an existing test save; for example, a save named wardrobe:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/tmp/kasuga-wardrobe-client \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=wardrobe \
  -PkasugaWardrobeDemo=true -PkasugaWardrobeCapture=true

This mode does not create a preview window and captures 960×720 Free Camera output. It produces, in order:

  1. The short-sleeve original Sapphire colorway.
  2. The same short-sleeve model in the Rose colorway.
  3. Swapped to the long-sleeve Mist model.
  4. Swapped back to the already-cached short sleeves, checking that the Model object is identical and the build counter does not increase.
  5. The vanilla MC sword rendered on the real right-wrist anchor.
  6. The same render after rotating the right wrist, verifying that the weapon follows.

Each stage waits 30 frames and then takes a screenshot; the report records the image differences for material, model, equipment and bone rotation. In a new session the automated mode performs two assembly builds in total; an interactive session that has already been exercised may reuse previous cache results. The success log is WARDROBE_EXAMPLE_PASS, together with report.json.passed=true; the failure log is WARDROBE_EXAMPLE_FAIL. A successful Gradle exit does not replace that client-side evidence. The automated mode exits MC when it finishes.

RibbonDress and this base body bind their same-named bones at different positions, so the example deliberately keeps the clothing's own bind skeleton, enables no physics and runs no full-body animation; this is not automatic body fitting or skeleton retargeting. The ayuchan comparison uses the matching long dress and strictly compatible shared bones. See assembly boundaries and Anchor and rigid equipment.

This is the recipe page. The implementation and verification record for this pass, plus the local performance baseline, are in wardrobe example verification record and performance baseline.

docs.title: Path 1: adding content with data-driven files (organization and best practices)
docs.text:
For content authors: add blocks, items, groups, state machines, and animation clips with JSON alone, without writing Java. Applies to: Minecraft 1.21.1 · NeoForge 21.1.203 · Parchment 2024.11.17 · Java 21. Line numbers in this page refer to the current working tree (the uncommitted data-driven reimplementation), baseline commit ec864a1. This page answers "how to organize files" and "why organize them this way". The complete list of fields is not here — see schema.md.

This page is written for someone with a concrete goal in hand: adding the blocks of one carriage, wiring up a fan, setting up a creative tab. Every step gives JSON fragments you can copy as-is and spells out the cost. Anything that takes Java to do (registering the factory behind a type, registering a new top-level field) lives in guide-extension.md and is not repeated here.

docs.title: 0. Separate the three concepts first (about 30 seconds)
docs.text:
The three words each have a clear identity in this system:

  • index manifest: a manifest file of "which files to parse". It lists paths only and contains no object definitions.
  • content file: the single source of truth for definitions of blocks, items, and groups. The top-level field name (blocks, items, registry_groups) decides which handler this set of definitions is handed to.
  • domain: content files are split into two domains by when they are read. Registration phase (register) content is read once during mod construction and written into Minecraft's registries; reload phase (reload) content is read on /reload and written into the reload bucket; state machines and animation clips belong here.

How the three relate:

flowchart LR
    IDX["index manifest<br>kasuga_lib/data_driven/*.json<br>{ on_register: [...], on_reload: [...] }"]
    IDX -->|on_register| REG["registration-phase content file<br>{ blocks, items, registry_groups }"]
    IDX -->|on_reload| REL["reload-phase content file<br>{ state_machines, animation_clips }"]
    GLOB["directory glob<br>data/<ns>/state_machines/*.json"]
    GLOB --> REL

This diagram holds one asymmetry, and it is the easiest pitfall in the whole page: state_machines/ has an extra directory-glob entry point, while animation_clips/ does not — the latter's files can only be listed by the index manifest (see section 6).

The authoritative table of field names, types, requiredness, defaults, and rule IDs D1–D6 is in schema.md. The examples in this page are copied from real fixtures and can be adapted directly.

docs.title: 1. Goal: get a batch of content loaded — how to organize the index manifest
1.1 The index directory is fixed and cannot be moved
docs.text:
Put the manifest into this four-segment path; the spelling must match exactly:

data/<your mod id>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/

The path is locked down by JsonTreeBuilder.indexDirectorySegments(modId) to {"data", modId, "kasuga_lib", "data_driven"} (JsonTreeBuilder.java:745-747). kasuga_lib uses an underscore, and so does data_driven; write kasuga-lib instead, or drop the kasuga_lib level, and the system concludes you have no index directory and then does nothing at all (leaving a single DEBUG line in the log). Every .json file under the directory is treated as a manifest and read in ascending filename order; index.json is only a conventional name, not a requirement (JsonTreeBuilder.listIndexFiles, :762-774).

So do not put content files in this directory — a content file gets parsed as a manifest and reports "missing on_register/on_reload".

docs.title: 1.2 One manifest per mod, or several?
docs.text:
Both work, and you can mix them. All .json manifests under the index directory for the same mod are read in full first and then consumed together; paths are joined in the order "ascending manifest filename → written order of the array inside the manifest" (JsonTreeBuilder.java:92-96, :296-301).

The trade-off:

  • Splitting has the benefit that each feature unit can carry its own manifest fragment. KuaYue has one data/kuayue/kasuga_lib/data_driven/cXX.json per carriage; after compilation these fragments merge into the same jar directory, and the system aggregates them as several manifests of the same mod (see section 9).
  • The cost of splitting is that filenames must be unique. Once several manifests are merged, files with the same name cannot overwrite each other (they are appended side by side, not overwritten), but you have to make sure each manifest lists only its own files, or content is parsed twice (the same path listed in more than one place within one mod is silently deduplicated, with no error, parseSource's parsedSources, :400-402).

docs.title: 1.3 What goes in on_register and on_reload
docs.text:
A manifest has only two top-level fields, each a string array:

Field What it lists When it is read on_register content files that go into Minecraft's registries, such as blocks, items, and groups during mod construction, once on_reload reload-phase content files, such as state machines and animation clips on every /reload

Both fields may be omitted, but at least one must be written; a "pure reload mod" that writes only on_reload is legal (JsonTreeBuilder.java:100-104, :323-326). An empty array [] also counts as "written" (rule D2). Omitting both records one error.

A minimal two-domain manifest:

{
  "on_register": [
    "kasuga_lib_content/groups.json",
    "kasuga_lib_content/blocks.json"
  ],
  "on_reload": [
    "animation_clips/fan_fsm_data_driven.json"
  ]
}

Array elements are paths relative to data/<your mod id>/, must carry the .json suffix, must not start with /, and must not contain an empty segment or a ./.. segment (JsonTreeBuilder.validateSourcePath, :383-392). They are always joined under data/<your mod id>/, so cross-namespace is structurally impossible.

Best practice: write the groups (groups.json) ahead of the block manifest so a human can see the dependency at a glance. But this has nothing to do with "order is semantic" — the group application phase comes before blocks anyway, see section 3.

docs.title: 1.4 Why leaving a file out means it never loads
docs.text:
The registration phase has no directory scan: buildForMod reads only the paths listed in on_register and does not walk your data/ directory (JsonTreeBuilder.java:105-110). A content file that really exists in the jar still never gets read as long as no manifest lists it, and nothing is reported either.

The reload side has different rules: state_machines/ has a directory glob, animation_clips/ does not. The difference is spelled out in section 6.

The cost: the index is a hand-maintained manifest, and "adding a file = editing the index" is what this design pays for "what gets loaded is fully controllable and auditable". Change the directory structure and forget the index, and the symptom is silently loading less, not an error. That is why the first thing in the verification steps of section 8 is counting entries in the log.

docs.title: 2. How to split content files
docs.text: Content files go anywhere under data/<your mod id>/ (they do not have to be squeezed in next to the index directory), and one file may hold several top-level fields at once. Files do not reference one another, so there is no recursion and no need for cycle detection (JsonTreeBuilder.java:372-373).

docs.title: 2.1 Split by type, or split by feature
docs.text:
Both hold up; the choice depends on whether the question you need to answer is "where is everything of this type" or "where is everything of this feature".

Split by type (one big file each for groups and blocks):

data/mymod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/index.json
data/mymod/content/groups.json        # all registry_groups
data/mymod/content/blocks.json        # all blocks
data/mymod/content/items.json         # all standalone items

Split by feature (each feature directory carries its own type files):

data/mymod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/panels.json     # on_register: content/panels/*
data/mymod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/lighting.json   # on_register: content/lighting/*
data/mymod/content/panels/groups.json
data/mymod/content/panels/blocks.json
data/mymod/content/lighting/groups.json
data/mymod/content/lighting/blocks.json

The trade-off:

  • Splitting by type makes reuse and cross-feature lookup convenient (one file is the complete set for one type), but files keep growing, several people editing one file conflict easily, and nothing reminds you not to stuff unrelated things in.
  • Splitting by feature keeps one feature's changes in one place, which suits units that can be delivered on their own, such as "one carriage = one feature"; the cost is that every feature has to list its own files in the index one by one.

Best practice: take "the smallest unit that can be delivered and verified on its own" as the splitting unit. Inside a feature unit, split further by type (groups.json + blocks.json); that keeps reusability and keeps index entries readable. KuaYue's carriages are split that way (section 9).

docs.title: 2.2 More files means listing them one by one in the index
docs.text: After splitting by feature, the manifest grows into one file per line — which is exactly what it is for: the manifest is the explicit declaration of "which files this feature contains". Do not stuff a whole block of content into one file just to keep the manifest short. A longer manifest is a readability cost, a stuffed file is a maintainability cost, and the former is easier to handle.

docs.title: 3. Goal: share properties across blocks — inheritance with registry_groups
docs.text: A group is a container for shared properties: write properties on a group and the blocks in it inherit them automatically.

docs.title: 3.1 Create a group and attach blocks to it
docs.text:
{
  "registry_groups": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:base_panels",
      "properties": {
        "no_occlusion": true,
        "strength": [1.5, 3.0]
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "mymod:detail_panels",
      "parent": "mymod:base_panels",
      "item_properties": {
        "tab": "mymod:main_tab"
      }
    }
  ]
}

A block names the group it attaches to with registry_group:

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:simple_panel",
      "type": "simple_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:detail_panels",
      "properties": {
        "destroy_time": 2.0
      }
    }
  ]
}

This passage is copied verbatim from the real fixtures modules/data-driven/src/contentTesting/resources/data/kasuga_lib/kasuga_lib_content/groups.json and blocks.json.

docs.title: 3.2 Inheritance chain: block level > child group > parent group > root
docs.text:
Properties are not "merged"; they are applied in turn along the parent chain. The parent group's properties are applied first, then the group's own, so definitions closer to the block take effect later and override what came before (Reg.applyProperties, Reg.java:103-114). Priority in one sentence:

Block level > child group > parent group > root group.

This order holds for both properties and item_properties. The real fixture inheritance_blocks.json shows three cases:

{
  "blocks": [
    { "id": "mymod:inherited_block", "type": "simple_block", "registry_group": "mymod:inherit_group" },
    {
      "id": "mymod:overridden_block",
      "type": "simple_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:inherit_group",
      "properties": { "strength": [5.0, 5.0] }
    },
    {
      "id": "mymod:item_inherit_override",
      "type": "simple_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:inherit_group",
      "item_properties": { "stacks_to": 1, "durability": 100 }
    }
  ]
}
  • inherited_block touches no property at all and inherits the group entirely.
  • overridden_block overrides the group value with a block-level properties.strength.
  • item_inherit_override overrides the group's stacks_to with a block-level item_properties, and adds a durability the group does not have.

One exception is worth noting on its own: the creative tab (tab). The group's item_properties.tab is recorded separately and used only when the block has no tab of its own (RegTypeHandler.java:89-97). So "block-level tab wins" works like most fields here, but the implementation goes through a different channel, and that is worth remembering when troubleshooting tab problems.

docs.title: 3.3 What happens with a missing parent group or a cycle
docs.text:
Both anomalies are caught and neither crashes, but the result may differ from what you expect:

  • The parent group does not exist → the group silently attaches to the root group (RegistryGroupHandler.store, :58-63). Blocks register as usual, they just inherit nothing. With no log message.
  • The ancestor chain contains a cycle → the loader does a topological sort first, and on detecting a cycle emits a WARN: Cycle detected among registry groups: [...]; the groups in the cycle fall back to their original order and end up attached to the root (JsonTreeBuilder.java:823-842).

The real fixture edge_cases_groups.json contains a ready-made cycle:

{
  "registry_groups": [
    { "id": "mymod:orphan_group" },
    { "id": "mymod:circular_a", "parent": "mymod:circular_b" },
    { "id": "mymod:circular_b", "parent": "mymod:circular_a" }
  ]
}

orphan_group explicitly has no parent and attaches to the root; circular_a/circular_b are each other's parent.

The cost and the advice: group inheritance saves a lot of repeated fields, but "silently attaches to the root" means a mistyped group id is not reported. So give group ids a namespace prefix (starting with mymod:), and make "the group definition" and "the block that references the group" appear as a pair in the same manifest, so changing an id changes both together.

docs.title: 4. Goal: know who wins on a duplicate id — last-wins
4.1 What counts as "the same id"
docs.text:
A duplicate is decided only within the same type field (blocks against blocks, items against items, registry_groups against registry_groups, embedded block entities against embedded block entities). The same name in different fields is not a conflict (DuplicateIdResolver's collision key is (typeName, identity), :73-100).

The three types compute identity differently:

Type What identity is Normalization blocks / items the ResourceLocation at registration no namespace or a minecraft: prefix → <your mod id>:<path>; any other namespace is kept as-is (EffectiveId.of, :39-52) registry_groups the entry's literal id, not normalized groups are internal nodes and do not go into a registry, so door and minecraft:door count as two groups (RegistryGroupHandler.resolveIdentity, :50-52) the embedded block entity the identity of the host block only two block_entity keys on the same block count as a duplicate (BlockEntityTypeHandler.resolveIdentity, :66-68)

Normalization is the easiest one to trip over: as blocks, foo and minecraft:foo are the same id and conflict with each other (EffectiveIdTest.explicitMinecraftNamespaceResolvesToTheOwningMod). But foo in blocks and foo in items do not conflict; they are two registration spaces.

docs.title: 4.2 "Later" means load order, not lexicographic order
docs.text:
The rule for duplicates is last-wins (the later definition wins). "Who is later" is decided entirely by load order:

  1. Several manifests of the same mod, by ascending filename;
  2. Inside one manifest's on_register array, by written order;
  3. Inside one content file's type array, by written order.

DuplicateIdResolverTest.lastMeansLastInSequenceNotLexicographicallyLastSource locks this down specifically: even when the later candidate comes from a file whose path sorts earlier lexicographically, it is still the winner. In other words, order is a semantic switch, not a layout preference.

docs.title: 4.3 Conflicting entries: isolated, no crash
docs.text:
When a duplicate is found (DuplicateIdResolver.describe, :109-115):

  • No crash: loading finishes as usual and the game starts normally.
  • The loser does not take effect at all: the earlier definition never reaches registration, so no ghost entry is left in Minecraft's registries.
  • No collateral damage: only the conflicting entry is dropped; other entries in the file and other types proceed as usual.
  • Evidence is kept: one WARN log line (giving the id, the type field, and the winner's and the loser's source files) plus one loading error recorded against that mod.

Best practice: treat order as an "override switch", not as "layout". When you have no intent to override, make sure ids are unique within the type and keep the WARN away; when you do intend an override (a base file plus a variant file), point out which one is the patch file in the manifest with a comment or a name. The cost is that such an override tells you nothing about "who got overridden" beyond that WARN, so override files should be as small and focused as possible.

docs.title: 5. Goal: bind a block entity to a block — how to use an embedded type
5.1 The block entity is embedded, not a top-level field
docs.text:
A block entity (BE) does not get a top-level field of its own; it is written in the block_entity key of the block entry:

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:be_test_block",
      "type": "be_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:data_driven_group",
      "block_entity": {
        "type": "my_be",
        "params": {
          "tick_interval": 4
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

(from kasuga_lib_content/block_entities.json.) block_entity accepts type (the BE factory) and params; after the host block is registered, the system creates the BE automatically and attaches it as its child node, and the BE id is automatically <block path>_be. So a block can embed at most one BE (BlockEntityTypeHandler.apply, :88-95).

FSM blocks have a common pattern: state_machine is written at the top level of the block entry, and the system forwards it into the BE's params:

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:my_fsm_block",
      "type": "fsm_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:data_driven_group",
      "state_machine": "mymod:my_machine",
      "properties": { "destroy_time": 2.0 },
      "block_entity": {
        "type": "fsm_be",
        "params": { "model": "mymod:models/my_cube.obj" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

(from modelling contentTesting's fsm_blocks.json; the forwarding logic is in BlockEntityTypeHandler.extractEmbedded, :33-44, covered by BlockEntityStateMachineExtractTest.)

docs.title: 5.2 "In the same file" or "in its own file"
docs.text:
The filename block_entities.json is a convention, and its top-level key is still blocks once you open it. So the choice here is file organization, not syntax:

  • Keeping blocks with BEs together with ordinary blocks puts the whole block picture in one place, which is convenient for comparison.
  • Opening a separate file (such as block_entities.json) for blocks with BEs shows "which blocks have entities" at a glance, and lets this kind of block evolve on its own.

Either choice must list the file in the manifest. The trade-off is review cost: a separate file makes the BE set stand out, but seeing "a block's full definition" then takes two files.

docs.title: 5.3 Anti-pattern: writing an embedded type as a top-level field
docs.text:
The following form is illegal:

{
  "block_entities": [ { "type": "my_be" } ],
  "blocks": [ { "id": "mymod:ok", "type": "simple_block" } ]
}

The result: the top-level block_entities is reported as an "unsupported top-level field", with the hint "it should be written in the block_entity key of a blocks entry"; the key point is that blocks in the same file still dispatches as usual (partial-apply), so this one mistake does not throw away the whole file (JsonTreeBuilderEmbeddedTypeDispatchTest.topLevelEmbeddedTypeIsReportedAndTheRestOfTheFileStillDispatches, JsonTreeBuilder.java:475-490).

Likewise, a single BE failing in the apply phase (a missing BE factory, for example) only emits a WARN and is skipped, leaving the other blocks in the same file alone (BlockEntityTypeHandler.apply, :81-100).

Best practice: always write block_entity next to its host block. A BE has no id of its own, so an "orphan BE" does not exist syntactically.

docs.title: 6. Goal: add state machines and animation clips — reload-domain content
docs.text: The reload domain has two kinds of content, and their top-level field names are each the only legal key.

docs.title: 6.1 State machines (state_machines): two entry points
docs.text:
A state machine file looks like this:

{
  "state_machines": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:fan_machine",
      "state_vars": [
        { "name": "cycle", "type": "bool", "default": false, "ephemeral": true, "reference": "mymod:fan/cycle" }
      ],
      "layers": [
        {
          "id": "gear",
          "mode": "base",
          "initial_state": "off",
          "states": [
            { "id": "off", "clip": { "id": "mymod:fan_clip", "loop": true } },
            { "id": "g1", "clip": { "id": "mymod:fan_clip", "loop": true } }
          ],
          "transitions": [
            { "id": "off_to_g1", "from": "off", "to": "g1", "trigger_on": "cycle", "cross_fade_seconds": 0.25 }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

(the full version of the real fixture modules/modelling/src/contentTesting/resources/data/kasuga_lib/state_machines/fan_machine_data_driven.json has 4 states and 4 transitions; a subset is taken here for space, with no field changed.)

A state machine has two entry points; use either one or both:

  1. Directory glob: put the file at data/<your namespace>/state_machines/*.json and it is discovered automatically (StateMachineDefinitionLoader.PATH = "state_machines", :39; the directory is declared by FsmReloadHandler.globDirectories(), :69-71). No need to list it in the index.
  2. The on_reload array: list the path in the manifest and it is read as well.

When both entry points hit the same file, the glob skips the one the index already lists, so the file is read once (ReloadOrchestrator.collectGlob, :348-367). The relative order of the two entry points is glob first, index second, and for the same id the later one still wins (ReloadOrchestrator class documentation, :77-91).

docs.title: 6.2 Animation clips (animation_clips): the index is the only entry point
docs.text:
{
  "animation_clips": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:fan_clip",
      "duration_seconds": 12.0,
      "functions": [
        { "bone": "fan", "channel": "rotate", "y": "11 * query.angle" },
        { "bone": "cover", "channel": "rotate", "z": "sin(rad(2 * query.angle)) * 30" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

(from animation_clips/fan_fsm_data_driven.json.)

animation_clips/ has no directory glob, so clip files can only be read through the manifest's on_reload array (AnimationClipLoader class documentation, :28-29). Put a clip file under data/<ns>/animation_clips/ and forget to list it in the manifest, and it is never loaded, with no hint at all.

Compare the real fixture modelling.json, which lists two entries under on_register and one under on_reload:

{
  "on_register": [
    "kasuga_lib_content/fan_formula_data_driven.json",
    "kasuga_lib_content/fsm_blocks.json"
  ],
  "on_reload": [
    "animation_clips/fan_fsm_data_driven.json"
  ]
}

The state machine file state_machines/fan_machine_data_driven.json is not in this manifest — the glob picks it up. fsm_blocks.json originally belonged to data-driven's contentTesting, and moved to the modelling side because the fsm_block / fsm_be factories live in modelling only (the content is still written with blocks as its top-level key).

docs.title: 6.3 A few rules for reload content
docs.text:
• One file can carry several top-level keys: writing state_machines and animation_clips in the same file is legal, and the two handlers each read their own key and register their own entries (ReloadOrchestrator.dispatch, :429-470). A genuinely unknown key (claimed by no reload type, a mistyped foo for instance) is reported as an unsupported-top-level-field error, but known keys still contribute as usual and do not drag down the whole file.
  • Reload paths go through the pack stack: paths in on_reload are resolved with ResourceManager.getResource, so data packs can override your reload content; on_register goes through the mod's jar (IModFile.findResource), which data packs cannot reach (ReloadOrchestrator.collectIndex, :369).
  • Dangling clip references are checked after the fact: once a reload round finishes, the loader checks whether the id that states[].clip points at exists in every state machine definition just registered, and if it is missing it emits a WARN and records it in the error bucket, while that state degrades to a static pose (FsmReloadHandler.afterReload, :95-116). The check does not block registration.

Best practice: keep state machines in state_machines/ for the glob to discover, which cuts manifest maintenance; clips must be listed in on_reload one by one, so make clip files coarser rather than finer (one file per feature) instead of letting the manifest grow to dozens of lines.

docs.title: 7. Anti-patterns and boundary checklist
docs.text:
What you write Symptom Cause / handling "sources": [...] in a manifest two errors: contains unsupported field 'sources' + declares neither 'on_register' nor 'on_reload', and that manifest contributes no path sources is a deprecated field, not an alias (JsonTreeBuilder.parseIndexManifest, :222-243; JsonTreeBuilderIndexSchemaTest.legacySourcesFieldIsReportedAsUnknown). Change it to on_register listing a state_machines file under on_register error: unsupported top-level field 'state_machines', with the hint "list this file under 'on_reload' instead" the conditional D9 hint; the registration domain does not recognize a reload-domain shape, and the hint points you at the other array (JsonTreeBuilder.java:474-491; JsonTreeBuilderReloadHintTest) listing registration content under on_reload error: unsupported top-level field 'blocks', with the hint to list it under on_register the reverse D9 hint (ReloadOrchestrator.dispatch, :441-446) the same path in both on_register and on_reload error, and that path is consumed by neither domain rule D6's fail-closed (JsonTreeBuilder.resolveIndexManifests, :308-316; JsonTreeBuilderIndexSchemaTest.crossListedPathIsConsumedByNeitherDomain) a top-level block_entities error + the hint to write it in the block_entity key of a blocks entry embedded types do not take a top-level field (section 5.3) a path written as /blocks.json, blocks (no suffix), a/../b.json error: path must be relative / path must include the '.json' suffix / path must not contain '.' or '..' validateSourcePath (:383-392; JsonTreeBuilderSourcePathTest.rejectsMalformedSourcePaths) the manifest points at a file that does not exist error: Source file not found ... the path is relative to data/<mod>/; first confirm the file really made it into the jar a content file placed in the index directory error: the file is parsed as a manifest and reports the two domain fields as missing the index directory holds manifests only a block type with no corresponding factory the block does not appear; log WARN No factory for type '...' log only, not into the error bucket (RegTypeHandler.apply, :70-74). The factory must be registered first, see guide-extension.md a block referencing a registry_group that does not exist the block still appears, but its properties/tab do not match expectations silently attaches to the root group, no log (section 3.3) a misspelled property name (such as sound_type) that property is ignored; log WARN Unknown block property / Unknown sound type log only, not into the error bucket (JsonPropertyParser, :50-57, :87-95) an element's parse throws during the registration phase (malformed fields in that element) error: Content file '<label>' for mod '<mod>': entry <i> in '<key>' failed to parse: <msg>; entry skipped only that element is dropped; sibling entries in the same file register as usual (JsonTreeBuilder.java:530, 592; isomorphic to the reload side's …; element skipped).

Best practice: distinguish "errors that go into the error bucket" from "errors that only emit a WARN". The former (index, path, field, duplicate id, apply failure) can be asserted red through getLoadingErrors; the latter (unknown factory, unknown property, missing group, group cycle) can only be found by reading the log. Lumping the two together will make you miss the second half of the problems.

docs.title: 7.1 Data-driven does not generate assets or localization
docs.text:
Data-driven registers the block / item / block entity itself only (blocks entries have no model / textures field, see schema.md section 2.3). For a block to display properly, its model, texture, and language still have to be provided in the resource pack following vanilla conventions, and the system does not generate them for you:

  • Model / texture: looked up following Minecraft conventions at assets/<namespace>/blockstates/<path>.json and assets/<namespace>/models/block/<path>.json, and you must supply them by hand; leave them out and you get a purple-and-black block.
  • Translation key: derived by convention as block.<namespace>.<path> (item.<namespace>.<path> for items), and you must add it in lang/*.json by hand; leave it out and the raw key name is displayed.

docs.title: 8. Goal: confirm you got it right — verification and troubleshooting
8.1 Count the entries in the log first
docs.text:
After startup the log should contain this line (INFO):

Loaded N JSON entries across M types for mod '<your mod id>'

JsonTreeBuilder.java:114. N is the total number of entries parsed, and M is the number of distinct top-level types with content. Turn DEBUG on and you also see the applied count per type (Applying N entries for type '<type>', :129). An N that is too small usually means a missed index entry or a wrong path. If the line is entirely absent, check the index directory path first (when the directory does not exist there is only one DEBUG line: No data-driven index directory for mod '...', :77).

docs.title: 8.2 Inspect the error bucket with a command
docs.text:
In game (permission level 2 required):

/kasuga_data errors
/kasuga_data errors <your mod id>

With no argument it prints a one-line summary for every non-empty bucket (both dimensions included: the mod dimension and the reload RELOAD_DATA[<namespace>] source dimension); with a mod id it prints that mod's per-entry failures in both dimensions (DataDiagnosticsCommands, :45-92). Registration-phase errors go into the mod dimension; reload-phase errors go into the Domain.RELOAD_DATA source dimension, keyed by namespace (ReloadOrchestrator.reportError, :566-573).

docs.title: 8.3 Assert in a test that the error bucket is empty
docs.text:
An integration test or a debugging tool can assert directly:

JsonTreeBuilder.getLoadingErrors("mymod")   // this mod's list of errors
JsonTreeBuilder.getLoadingErrorsByMod()     // bucketed by mod

Turning "silent errors" into a red light is the least-effort approach. Error buckets are isolated per mod, and one mod's buildForMod clears only its own bucket (JsonTreeBuilderLoadingErrorTest.errorsAreIsolatedPerMod).

docs.title: 8.4 A troubleshooting order table
docs.text: Symptom Look first at no Loaded ... JSON entries at all is the index directory's four-segment path right? is there a .json in the directory? N smaller than expected is the manifest missing an entry? Source file not found? the block does not appear No factory for type? (WARN); are the block item, blockstate, and model assets all present? properties are wrong Unknown block property (WARN); is registry_group written correctly (silent attach to root)? an id takes effect as something other than what you wrote the duplicate-id WARN; look at the winner/loser source files (section 4) the state machine does not take effect is the file in state_machines/? or is it listed in on_reload? the clip does not take effect almost always it is not listed in on_reload — clips have no glob (section 6.2) the state machine runs but the animation is frozen look for the unresolved clip references after reload WARN (section 6.3)

docs.title: 9. Production-scale reference: how KuaYue organizes carriages
docs.text:
This section only observes the KuaYue repository's modules/train-parts/resources/carriages/ read-only; nothing is modified.

KuaYue's 11 carriages (22/25/25b/25g/25k/25t/25z/cr200j/freight/jy30/m1) show what "split by feature, each feature carrying its own manifest fragment" looks like in a real project. Each carriage is an independent resource-compilation module, and its source directory top level holds blockstates/, data/, lang/, loots/, models/, recipes/, tags/, textures/ and module.toml — there is no assets/; only after resource compilation does it merge into the assets//data/ layout in the output. Model assets, localization, loot tables, and data-driven content are delivered together inside the same carriage directory.

For the data-driven part there are three files per carriage (exception: jy30 has module.toml but no data-driven content at all, so it does not take part in data-driven):

carriages/22/
├── module.toml                                              # module root marker
└── data/kuayue/
    ├── kasuga_lib/data_driven/c22.json                      # index manifest (one per carriage)
    └── carriages/c22/
        ├── groups.json                                      # this carriage's groups
        └── blocks.json                                      # this carriage's blocks

The manifest content is "groups first, blocks after":

{
  "on_register": [
    "carriages/c22/groups.json",
    "carriages/c22/blocks.json"
  ]
}

The group (c22):

{
  "registry_groups": [
    {
      "id": "kuayue:c22_panels",
      "properties": {
        "no_occlusion": true,
        "strength": [1.5, 3.0],
        "map_color": "blue"
      },
      "item_properties": { "tab": "kuayue:train_panel_tab" }
    }
  ]
}

The blocks (c22, excerpt):

{
  "blocks": [
    { "id": "kuayue:22_floor", "type": "slab", "registry_group": "kuayue:c22_panels" },
    {
      "id": "kuayue:22_large_window",
      "type": "train_openable_window",
      "params": { "wide": 2 },
      "registry_group": "kuayue:c22_panels"
    }
  ]
}

How it is split, and why:

  • The splitting unit is one carriage, because a carriage can be delivered and verified on its own, and the whole carriage's assets (models, language, block definitions) travel together anyway.
  • One manifest per carriage (c22.json, c25.json, …; the filenames all differ). At compile time they merge into the same jar directory, and the framework aggregates them as several manifests of the same mod. This answers exactly the question in section 1.2: "several manifests per mod" in production is split by delivery unit.
  • Inside a carriage, split further into two files by type (groups.json + blocks.json) rather than stuffing groups and blocks into one — that keeps the readability of "split by type" while putting groups before blocks, matching the framework's "groups are applied first" phase order.
  • A block's type is a factory KuaYue registers itself (slab, train_panel, train_openable_window, and so on), not one of the library's built-in test factories — this is exactly the extension point described in guide-extension.md used in production.

A lesson unrelated to data-driven content, but one that makes content "vanish into thin air": the two carriage directories cr200j and freight have no module.toml. The resource compiler only walks directories that contain module.toml (ResourceCompilerMain.java:24-39; ResourceScanner.scanModule, :43-58), so the content in these two directories (index and data-driven files included) never makes it into the jar, and the blocks in them are never registered. Transferring this to your own project: even with the manifest written correctly, confirm that the directory carrying it is really picked up by your resource compilation/packaging pipeline.
