Textures and immutable raw metadata borrow the source resources, and Textures are deduplicated by object identity. Material and frame state stay independent between parts. Do not modify the shared definitions of a cache result; each character's transform, morph, material frames, animation clock and physics state live in the ModelInstance.

Numeric/numeric-string Pose material references are remapped from source material indices to output Materials; invalid numeric references are ignored. MaterialResolver.forInstance supports Material references that belong directly to the current MaterialSetInstance. Custom named material references are passed through as-is, and the host can handle them with a custom MaterialResolver.

docs.title: Dynamics merging
docs.text:
Inheritance and fixed axes are converted to output Bones; identical constraints on the same output bone are reused, conflicting constraints are an error. A shared IK whose controller, effector, links and all solver settings match reuses the body chain; otherwise a part-prefixed chain is generated. Diamond closures are preserved; fully identical closures are reused, and conflicts and overlapping chain relationships continue to be validated by the generic Builder. When a full-skeleton garment uses the body's existing dynamics, you can also pass includeDynamics(false) explicitly.

Physics coordinates and sizes are converted by each source's Physics.unitScale, and the output has unitScale = (1,1,1); angles are still in radians. Rigid bodies bound to the same output bone with all properties identical are reused; a rigid body with no bound bone is kept independently. Joint indices are remapped, and fully identical joints are reused; a self-connection after mapping is an error. Bind-following bones are merged. If any source with physics bodies requires a profile, the result requires an explicit profile; when any source needs affine writeback, the combined physics uses affine writeback. profileRadiusScale must agree across non-empty sources, and a conflict is an error. The profile and drag interfaces use output physics indices, and source indices are converted through Remap.

docs.title: ModelAssemblyCache
docs.text:
new ModelAssemblyCache(); // 32 entries, 1_000_000 vertices
new ModelAssemblyCache(int maximumEntries, long maximumVertices);
new ModelAssemblyCache(int maximumEntries, long maximumVertices, ModelAssembler assembler);

ModelAssembly getOrAssemble(ModelAssembly.Request request);
int invalidate(Model source);
int invalidate(String partId);
void clear();
ModelAssemblyCache.Stats stats();

Both capacities must be positive. The LRU is limited by both the entry count and the vertex count of merged Models; the statistics are not byte sizes or GPU memory usage. A single result that exceeds the vertex budget can still be used, but is not cached. All operations are synchronous, and concurrent requests assemble only once; different misses also run serially, so the assembly service should be used on a loading/worker thread.

The cache key covers part order, the object identity and revision of source Models, bone mappings, the final hidden face set, the dynamics switch, the same-name matching switch and the bind tolerance. Invalid resources/assembly exceptions are not stored in the cache. invalidate returns the number of removed entries; clear drops references but keeps the cumulative statistics. Stats provides hits(), misses(), builds(), entries(), vertices(); builds counts only successful assemblies.

The cache owns CPU shared definitions, has no GPU resources and needs no close. Invalidation/eviction does not modify already returned results; a host still using an old ModelInstance is responsible for its render resource lifecycle. On a resource reload, stop the old instances and invalidate the corresponding cache entries first, then release the borrowed Texture/metadata.

docs.title: Extension interfaces
docs.text:
@FunctionalInterface
interface ModelAssembler {
    ModelAssembly assemble(ModelAssembly.Request request);
    static ModelAssembler standard();
    static ModelAssembler standard(MorphRemapper morphs);
}

@FunctionalInterface
interface MorphRemapper {
    MorphType<?, ?, ?> remap(MorphType<?, ?, ?> source, ModelAssembly.Remap mapping);
    static MorphRemapper standard();
}

The standard implementation supports the existing vertex position/normal/UV/tangent, bone transforms, material color/specular/ambient/rim, material frames/ sprite frames, Flip and nested Group morphs. Unknown morph types are an error; custom types copy their references and parameters through a remapper, then fall back to the standard implementation. There is no model format allowlist.

MorphRemapper defaults = MorphRemapper.standard();
ModelAssembler assembler = ModelAssembler.standard((morph, mapping) -> {
    // You can handle your own morph types here, remapping targets, identities and parameters.
    return defaults.remap(morph, mapping);
});
ModelAssemblyCache cache = new ModelAssemblyCache(32, 1_000_000, assembler);

A custom assembler must return a request equal to the input request, otherwise the cache refuses to store it. Resources should be read-only during assembly; the remapper is used only in the assembly/extension copy phase, and playback uses the result's immutable mappings.

docs.title: Local real-asset probe and cache benchmark
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelAssemblyProbe -PkasugaAssemblyFixtures=/absolute/path/to/extracted-fixtures
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderGlTest -PkasugaAssemblyFixtures=/absolute/path/to/extracted-fixtures

This optional probe covers the current nine-pack test assets: the extracted directories are pack_1 to pack_9, pack_6/7 are base bodies and pack_3 is compatible dress clothing; it only calls the production PMX conversion and the generic assembly, and does not decode or display the asset textures. It checks all PMX loading and base body/part bind compatibility, then verifies the compatible dress, the assembly of 1/10/100 real small parts, neutral skinning positions, cache sharing and source invalidation. The stress case shares only bind-compatible bones, and the remaining bones keep the part namespace; this cannot be read as 100 different garments having been fitted to the base body. When RibbonDress short sleeves/long sleeves are present it also measures their assembly with a separate bind skeleton alongside the base body; when pack_8/**/13.pmx is present, hair is included. For actually swapping textures and clothes, and rendering hair and an MC weapon see real-asset example.

The default report is build/reports/modelAssemblyProbe/report.json; kasugaAssemblyReport can specify the output, and kasugaAssemblyOrder=cached-first or the default uncached-first controls the measurement order, making it easy to repeat in an alternating order on a fresh JVM. It records the first assembly, a rebuild after warm-up, a cache lookup for an existing request, building a request plus a cache lookup, and allocations on the current thread. Timings exclude file loading and texture decoding; the p50/p95 of batch means differ from a per-call latency distribution. Allocations do not include GPU/native memory. These numbers only verify CPU assembly and caching, and do not represent game FPS or a per-frame skinning/draw speedup.

The optional GL path compares CPU and production GPU skinning over all merged vertices of the compatible base body + dress, including real bind types and bone rotations; it uses transform feedback and disables rasterization, and outputs no base body image. The success marker is REAL_OVERLAY_SKINNING_PASS.

docs.title: Generic model posing and animation API
docs.text: The runtime interface does not require the Model to come from any particular format, and ModelData / BoneData may be null. For the principles see model subsystem boundaries; for IK, inheritance, fixed axes and physics definitions see Skeleton Dynamics.

docs.title: Model and format integration
docs.text:
Interface Package Behavior AnimationLibrary Model.getAnimations() lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.structure Named clip library shared by Model ModelPosing ModelInstance.getPosing() lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic Lazily creates this instance's generic pose controller; obtaining it does not itself install a driver void ModelData.configureSkeleton(Skeleton) lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.structure.data Converts skeleton capabilities when the Model is constructed; default is an empty implementation void ModelData.configureModel(Model) same as above Integrates the generic subsystems after the Model's public fields are initialized; default is an empty implementation

The glTF Converter registers the animations it loads into the clip library; tracks that were not loaded are not in the library. glTF's weights track shares this entry point with TRS, and supports STEP, LINEAR and CUBIC_SPLINE. POSITION / NORMAL morph targets are registered per node instance as GltfAsset.MorphId(nodeIndex, targetIndex); different nodes of the same mesh are controlled independently. The default weight is taken in order from node.weights, mesh.weights, or all zeros, and is baked into the static geometry; the sampler outputs offsets relative to the default value, and the default shape is restored when playback stops. Weights may be negative or greater than 1, and assembly and cross-fade preserve their linear meaning. Custom samplers can write finite signed weights with Pose.Builder.morphWeight(id, weight); morph(id, value, factor) keeps its original normalized activation semantics. The Blockbench Loader registers the animations inside the file into the same library. Unnamed clips in both formats use animation_<file index>. VMD/VPD, generic AnimationClip or custom formats are integrated through sampler/data; there is no need to create a new model type. Bone names, morph identities and material references must still match the target model; this interface does not automatically retarget skeletons with a different topology.

docs.title: AnimationLibrary
docs.text:
Package: lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.animation.

new AnimationLibrary();
<T> AnimationLibrary.Clip<T> register(String name, AnimationSampler<T> sampler, T data);
AnimationLibrary.Clip<?> get(String name);
boolean contains(String name);
Map<String, AnimationLibrary.Clip<?>> clips();

new AnimationLibrary.Clip<T>(String name, AnimationSampler<T> sampler, T data);
float AnimationLibrary.Clip.duration();
Pose AnimationLibrary.Clip.sample(float seconds);
Pose AnimationLibrary.Clip.sample(float seconds, Namespace namespace);
AnimationLibrary.Clip<Pose> AnimationLibrary.pose(Pose pose);

The name passed to register must be non-empty and must not be all whitespace; registering the same name replaces the existing binding; get returns null on a miss. clips() returns an unmodifiable view. Register at build/load time, and create players only after registration is complete; registration is not a thread-safe operation. sampler/data must be non-null; the integrating party guarantees the immutability of external data. The library does not copy the original animation, nor does it rewrite its interpolation mode. Clip times and durations are in seconds, and the shared player checks whether the duration is finite when playback actually starts. AnimationLibrary.SAMPLER is the shared clip adapter used by AnimationPlayer/FSM. The FSM's formula Namespace is passed through to the original sampler; a named binding does not lose the formula context. pose produces an unnamed, zero-duration constant clip.

import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.ModelInstance;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.fsm.Pose;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.math.Transform;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.typo.miku_miku_dance.vmd.VmdSampler;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.typo.miku_miku_dance.vpd.VpdSampler;

// model is a Model from any source; motion / vpd are data already read by the corresponding Reader.
model.getAnimations().register("dance", new VmdSampler(), motion);
model.getAnimations().register("stance", VpdSampler.INSTANCE, vpd);
ModelInstance instance = new ModelInstance(model, null, null, null, null, null);
instance.getPosing().play("dance", true);

// A static pose can also use the generic Pose directly.
instance.getPosing().pose(new Pose.Builder()
        .bone("head", new Transform(), lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.fsm.ApplyMode.REPLACE)
        .ikEnabled("left-arm", false).build());

docs.title: ModelPosing
docs.text:
Package: lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic; implements PoseDriver.

Method Behavior new ModelPosing(ModelInstance instance) Usually use instance.getPosing(); does not check the model format boolean hasClip(String name) Queries the model clip library String currentClip() Current clip name; null for a static pose or after stopping boolean play(String name, boolean loop) Plays from the start and installs as the instance driver; returns false for a missing name and keeps the current driver boolean follow(String name, AnimationTimeline timeline) Follows an external timeline and installs a driver; does not advance the shared clock a second time void pose(Pose pose) Installs a driver and keeps sampling a constant pose; pose must not be null void stop() The next render sample restores the bone/morph/IK channels written by that driver to their defaults; material frames are kept void pause(), void resume() Pauses/resumes the playback clock void seek(float seconds) Seeks to a finite, non-negative number of seconds void setSpeed(float speed) Finite, non-negative multiplier; 0 freezes the clock boolean isPlaying() Whether the clock keeps advancing; a static pose is still sampled continuously float currentTime() Current clock seconds; not taken modulo when looping AnimationTimeline timeline() Current timeline, for other targets to follow void tick(float dt) Usually advanced by ModelInstance.animate(dt) void sample(float partialTick) Usually called by the instance's render sampling entry point

Each instance holds its own player, timeline and PoseSink; a static pose and a named clip switch reuse the same sink, so channels that disappear from the previous pose are cleared automatically. Playback control and tick run serially, and the render sample consumes the clock snapshot published by the shared player. stop's reset runs during the sampling phase and cannot replace sampling or instance updates. The current PoseDriver is still a single slot; installing a ModelPosing replaces the current driver. The shared drivers implement RebindablePoseDriver; for resource switching and clock preservation see input migration. When animation layering is needed, use the FSM's State.clip(AnimationLibrary.SAMPLER, clip, loop) and State.pose(Pose).

docs.title: Pose IK channels
docs.text:
Package: lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.fsm.

new Pose(Map<Object, Pose.Morph> morphs, Map<String, Pose.Bone> bones,
         Map<Object, Pose.Frame> frames, Map<String, Boolean> ikEnabled);
Map<String, Boolean> Pose.ikEnabled();
Pose.Builder Pose.Builder.ikEnabled(String chain, boolean enabled);
State<Owner> State.ikEnabled(String chain, boolean enabled);
boolean SkeletonInstance.clearIkEnabled(String chain);

The original three-parameter Pose constructor is kept, and the IK map defaults to empty. The keys of the map are IK chain names, not model format or file bone indices. VmdSampler automatically writes the IK state of the property track into the Pose, so there is no need to write the skeleton separately after playback. pose.ik_enabled in FSM JSON is an optional object from names to booleans, defaulting to {}.

A switch takes the earlier end while the cross-fade alpha is less than 0.5 and the later end otherwise; a one-sided channel keeps that side's value. As with material frames, BASE/ADDITIVE use the last value and OVERRIDE takes precedence; BoneMask applies only to bone transforms and does not mask IK chain switches. PoseSink ignores unknown chains; when a channel disappears it clears only the chains it wrote itself, and other manual switches are kept. clearIkEnabled restores the chain's default enabled state and returns true when an explicit state was removed.

docs.title: Name migration
docs.text:
Original interface Current interface GltfAnimationPoseDriver ModelInstance.getPosing() / generic ModelPosing MmdRagdoll lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.physics.SkeletonRagdoll MmdPhysicsScene ModelPhysicsScene in the same package MmdPhysicsClusterManager ModelPhysicsClusterManager in the same package SkeletonInstance.getPmxBones() Format Readers maintain their own file index mapping; the instance exposes only the generic Skeleton/Bone

These format-specific runtime entry points have been removed. The parameters and capabilities of the physics interfaces are preserved; callers referencing the old types need to update imports and recompile. glTF's STEP/LINEAR/CUBIC_SPLINE continues to be sampled exactly by GltfSampler.

docs.title: Final main frame WYSIWYG output
docs.text:
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.FrameOutputMode;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.mc.MinecraftFrameOutputs;

var output = MinecraftFrameOutputs.open(FrameOutputMode.MIRROR, frame -> {
    var texture = frame.resource();
    consumeTexture(texture); // implemented by the caller, consumed synchronously on the render thread.
});
output.close(); // released on the render thread.

MIRROR delivers to both the FBO and the display window; OFFSCREEN_ONLY skips the screen blit for that frame after a successful delivery, while the game loop and window events keep running. After all exclusive outputs are closed, normal display resumes; when no exclusive output succeeds, it falls back to the native window output.

The default view minecraft:main is intercepted at the final RenderTarget.blitToScreen in Minecraft.runTick, after the world, post-processing, HUD, GUI, loading screen, and debug overlay have been drawn. It reuses the native final blit and provides the final WYSIWYG frame, with no need to render the world again just to capture it. Additional camera views deliver through their own world/Iris composition.

docs.title: Creating a camera and its lifecycle in one call
docs.text:
All create, update, pause, resume, and close operations happen on the render thread. Other threads schedule work with Minecraft.getInstance().execute(...); the first creation requires a loaded level.

import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.WorldCameraView;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.camera.CameraRenderSettings;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.mc.MinecraftCameras;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

var settings = new CameraRenderSettings(
        12,
        CameraRenderSettings.Quality.FANCY,
        new CameraRenderSettings.Shader(
                Path.of("/absolute/path/to/shader-pack.zip"),
                Map.of("SHADOW_QUALITY", "1")), // an option name defined by the selected shader pack.
        List.of(Path.of("/absolute/path/to/resource-pack.zip")),
        2,    // mipmap level 0..4
        true  // ambient occlusion
);
var camera = MinecraftCameras.create("capture:wide", () ->
        new WorldCameraView(100, 80, 100, 45, 15, 0, 70, 1280, 720),
        settings, frame -> consumeTexture(frame.resource()));

camera.pause();
camera.updatePose(new WorldCameraView(110, 82, 100, 90, 10, 0, 50, 1920, 1080));
camera.resume();
camera.close(); // closes both the producer and the outputs it owns.

The consumer is a placeholder example function. With no shader pack, use CameraRenderSettings.Shader.disabled(). The overload that omits settings uses render distance 8, Fancy, no shader pack, base vanilla/mod materials, mipmap 0, and AO on. The pose can be a fixed record or a provider sampled once per frame.

WorldCameraView parameters are absolute world x/y/z coordinates, yaw/pitch/roll, vertical FOV, and width/height. Angles are in degrees; yaw/pitch follow MC. Values must be finite, FOV must be in (0, 180), and dimensions must be positive and no larger than the GL maximum texture size. A new size automatically replaces the render and output FBOs. The view ID must be non-empty and unique and must not be minecraft:main.

CameraHandle.state() is one of READY, PAUSED, FAILED, CLOSED; failure() stores the fault. READY means the registration is usable; when resources load asynchronously for the first time, the first frame may not have been delivered yet. A failure in the provider, resource loading, drawing, or the consumer removes that camera view and releases its resources, keeping the exception. close() is idempotent; pausing stops the output and withdraws the server subscription, and resuming subscribes again.

Resource configuration is fixed at creation; to change packs, quality, or render distance, close and recreate. Position, FOV, and size are modified dynamically through updatePose. At the lower level you can also call MinecraftWorldViews.register and MinecraftFrameOutputs.open(viewId, ...) separately, or add multiple consumers to the same view; lower-level producers/consumers must be closed separately. A camera view with no consumer, or one that is not enabled, is not re-rendered and not sampled.

docs.title: Same-process isolation and render timing
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[host frame / shared animation token] --> B[camera view A world / resource / Iris scope]
    B --> C[A world and Iris final composition]
    C --> D[A consumer]
    D --> E[camera view B independent scope and output]
    E --> F[restore main view and render]
    F --> G[main post-processing / HUD / GUI]
    G --> H[final main frame output]
Configuration or resource Isolation Position, orientation, FOV, size Per-camera-view Camera, projection, and color/depth FBO Chunks and lighting Per-camera-view ClientLevel, ClientChunkCache, light engine Terrain and entity drawing Per-camera-view LevelRenderer, RenderBuffers, mutable entity/block entity dispatcher Render distance Per-camera-view 2..32 chunks, independent server subscription and client render distance Iris shader pack Per-camera-view ShaderPack, PipelineManager, material settings, uniform time, capture, and shadow state Materials and models Per pack stack independent resource manager, TextureManager, ModelManager, atlas Quality Per-camera-view Fast/Fancy, leaf type, AO, mipmap Fog and clouds Per-camera-view fog history; Iris/Sodium cloud format flags stored per CloudRenderer instance

Camera views with the same pack stack/mipmap share loaded models/atlases and release them by reference count; the mutable renderer/dispatcher is held per camera view. Resource packs stack in list order, with later ones taking priority. Base resources keep vanilla/mod resources and do not inherit the user/server packs selected by the main view; required packs must be written explicitly into resourcePacks. Both directories and zips are supported. Player skins/capes/elytras downloaded on connect, plus the shared light texture, font glyphs, particle atlas, and mod-generated textures with no file resource, are borrowed resources and are not deleted with the camera view. A camera view's own atlas takes priority and is not replaced by the main view's atlas.

Iris entry points route to their respective instances inside the scope, and some static state is isolated through switching and restoration. Chunk build tasks capture the camera view's resources, materials, and quality when created and restore the context when running on a worker. Vanilla rebuild tasks also hold a resource lease, returned only after cancellation or the end of CPU building, so closing a camera view does not release models/materials still being read by async tasks. The vanilla ViewArea is positioned at the actual camera view coordinates. This requires sequential rendering in the same context and does not support drawing camera views concurrently on multiple threads.

The host tick and RenderFrameEvent.Pre/Post still run only once per frame, model animation is deduplicated by the shared frame token, and visibility marks are cleared before each camera view draws. Inside the scope the MC world, renderer, buffers, targets, camera, and resource getters point to the current camera view, and world stages receive the camera view's frustum and matrices. Custom time histories can be partitioned with WorldRenderPipelineContext.viewId().

Leaving the scope restores the main state as well as GL read/draw FBO, viewport, projection, and draw/fog state. Closing inside a callback defers release until the current delivery ends. Switching worlds destroys the old session, which is rebuilt from the current world next time; MC shutdown releases everything. Vanilla in-flight builder packs are released when returned, and Sodium releases its native buffers, sky VBO, pipeline, and FBO after stopping its terrain workers.

docs.title: Distant chunks and entities
docs.text:
The server must also have KasugaLib with this feature installed; the integrated server in single player uses the protocol as well. A server without the channel support makes the camera view fail explicitly rather than pretending the distant world was loaded.

The server manages subscriptions by camera UUID, epoch, dimension, and center, requests FULL/non-ticking chunk tickets in batches, and does not block the main thread waiting for generation. Per subscription it requests at most 8 tickets and sends 4 completed, light-ready snapshots per tick; block/lighting changes trigger resends. The client feeds chunks, heightmaps, lighting, and block entities into its own ClientLevel. Movement discards caches outside the range and data from stale epochs, and cleans up the light/Sodium tracker. Pausing, closing, logging out, dimension changes, and heartbeat timeouts withdraw the server tickets.

Entities are synced to the camera-view world every 5 ticks — spawn, position, head rotation, full metadata, equipment, attributes, passengers, and existing leashes. The copy interpolates independently, does not consume the vanilla packDirty, and keeps tracking the main player entity. This subscription is not a new player connection: distant areas can be loaded/captured, but non-ticking tickets do not extend the server simulation range for AI/redstone.

docs.title: Output rules and boundaries
docs.text:
OutputFrame<FrameTexture> provides the view ID, the per-view frame number, the size, and the color texture. The color is RGBA8 with opaque alpha, OpenGL bottom-left origin, and no depth attachment. The router owns the color target per view; all subscriptions for the same frame receive the same OutputFrame and resource object, borrowed for reading only and not writable, resizable, or deletable. The next frame overwrites it, and a resize or the closing of the last subscription deletes the old objects; when unsubscribing inside a callback, release is deferred until the current delivery ends. Keeping the frame outside the callback requires copying it on the spot into your own GPU/CPU storage; the DEBUG preview also copies first and composites afterwards. Consumers run on the render thread and should not wait on encoding/network; you may implement your own PBO/fence readback and a bounded worker queue, and a bare texture ID must not be handed to an async thread without the current GL context.

The resources in the table above are isolated, but this is not a copy of the full client:

  • An additional camera view outputs world stages and the Iris final composition, but not the HUD/GUI, the hand, glowing outlines, or the main view's GameRenderer.postEffect. The complete main frame goes through the final output entry point.
  • Quality supports Fast/Fancy, AO, and mipmap, but not all options (Fabulous, particle presets, separate cloud toggles, etc.). The main light texture, fonts, particle engine, and the vanilla core shader loader are shared; a pack that modifies fonts, particles, or core shaders cannot be considered fully isolated, and a distant camera view also has no independent server particle event stream.
  • Resource-pack overlays metadata, third-party reload listeners, mod entity pairing payload/attachment, effect, and audio protocols are not fully replicated.
  • Third-party code that reads static state directly, caches the main world, or advances logic in a world stage still needs adaptation; effects with a time history should be managed by view ID.
  • Multi-camera with a high render distance increases generation, network, CPU/GPU/VRAM load. Permissions, subscription counts, and resource budgets on public servers are constrained by higher-level policies.

docs.title: How to drive the FBO data flow without showing a window
docs.text: After a headless launch, the same FBO API below is used. MinecraftCameras.create comes with an offscreen consumer; MinecraftFrameOutputs.open subscribes to the final main frame. The launcher keeps one main-frame OFFSCREEN_ONLY output, including the loading screen, so closing the caller's output does not show the MC window. The launcher's and the caller's main-frame subscriptions share one capture target and do not copy an extra frame. On a normal desktop launch the main-frame subscription may be OFFSCREEN_ONLY, and display resumes after closing it.

docs.title: Direct transfer inside the GPU
docs.text:
var camera = MinecraftCameras.create("export:camera", () ->
        new WorldCameraView(100, 80, 100, 0, 20, 0, 70, 1280, 720), frame -> {
    FrameTexture texture = frame.resource();
    // In this callback and the current GL context, sample/composite with texture.textureId(),
    // or blit from texture.framebufferId() to an FBO held by the caller.
});

Synchronous read-only consumers share the handle above directly without copying first. For example, when one camera view subscribes to two preview windows and one GPU compositor at the same time, the router creates only one output color texture and performs the final capture once per frame; presenting to each screen still needs one blit per window. Closing one consumer does not release the frame other consumers are using, and a consumer exception only cancels its subscription. If the capture itself fails, all subscriptions of that view are cancelled while other camera views keep working.

A texture ID is a GL object handle, not a pointer the CPU can dereference, and is meaningful only in the corresponding GL context/share group of this process. Even for read-only use, a CPU encoder still needs a readback. If a later frame or an async consumer needs it, you must copy it into your own FBO inside the callback and manage the copy target and fence on the GL/render thread; a borrowed ID must not be put directly into a background queue. The DEBUG preview's OutputFramebuffer.capture plus glBlitFramebuffer is a real GPU copy example, see DualCameraDebug in the modelling module.

docs.title: CPU byte stream: a minimal working recording example
docs.text:
RgbaReadback.copy(FrameTexture) is provided: inside a callback it returns a caller-owned, tightly packed RGBA8 byte[], already flipped to the top-left origin, with no stride padding. It restores the read FBO, read buffer, pixel-pack buffer, and pack parameters; after it returns, the byte[] can be handed to a thread without a GL context. The implementation is a synchronous glReadPixels that waits on the GPU, suitable for functional verification; high-throughput recording should switch to multi-slot PBO/fence readback.

The snippet below fixes 1280×720 and writes one camera view to an encodable raw RGBA file; creating/closing the camera happens on the render thread and disk writes happen on a separate thread. The caller should create the output directory first:

import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.WorldCameraView;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.gl.RgbaReadback;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.mc.MinecraftCameras;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;

var queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<byte[]>(2);
var running = new AtomicBoolean(true);
var writer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
// Keep the future; check get() afterwards so disk errors become visible.
var writeResult = writer.submit(() -> {
    try (var stream = Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("capture.rgba"))) {
        while (running.get() || !queue.isEmpty()) {
            byte[] rgba = queue.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            if (rgba != null) stream.write(rgba);
        }
    }
    return null;
});
var camera = MinecraftCameras.create("export:camera", () ->
        new WorldCameraView(100, 80, 100, 0, 20, 0, 70, 1280, 720), frame -> {
    if (writeResult.isDone()) {
        try { writeResult.get(); }
        catch (Exception failure) { throw new IllegalStateException("Output writer failed", failure); }
        throw new IllegalStateException("Output writer stopped");
    }
    if (queue.remainingCapacity() == 0) return; // drop the frame when the bounded queue is full; do not block the host.
    queue.offer(RgbaReadback.copy(frame.resource()));
});

// End of recording: close the camera on the render thread, then tell the writer to drain the remaining data.
try { camera.close(); }
finally { running.set(false); writer.shutdown(); }
// Wait for writeResult.get() on a background control thread; do not wait on disk on the render thread.

The output file is ordered frame by frame and row by row as RGBA; one frame is 1280 * 720 * 4 bytes. It can be converted to video with FFmpeg:

ffmpeg -f rawvideo -pixel_format rgba -video_size 1280x720 -framerate 60 \
  -i capture.rgba -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p capture.mp4

The 60 here is the playback interpretation of the file's frame sequence and does not guarantee that MC samples at 60 FPS; a full queue drops frames, and the game also ticks in real time. Offline rendering that needs an exact duration/fixed time step additionally requires scheduling time, timestamp-based frame filling or offline stepping, and an encoder backpressure policy. The resolution must stay fixed during a continuous stream; after a resize the encoder must be reconfigured or a new segment started.

To export only the final main frame, replace the create above with:

var output = MinecraftFrameOutputs.open(FrameOutputMode.OFFSCREEN_ONLY, frame -> {
    byte[] rgba = RgbaReadback.copy(frame.resource());
    // Deliver under the same bounded-queue rule; use frame.width()/frame.height() for the size.
});
// Call output.close() when done.

The flow is world/Iris → one final blit per view → shared output FBO → synchronous read-only callback → own GPU copy or RGBA bytes → bounded background queue → encoding/disk/network. Additional camera views do not include the HUD; the main view includes the complete final frame. The public API's texture output and readback are implemented; the example video encoding is the caller's job.

docs.title: Read-only consumers share the completed frame
docs.text:
The output router now captures and holds storage per view. All subscriptions for the same frame receive the same OutputFrame<FrameTexture>, and the shared target is released only after the last subscription closes; closing or replacing a subscription inside a callback does not delete the borrowed texture early. The first registration chooses the target factory, and GPU storage is allocated only on the first valid output. Different views still own their own output targets.

N synchronous read-only subscriptions on the same view Before After Output color texture / FBO N copies 1 copy Final capture per frame N times 1 time Alpha initialization operations per frame capture 2N clears 2 clears Consumer calls N times N times

The nominal size of the RGBA8 color storage is 4 × width × height bytes; about 7.91 MiB at 1080p and about 31.64 MiB at 4K. The table does not count driver metadata, world render targets, window presentation, or the consumer's own copy/encoding storage. The MIRROR main frame still needs the normal screen blit, and each auxiliary window still needs presenting; the shared capture does not save these consumers their work.

This change did not add CPU zero-copy or asynchronous readback. A GPU texture ID is not a CPU address, and RgbaReadback.copy still performs a synchronous GPU readback, a Java array copy, and a Y flip. A read-only GPU consumer can just borrow the handle; cross-frame, asynchronous consumption needs its own storage and synchronization mechanism.

This round's JVM check ran 633 cases, 0 failures/errors, 1 skipped, the standalone GL 10 suites passed, and renderingReleaseCheck passed. The new GL assertions empirically show that three subscriptions allocate only one output target and capture once per frame, that correct RGB/alpha can still be read after a consumer failure, and that resize and closing the last subscription release the old GL objects. The real MC menu check passed for shared frame identity, pixel-exact complete GUI consistency, resize, replacing a subscription inside a callback, release on the last subscription, and consumer-failure fallback. These results verify capture counts and resource ownership; they do not measure standalone GPU time in milliseconds. The earlier JFR data is the whole-frame result from before the change and cannot be used to claim a specific FPS gain from this shared capture.

The shared-capture version also re-passed the macOS MC + Iris/Sodium multi-camera window regression (FRAME_WINDOWS_SMOKE_PASS, independent close and resize) and the hidden-window launch regression (HEADLESS_CLIENT_SMOKE_PASS, main frame plus two camera view outputs). This round did not rerun the Linux no-display-server test; the earlier Linux record belongs to a previous launcher verification.

This document is the contract page of the offscreen and multi-camera topic. For startup, verification, and performance walkthroughs see the offscreen rendering walkthrough; for the principles see offscreen output and multi-camera principles.

docs.title: Model Variant Selection (Multiplexer) Reference
docs.text:
Interfaces, configuration, and call reference. For the mechanics see multiplexer.md.

Multiplexer is a stateless variant selector: a set of Variant nodes plus guarded transition edges. It picks the current variant (such as a block's appearance/model) from the context. The definition itself holds no runtime state — one block type shares one definition, with one MuxState per instance.

Multiplexer is a code definition (Java DSL), not JSON. FSM is the data-driven JSON one (see fsm.md).

docs.title: When to use Multiplexer and when to use FSM
docs.text:
Multiplexer FSM Driving mechanism Context snapshot selects the variant (ctx.property(...)) Layered state machine + tick advance + actions State None (definition); one MuxState per instance One complete StateMachine per instance Suited to Switches, gears, redstone states, model variant switching Animation timing, attack chains, locomotion Definition location Java code data/<ns>/state_machines/*.json

Use Multiplexer for a simple "powered / unpowered model swap"; use FSM when you need state duration, actions, and multi-layer blending.

docs.title: Core API (lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.multiplexer)
docs.text:
// 1. Definition (shared, one per type)
Multiplexer<MyContext, MyVariant> def = Multiplexer.define(MyVariant::new, mux -> {
    MyVariant off = mux.variant("off", v -> { /* variant config: model/material... */ });
    MyVariant on  = mux.variant("on",  v -> { });
    mux.transition(off, on, t -> t
            .when(ctx -> ctx.property("powered").equals("true"))
            .crossFade(0.2f));
    mux.transition(on, off, t -> t.when(ctx -> ctx.property("powered").equals("false")));
    mux.initial(off);
});

// 2. One state per instance
MuxState<MyVariant> state = def.newState();

// 3. Advance each tick (advance the cross-fade + evaluate guards; a guard hit switches)
def.advance(state, context, dt);

// The currently selected variant (during a transition it is the target variant)
MyVariant current = state.current();

docs.title: Builder methods
docs.text: Method Description variant(id, config) Defines a variant and returns a typed handle transition(from, to, config) Adds a transition edge; TransitionBuilder: ↳ .when(Predicate<C>) Guard; empty = always true ↳ .crossFade(seconds) Cross-fade duration in seconds; 0 = switch immediately ↳ .onSwitch(Consumer<MuxState>) Callback on switch initial(variant) Initial variant

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text: Method Description newState() Creates a per-instance MuxState (starting at initial) advance(state, ctx, dt) Advances the cross-fade + evaluates guards, switching on a hit; call every tick select(ctx, state) Read-only: which variant would be selected now (does not change state) state.current() Current variant state.inTransition() / state.to() In transition / target variant (during the cross-fade)

docs.title: Minecraft side
docs.text: The MC implementation uses McContext (wrapping block states/redstone and so on into a context snapshot) + McVariant (model/material variant) + McMultiplexer; the core Multiplexer does not depend on Minecraft. A block type creates one McMultiplexer at registration, each BE calls newState(), and in #onDataChanged or tick it calls advance(state, ctx, dt) and feeds state.current() to rendering to select the variant.

docs.title: Composition with FSM
docs.text: Multiplexer selects "which model variant to use", FSM drives "the animation timing of that model". The two compose: Mux selects the variant → the ModelInstance for that variant mounts an FSM PoseDriver to run animation.

docs.title: KasugaLib PMX → PBR Conversion
docs.text:
Interfaces, configuration, and call reference. For the mechanics see pbr.md.

This page covers KasugaLib's current PMX stylized PBR conversion pipeline, the implementation changes in this round, observability and troubleshooting, and how to customize it with the player configuration and the Java API.

docs.title: 1. How It Works
docs.text:
PMX source materials mainly provide a base texture, a diffuse color, a specular color, and a specular strength; they do not directly contain complete PBR textures. KasugaLib performs one pre-bake during the client resource load phase:

  1. Read the numeric properties of the PMX material and generate automatic conversion parameters.
  2. Apply the Java registration rules and the player JSON rules in order.
  3. Generate a normal texture from the luminance gradient of the base texture.
  4. Generate a specular texture that matches the current LabPBR/Iris path.
  5. Pack the base color, normal, and specular into three corresponding atlases.
  6. Write the result to the disk cache; later resource reloads reuse it first.

docs.title: Automatic parameters
docs.text:
• smoothness: mapped from the PMX shininess.
  • f0_code: generated from the average of the PMX specular color; the automatic value is limited to 4–90, and no metal is guessed automatically.
  • subsurface: default 0.
  • normal_strength: default 0.08.
  • emission: default 0.

docs.title: Output channels
docs.text:
Normal texture:

Channel Content R Encoded tangent-space X G Encoded tangent-space Y B AO, currently 255 A Height, currently 255, that is, parallax height is not enabled

Specular texture:

Channel Content R Perceptual smoothness G Dielectric F0 or the LabPBR metal code B Porosity/SSS; non-zero SSS maps to 65–255 A Emission

Normal sampling uses repeat/wrap at texture edges, matching the repeatable-UV behavior of PMX.

docs.title: Independent material variants
docs.text:
The atlas identity is decided jointly by "source texture + final PBR parameters":

  • Same source texture, same parameters: reuse the same variant.
  • Same source texture, different parameters: generate an independent variant and independent normal/specular sprites.
  • If the same atlas identity is bound to a different source image or different parameters again: throw a conflict error immediately, instead of averaging silently.

docs.title: GPU, CPU, and caching
docs.text:
• Prefer generating both the normal and specular outputs in a single pass on the render thread through an offscreen framebuffer and MRT.
  • When the GPU shader is unavailable, this session switches automatically to the deterministic CPU reference baker.
  • The GLSL of the GPU baker lives in assets/kasuga_lib/shaders/pbr/stylized_bake.vsh and stylized_bake.fsh.
  • The GPU baker explicitly saves, clears, and restores GL_PIXEL_PACK_BUFFER, GL_PIXEL_UNPACK_BUFFER, and the pack/unpack row-length/skip state.

docs.title: Load performance
docs.text:
• Fixed the linear indexOf lookup in PMX vertex deduplication, replacing the near-O(n²) path of large models with a hash index.
  • Unused copies of base textures are no longer put into the PBR atlas repeatedly.
  • The PBR disk cache is prefetched in parallel by the resource load threads; only misses go back to the render thread for GPU baking.
  • The content hash of the same source image and profile is reused within a single load.
  • BufferedImage is converted to NativeImage directly, instead of being encoded to an in-memory PNG and decoded again.
  • The CPU fallback runs at most two bakes at a time, so it does not occupy all resource load threads.
  • In-world resource reload uses generation-based publishing: new models are built in the background first, and are atomically swapped on the game thread only after the atlas and the sprite mappings are all ready; Kasuga model drawing is paused during the reload, and the old backend instances of the replaced models are cleaned up.

docs.title: Startup indicator
docs.text:
Minecraft's resource loading screen additionally shows KasugaLib's current stage and progress, including:

  • scanning model resources;
  • the current model resource;
  • the current PMX name and the PMX count inside the ZIP;
  • reading PBR cache entries;
  • the number of GPU bakes for cache misses;
  • PBR atlas packing.

docs.title: Batch log
docs.text:
After each PBR preparation finishes, one summary log line is emitted, for example:

Prepared 91 stylized PBR variants from 74 source textures (59.4 MP, 17 shared-source variants): GPU 0, CPU 0, disk hits 91, failures 0, elapsed 880.3 ms

Field meanings:

Field Meaning variants Number of configured variants in the final atlas source textures Number of distinct source images MP Total processed pixels, counted per variant shared-source variants Number of variants added because the same source image uses different parameters GPU Number of items newly generated on the GPU in this batch CPU Number of items newly generated by the CPU fallback in this batch disk hits Number of disk cache hits in this batch failures Number of items that failed in this batch and used the default PBR map elapsed Total time of cache prefetch and baking of misses

A first load usually shows a GPU count; a warm-cache load usually shows GPU 0, CPU 0 and a high disk hits.

docs.title: Client commands
docs.text:
/kasuga_pbr status
/kasuga_pbr reload_config
/kasuga_pbr rebake

status prints:

  • ready, failed, total: status counts of cache keys within this session;
  • GPU, CPU: number of items actually newly baked;
  • disk-cache: number of disk cache hits;
  • memory-cache: number of in-memory result hits within the same resource load;
  • requests: total number of requests the coordinator received, including cache prefetch and atlas consumption;
  • key: cumulative time of generating content cache keys;
  • read: cumulative time of decoding disk PNGs;
  • GPU-time, CPU-time: cumulative time of the corresponding baker;
  • write: cumulative time of writing to the disk cache.

reload_config reloads the player configuration and triggers a resource reload. rebake deletes the whole Kasuga PBR disk cache, clears the session statistics, and triggers a full resource reload.

When either command runs inside a world, Kasuga models are temporarily hidden during the resource reload. New models are not published before the atlas is ready, so the render thread never observes a missing sprite; after the reload finishes, backend instances are recreated with the new configuration. On every platform, macOS included, cache misses uniformly prefer the GPU baker; only when the GPU shader or a GL call fails does it fall back to the CPU.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. No change after editing parameters: run /kasuga_pbr reload_config. Parameters take part in the cache key, so clearing the cache by hand is usually unnecessary.
  2. Suspected corrupt old cache: run /kasuga_pbr rebake.
  3. GPU=0: if disk-cache is high, this is a normal cache hit; if a GPU unavailable log appears, check for OpenGL/shader errors, as the system will use the CPU fallback.
  4. failures > 0: search the log for Failed to bake stylized PBR texture; the log entry contains the cache key and the exception.
  5. Atlas too large: compare variants with source textures. A large difference usually means many materials use different configurations.
  6. Startup still slow: use the indicator to tell whether it is stuck on PMX, cache reading, or atlas, and compare the staged timings in the batch log and /kasuga_pbr status.

docs.title: 4. Player JSON Customization
docs.text:
The configuration file is located at:

<game directory>/config/kasuga-pbr.json

The file is generated automatically when it does not exist. Base structure:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "defaults": {},
  "rules": []
}
  • enabled: false: disables the player configuration layer; PMX automatic conversion and other Java rules are still kept.
  • defaults: conversion parameters that override all PMX materials.
  • rules: applied top to bottom in array order; a later matching rule can override the earlier result.
  • A rule only needs the fields it wants to match and override.

docs.title: Match fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description enabled boolean Set to false to temporarily disable a single rule model string glob Full model ResourceLocation texture string glob Original texture ResourceLocation, not the hashed variant ID local_name string glob PMX local material name english_name string glob PMX English material name material_index integer PMX material index, starting from 0 min_shininess number Lower bound of PMX shininess, inclusive max_shininess number Upper bound of PMX shininess, inclusive

String matching is case-insensitive and supports * and ?. Omitting a match field means that field is unconstrained.

Material names and texture names can serve as auxiliary filter conditions, but using them as the only basis for classifying materials is not recommended. For a specific model, prefer model + material_index; for cross-model rules, prefer PMX numeric ranges or the structured context in the Java API.

docs.title: Output fields
docs.text:
Field Range Description smoothness 0–1 Perceptual smoothness f0_code 0–255 LabPBR specular G channel code subsurface 0–1 Subsurface scattering strength normal_strength 0–1 Strength of the normal derived from the base color luminance emission 0–1 Emission strength

Out-of-range values are clamped automatically by PbrConversionSettings.

LabPBR predefined metal codes:

Metal f0_code Iron 230 Gold 231 Aluminum 232 Chrome 233 Copper 234 Lead 235 Platinum 236 Silver 237 Use albedo as the metal color 255

0–229 is used for dielectric F0. Automatic conversion does not produce metal codes above 230.

docs.title: Configuration example
docs.text:
The example below applies stylization to the material indices of one specific model:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "defaults": {
    "normal_strength": 0.06
  },
  "rules": [
    {
      "model": "kasuga_lib:models/pmx/test2.mmd.zip/unfading_flowers_miku_black.pmx",
      "material_index": 12,
      "smoothness": 0.72,
      "f0_code": 230,
      "normal_strength": 0.035
    },
    {
      "model": "kasuga_lib:models/pmx/test2.mmd.zip/unfading_flowers_miku_black.pmx",
      "material_index": 18,
      "smoothness": 0.38,
      "subsurface": 0.45,
      "normal_strength": 0.025
    },
    {
      "model": "kasuga_lib:models/pmx/*",
      "min_shininess": 96,
      "smoothness": 0.85
    }
  ]
}

After saving, run:

/kasuga_pbr reload_config

docs.title: 5. Java API Customization
docs.text:
The public API lives in:

lib.kasuga.rendering.models.mc.api.pbr

Main types:

  • PbrConversionSettings: immutable final conversion parameters, clamped automatically at construction, with with... methods.
  • PbrMaterialContext: read-only snapshot of the current model, texture, material index, PMX names, colors, shininess, flags, and texture dimensions.
  • PbrConversionRule: conversion function.
  • PbrConversionRegistry: rule registration, unregistration, and ordering.
  • PbrMetalPreset: LabPBR metal code enum.

docs.title: Registering rules
docs.text:
import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.mc.api.pbr.PbrConversionRegistry;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.models.mc.api.pbr.PbrMetalPreset;
import net.minecraft.resources.ResourceLocation;

PbrConversionRegistry.Registration registration = PbrConversionRegistry.register(
        ResourceLocation.fromNamespaceAndPath("example_mod", "character_materials"),
        500,
        (context, current) -> {
            if (!context.modelId().getNamespace().equals("example_mod")) {
                return current;
            }
            if (context.materialIndex() == 4) {
                return current
                        .withMetal(PbrMetalPreset.SILVER)
                        .withSmoothness(0.82f)
                        .withNormalStrength(0.04f);
            }
            if (context.shininess() < 8.0f && context.diffuseAlpha() < 1.0f) {
                return current
                        .withSmoothness(0.3f)
                        .withSubsurface(0.2f);
            }
            return current;
        }
);

When the rule is no longer needed, call:

registration.close();

You can also register again with the same ID; the old rule is removed first.

docs.title: Priority and error behavior
docs.text:
• Rules run from the smallest priority to the largest.
  • Rules with the same priority run in string order of the rule ID.
  • The player JSON configuration is registered at priority 1000.
  • To provide a base value before the player configuration, use a priority smaller than 1000.
  • To force an override of the player configuration, use a priority greater than 1000; this reduces the player's ability to customize and should be used with care.
  • When a rule returns null or throws a runtime exception, KasugaLib logs a warning and keeps the result of the previous rule, then continues.

docs.title: PbrMaterialContext fields
docs.text:
Code rules can access:

  • modelId, textureId, materialIndex;
  • localName, englishName, metadata;
  • diffuse RGBA;
  • specular RGB;
  • ambient RGB;
  • shininess;
  • noCull, receivesShadow;
  • textureWidth, textureHeight.

Prefer rules that use the stable combination of model ID, material index, and PMX numeric values. If names must be used, constrain the model ID as well and allow for fallback behavior when the model version changes.

docs.title: 6. Compatibility and Caveats
docs.text:
• Baking currently happens during the client resource load/reload phase and does not run every frame.
  • The PBR atlas is matched to the Iris shader path; without Iris or a shader pack the base-color model is still usable, but whether the PBR channels produce a visual effect depends on the actual rendering path.
  • Using many different configurations on the same base texture increases the atlas area and VRAM usage. Reuse identical parameter combinations as much as possible.
  • When changing the channel semantics or the algorithm of a baker, PbrBakeProfile.VERSION must be bumped so that old disk caches are invalidated.
  • rebake deletes the whole Kasuga PBR cache, which makes the next load expensive; use it only for troubleshooting or an algorithm upgrade.

docs.title: Physics, IK, and ModelTickLoop API
docs.text:
Interface, configuration, and call reference. For the underlying principles see physics.md.

Native physics in Kasuga modelling is handled by the official Box3D C17 engine. The Java layer only handles object mapping, fixed steps, Minecraft collision data, animation targets, and bone writeback; there is no Java fallback integrator or contact solver.

The currently vendored version is pinned to the official Box3D main commit 30c67b5e6d0a3a66f0f506c69ce9e9e0587e3b7c. The source and the license are in modules/modelling/src/main/native/box3d and modules/modelling/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md respectively.

CMake and the Box3D native library are both optional capabilities. When the build machine cannot find CMake, Gradle emits a warning, skips the Box3D JNI compile, and still produces a modelling package without native physics. At runtime the capability can be queried through NativeBox3D.available(); when the native library is missing, the high-level enablePhysics/attach APIs return null, the deployment and block-generation APIs return empty results, and the physics commands show the reason they are disabled, while the remaining model loading, rendering, and animation features are unaffected.

docs.title: 1. Per-Frame Evaluation Order
docs.text:
All procedural stages hang off the single ordered ModelTickLoop pipeline. The framework provides ordering through standard slots, and modules such as physics and IK implement only their own internal logic:

kasuga:apply -> [user pre-IK modules] -> kasuga:ik -> [user post-IK modules]
  -> kasuga:physics -> [user post-physics modules] -> kasuga:anchor

The complete data flow within one frame for a model with physics:

PoseDriver.sample(partialTick)
  -> SkeletonApplyModule (flush pending transforms)
  -> pre-IK modules (write transient IK targets; modules that need pending transforms flushed go before apply)
  -> IkModule (hierarchy evaluation + generic Caliko IK; skipped while physics takes over the pose)
  -> post-IK modules (read the same-frame IK results, submit controller forces)
  -> RagdollModule (Box3D fixed steps + bone writeback)
  -> post-physics modules (observe the final pose)
  -> AnchorModule (recompute the world transform of the display child anchor)
  -> renderer upload

MinecraftRagdollRuntime samples the animation first and then advances physics in RenderFrame.Pre; the backend's later sample consumes the mark already prepared for this frame and does not overwrite the physics results with the animation again. Animation/IK targets are evaluated and cached by input mutation epoch, so when the input stays the same the fixed steps reuse the same animation target; the native force accumulation and fixed-step execution are still managed by the world.

In manual mode you can call:

instance.animate(gameTickSeconds);
instance.sample(partialTick);
instance.simulatePhysics(frameSeconds);   // goes through tickLoop.tick(dt) internally
instance.tick(frameSeconds);              // advances the whole pipeline directly

Use this when animation sampling and physics advancement must happen in one call:

instance.evaluatePhysicsFrame(partialTick, frameSeconds);

docs.title: 2. Generic Rigid Body API
docs.text:
Main package:

lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.physics.core

docs.title: 2.1 Shape and Body
docs.text:
BodyShape is a body-local sealed API:

  • BodyShape.Sphere(center, radius)
  • BodyShape.Box(center, rotation, halfExtents)
  • BodyShape.Capsule(centerA, centerB, radius)

SimBody.collisionShapes() can return any number of child shapes, so one native body can be a compound body. The compatibility fields shape() and shapeSizeRef() are still mapped automatically to one centered primitive.

GenericRigidBody is the default implementation for non-PMX content:

GenericRigidBody sphere = GenericRigidBody.sphere(0.3f, 2f)
        .at(0f, 4f, 0f)
        .friction(0.7f)
        .restitution(0.1f)
        .damping(0.05f, 0.1f)
        .filter(2, 1 << 5);

GenericRigidBody compound = GenericRigidBody.compound(List.of(
        new BodyShape.Box(new Vector3f(-0.5f, 0f, 0f), new Vector3f(0.25f)),
        new BodyShape.Box(new Vector3f( 0.5f, 0f, 0f), new Vector3f(0.25f))
), 4f);

GenericRigidBody movingPlatform = GenericRigidBody.kinematic(List.of(
        new BodyShape.Box(new Vector3f(1f, 0.1f, 1f))
));

Runtime state methods include position(), rotation(), teleport(...), setLinearVelocity(...), and setAngularVelocity(...). The *Ref() methods on SimBody return internal mutable storage and are meant only for high-frequency adaptation and state synchronization.

docs.title: 2.2 World Lifecycle and Fixed Step
docs.text:
try (RigidBodyWorld world = new RigidBodyWorld(
        List.of(sphere, compound), List.of(), RigidBodyWorld.DEFAULT_SUBSTEP_COUNT)) {
    world.setSimulationHertz(120f);
    world.setGravity(new Vector3f(0f, -9.80665f, 0f));
    world.addGroundPlane(0f, 0.8f, 0f);
    world.step(deltaSeconds, RigidBodyWorld.KinematicDriver.none());
}

Object and joint management:

  • add(SimBody) / remove(SimBody)
  • add(BallJoint) / remove(BallJoint) (the ball joints PMX/gltf ragdolls use)
  • add(PhysicsJoint) / remove(PhysicsJoint) (weld/distance/revolute/prismatic, see 2.2.1)
  • bodies() / joints() / physicsJoints()
  • excludePair(bodyA, bodyB)
  • close()

When a body is removed, both kinds of joint attached to it are destroyed automatically.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Generic Joint Types
docs.text:
The four common Box3D joints have been ported in full through JNI (all constraint solving happens inside native code):

// Weld: rigidly bonds two props (0 hertz = hardest), softness adjustable
WeldJoint weld = WeldJoint.atCurrentPose(blockA, blockB).build();
world.add(weld);

// Distance: rope/spring/winch, supports spring, length limits, and motor
DistanceJoint rope = DistanceJoint.between(anchor, payload)
        .length(1f)
        .spring(true, 3f, 0.9f)
        .limits(true, 0.5f, 1.5f)
        .motor(true, 1f, 50f)      // winch reeling in the rope
        .build();

// Revolute: hinge (door, lid, windmill), can carry angle limits and a motor
RevoluteJoint hinge = RevoluteJoint.between(frame, door)
        .hingeAxis(new Vector3f(0, 1, 0))
        .limits(true, -(float) Math.PI * 0.25f, (float) Math.PI * 0.25f)
        .motor(true, -6f, 40f)
        .build();

// Prismatic: slide rail (piston, drawer), can carry travel limits and a motor
PrismaticJoint piston = PrismaticJoint.between(rail, slider)
        .slideAxis(new Vector3f(1, 0, 0))
        .limits(true, -1.2f, 1.2f)
        .motor(true, 2f, 200f)
        .build();

Runtime tuning goes through each joint's setters (setLimits, setMotor, setSpring, setLength); calling a setter on a joint that is not bound to a world throws IllegalStateException.

KinematicDriver.beginStep(world) runs before every fixed step; kinematicTarget(body) returns the target position and rotation of that same step. lastFixedStepCount(), droppedSimulationTime(), and interpolationAlpha() are used to diagnose the fixed step.

Main tuning parameters:

  • setSimulationHertz(10..1000)
  • setSubstepCount(1..50)
  • setMaxFixedStepsPerUpdate(1..1000)
  • setConstraintTuning(hertz, dampingRatio)
  • setSpeedLimits(linear, angular); the current Box3D only provides a world linear speed mapping
  • setRestitutionThreshold(value)
  • setSleepingEnabled(boolean) / setSleepingThresholds(...) / wake()
  • setContinuousCollisionEnabled(boolean)
  • setCollisionsEnabled(boolean)
  • setSelfCollisionsEnabled(boolean)

setSolverIterations is a compatibility entry point for old configurations. Box3D does not expose an iteration count of the same name, so it only validates and stores the value.

docs.title: 2.3 Impulse, Force, and Body Control
docs.text:
All vectors are in world coordinates:

world.applyImpulse(body, impulse);
world.applyImpulse(body, impulse, worldPoint);
world.applyAngularImpulse(body, angularImpulse);

world.applyForce(body, force);
world.applyForce(body, force, worldPoint);
world.applyTorque(body, torque);

world.setGravityScale(body, 0.25f);
float scale = world.gravityScale(body);
world.setAwake(body, true);
boolean awake = world.awake(body);

An impulse changes velocity immediately; force/torque is integrated by the next native Box3D step. The methods return false when the body does not belong to that world, when the body is not dynamic, or when an input is not a finite number. A negative gravity scale inverts that body's gravity.

docs.title: 2.4 Collision, Contact, and Query
docs.text:
Static environment entry points:

  • addPlaneCollider(normal, offset, friction, restitution)
  • addGroundPlane(y, friction, restitution)
  • addStaticBoxCollider(minimum, maximum, friction, restitution)
  • addEnvironmentMesh(friction, restitution)
  • setCollisionEnvironment(CollisionEnvironment)

StaticEnvironmentMesh incrementally synchronizes Minecraft terrain through putCell/removeCell; Java does not do the collision solving.

Queries:

Optional<RayHit> hit = world.raycast(origin, direction, maximumDistance);
List<BodyContact> contacts = world.contacts(body);

RayHit returns the Java SimBody, the world hit point, and the distance. BodyContact fields:

Field Meaning body the body from the query's point of view other the other Java body; empty for native static terrain point world contact point normal unit normal pointing from other to body separation negative means penetration normalImpulse normal impulse of the current solver point totalNormalImpulse normal impulse including the accumulated warm start normalVelocity pre-solve normal velocity touching() the separation or the impulse shows a current contact

Summary counts are available through selfContactCount() and staticContactBodyCount().

docs.title: 2.5 Ray Drag
docs.text:
world.setDragSettings(DragSettings.DEFAULT);
world.beginDrag(hit);                 // or beginDrag(body, worldPoint)
world.updateDragTarget(target, frameSeconds);
world.endDrag();

Drag creates a kinematic anchor and a spherical joint inside native Box3D; it does not teleport the body and does not run a Java stabilizer. A world currently has only one drag target at a time.

docs.title: 3. PMX and glTF ragdoll API
docs.text:
SkeletonRagdoll ragdoll = instance.enablePhysics();
// or generate only the body capsules registered in the profile
SkeletonRagdoll profiled = instance.enablePhysics(profile);

Queries:

  • bodies() / joints()
  • body(definitionIndex): index into the generic bodies list; the MMD Reader keeps the original rigid body order, the glTF Reader keeps the node order
  • body(Bone) / body(boneName)
  • animationTarget(body): the body target after this frame's animation + IK and before physics
  • raycast(...)

SkeletonRagdoll forwards the generic impulse, force, torque, gravity, collision, drag, fixed-step, sleep, and environment controls directly. Body additionally provides position(), rotation(), shapeSize(), velocity, toWorldPoint(...), toLocalPoint(...), teleport(...), and velocity setters.

Mode semantics:

  • PMX mode 0: kinematic, follows the animated bones.
  • PMX mode 1: dynamic, full physics writeback.
  • PMX mode 2: dynamic, keeps the animated translation and writes back the physics rotation.
  • profile ragdoll: both PMX and glTF can generate capsules and semantic masses from the shared UML bone segments; internal self-collision is off by default. PMX can keep the author-made skirt/hair rigid body chains through include_secondary_bodies; these secondary-motion rigid bodies keep the PMX-internal filter relationships in an independent collision group/mask namespace and attach to the main body one-way through a kinematic proxy, so they do not inherit the main body's negative group filters and do not drag the main body back. glTF must supply an explicit profile, and does not guess human topology from bone names.

For the configuration format, profile roles, and Minecraft deployment see mmd-ragdoll.md.

MMD/glTF ragdolls use a per-instance double world anchor and origin-local float physics coordinates. The Minecraft block mesh, rays, mouse drag, and entity attachment points all subtract that anchor first; rendering also uses a double camera-relative displacement. This avoids magnifying small colliders, bone segments, and joint error to centimeters or even whole blocks anywhere from a hundred thousand blocks out to the world border.

docs.title: 4. IK API
docs.text:
SkeletonInstance supports persistent external targets:

skeleton.setIkTarget("右足ＩＫ", worldTarget, 1f);
skeleton.clearIkTarget("右足ＩＫ");
skeleton.clearIkTargets();

skeleton.setIkEnabled("右足ＩＫ", false);
skeleton.resetIkEnabled();

weight ranges over [0,1] and blends between the chain controller's position and the external world target. The name denotes a generic IK chain name, and an undefined chain returns false. For the full construction, limits, closure, and diagnostics see Skeleton Dynamics API.

setFrameIkTarget(...) and clearFrameIkTargets() are the tick loop's transient entry points. ModelTickLoop.tick clears them at the start of every evaluation; the pre-IK modules write them again, and IK and physics then consume them together within that same evaluation. Ordinary callers should usually use IkTargetModule instead of managing the lifecycle directly.

docs.title: 5. ModelTickLoop Modules
docs.text:
Every ModelInstance carries its own ModelTickLoop pipeline (instance.getTickLoop()), with four built-in modules installed by default:

Slot Module Responsibility kasuga:apply SkeletonApplyModule flushes pending transforms into the skeleton; the identity slot skips, and does not overwrite bones the animation already wrote kasuga:ik IkModule hierarchy evaluation + generic Caliko IK; when physics is enabled physics takes over the pose and this slot skips automatically kasuga:physics RagdollModule advances the SkeletonRagdoll (Box3D) and writes back; no-op when physics is not enabled kasuga:anchor AnchorModule recomputes the anchor world transform and notifies the display children

User modules attach between the standard slots with typed helpers, and ordering is provided entirely by the pipeline:

ModelTickLoop loop = instance.getTickLoop();
loop.addPreIk("my-target", module);      // by default after apply, before IK
loop.addPostIk("my-controller", module); // after IK, before physics
loop.addPostPhysics("my-observer", module); // after physics, before anchor
loop.module(ModelTickLoop.SLOT_ANCHOR, AnchorModule.class); // fetch a built-in module instance

When you need to write pending transforms and have the default apply consume them, use loop.getPipeline().addBefore(ModelTickLoop.SLOT_APPLY, "my-pose", module). You can also use addFirst/addLast/addBefore/addAfter/remove through loop.getPipeline() to insert anywhere. tick() clears the transient IK targets at the start, so their lifetime is exactly one tick.

docs.title: 5.1 IkTargetModule
docs.text:
IkTargetModule hand = new IkTargetModule("右手ＩＫ", new Vector3f(1f, 2f, 0f), 1f);
instance.getTickLoop().addPreIk("hand", hand);

hand.setTarget(new Vector3f(1.2f, 2f, 0f));
hand.setTarget(target, 0.6f);
hand.setEnabled(false);

It writes the transient world target only in the pre-IK stage, and does not modify authored animation data.

docs.title: 5.2 ActiveRagdollModule
docs.text:
This controller pulls dynamic bodies toward the same-frame animation/IK body targets in the post-IK stage: it first calls SkeletonRagdoll.evaluateAnimationTarget() to refresh the kinematic targets, and then computes the PD spring force/torque; integration, collision, joints, and sleep are still all executed by Box3D in the physics stage.

Control all dynamic bodies:

ActiveRagdollModule active = new ActiveRagdollModule(
        5f,    // frequency Hz
        1f,    // damping ratio
        800f,  // maximum force
        250f   // maximum torque
);
instance.getTickLoop().addPostIk("active-ragdoll", active);

Control only the bodies of the given bones:

var upperBody = new ActiveRagdollModule(
        List.of("上半身", "首", "頭"), 6f, 1f, 600f, 180f, 0.7f);

At runtime you can use setWeight, setSettings, and setEnabled. An empty bone set means all dynamic bodies.

IkTargetModule and ActiveRagdollModule can be used together: the former modifies the targets first, Caliko solves the generic IK chains, and the latter then makes the Box3D bodies follow the post-IK pose. This is the recommended combination of animation, IK, and active physics.

docs.title: 5.3 AnchorModule and Display Children
docs.text:
Anchor in the model library (uml.structure.skeleton.Anchor) is a display-child anchor bound to a skinned bone, for example the sword a player holds. SkeletonInstance.anchorTransform(name) blends the bound bone's bind→current delta with the same rules as BDEF skinning to obtain the anchor world transform:

// hand the hand anchor's world transform to the host rendering logic every frame
instance.attachToAnchor("hand_r", worldTransform -> {
    if (worldTransform == null) { /* anchor is invalid, hide the held item */ return; }
    placeHeldItem(worldTransform.getPosition(), worldTransform.getRotation());
});
instance.detachFromAnchor("hand_r", attachment);

AnchorModule pushes these transforms in the last stage of every pipeline (kasuga:anchor), so an anchor always follows the final pose (including IK and physics). You can also call instance.anchorTransform(name) directly to query it immediately.

docs.title: 6. glTF Animation Compatibility
docs.text:
.glb and .gltf are registered as built-in resource pipelines. The parser API is in lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.typo.gltf:

GltfAsset asset = GltfLoader.load(path);                    // does not read animation tracks
GltfAsset animated = GltfLoader.load(path, Set.of("walk"));
GltfAsset all = GltfLoader.loadAllAnimations(path);
Model model = GltfModelConverter.convert(all);

GltfModelConverter merges all glTF nodes into one shared UML Skeleton and remaps every skin's JOINTS_0 to global Bones, so the existing CPU/GPU skinning and tick loop modules can be used directly. The Minecraft resource pipeline places embedded base-color images into the existing texture atlas.

ModelInstance instance = ...;
var animation = instance.getPosing();
animation.play("walk", true);

For the generic entry point see ModelPosing; the glTF sampler supports translation/rotation/scale/weights, STEP, LINEAR, and CUBIC_SPLINE. Resource-pack streaming of .gltf supports only embedded/data URIs; when you need external .bin or image URIs use the Path API, or package the asset as .glb.

In Minecraft you can place a <model>.gltf.json manifest next to the model:

{
  "model_scale": 1.3,
  "ragdoll": "example:ragdolls/character.json"
}

model_scale applies to the vertices, the bones, and the generated ragdoll at the same time; ragdoll points to a profile/simulation configuration. The deployment logic reads only the manifest and does not choose a profile by file name or model name. The generic command is:

/kasuga_ragdoll deploy example:models/character.glb

docs.title: 7. Minecraft Physics Block
docs.text:
MinecraftBlockRigidBody converts every voxel AABB of BlockState#getCollisionShape into one body-local BodyShape.Box, instead of always using the full unit cube. Slabs, fences, pillars, and combined shapes therefore keep their real collision gaps. The visual is still drawn by the vanilla block renderer.

MinecraftBlockPhysics uses one shared Box3D world:

  • physics blocks collide with each other in real native collision;
  • terrain is incrementally synchronized into static Box3D boxes by MinecraftBlockRagdollEnvironment;
  • collision groups: props sit in group 1; the local player AABB is a group 15 dynamic proxy and, through a non-collision mask, excludes group 0 (terrain and other default bodies), so the solver noise between the player and the terrain is not passed on to a ground-hugging prop through the proxy. Spectators and dead players get no proxy;
  • ground feel is synthesized from the contact writeback: the correction takes only the deepest contact's MTV (split by orientation — a top-face contact only lifts vertically and produces no horizontal drift; a side-face contact blocks walking just like a real wall), and the proxy's own solver displacement is not fed back to the player, so walking is not pushed back into "sliding" by the solver; while support holds, onGround is reset every frame and fallDistance is zeroed (vanilla clears that state every tick because no real block is underfoot), which makes ground friction, jumping, and fall-damage checks match real blocks;
  • the default cap is MAX_PROPS = 256, and a prop is released automatically when it falls out of the level or the dimension changes;
  • a block with an empty collision shape is not generated.

Debug commands:

/kasuga_physics block [1-32]
/kasuga_physics status
/kasuga_physics clear

This is a client-side playground. To the local player it shows as a pushable, standable collision prop, but it is not a server-registered Block/Entity and takes no part in server-authoritative collision, saving, chunk serialization, or multiplayer synchronization. If you need "like a normal block" semantics that include those network and save behaviors, add a server-side entity and a synchronization protocol above it; do not treat the current local collision bridge as an anti-cheat security boundary.

docs.title: 8. Current Limitations
docs.text:
• Box3D has no built-in Minecraft fluid volume/buoyancy API; the old Java buoyancy model has been deleted.
  • A PMX six-axis joint is currently mapped to a spherical joint; the rotation box is approximated as cone/twist, and the three translation axes are tightened to a fixed anchor.
  • A world currently has only one drag constraint.
  • glTF morph targets already convert POSITION / NORMAL and their weight animations; TANGENT, TEXCOORD / COLOR targets, a second set of skin weights, non-triangle primitives, and material extensions are not converted yet.
  • The glTF parser stores the metallic/roughness factor, but the current Minecraft adapter only uploads base-color directly; Kasuga's stylized PBR conversion still uses its own rules and atlas baker from pbr.md.

For the render pipeline, shader, and effect APIs see effect-rendering.md.

docs.title: Model Material Alpha Rendering Reference
docs.text:
Interfaces, configuration, and call reference. For the mechanics see render-alpha-passes.md.

Model materials are now split into three classes by the alpha contract of glTF/generic materials:

Class GPU state Fragment behavior Order OPAQUE No blending, depth write Ignores the sampled alpha, outputs 1 AFTER_ENTITIES priority 0 MASK No blending, depth write Fragments below the material alphaCutoff are discarded, the rest output 1 AFTER_ENTITIES priority 1 BLEND OIT accumulation/revealage, no depth write Drops only the near-invisible alpha <= 1/255, keeps the actual alpha AFTER_TRANSLUCENT_BLOCKS, WBOIT needs no sorting

BackendInstance creates a separate FlatModelData and vertex buffer for each non-empty pass, so a model with several materials does not redraw incompatible geometry into the wrong RenderType. OPAQUE/MASK can still go into the global batch, but the batch key includes the alpha pass; BLEND does not go into the global batch, so that the two OIT geometry submissions and the ordinary batching state do not get mixed together.

glTF's alphaMode and alphaCutoff are passed to the backend by GltfMaterialData. Older loaders without a transparency contract default to OPAQUE; the PMX loader infers OPAQUE/MASK/BLEND from the diffuse alpha and the texture alpha.
