The non-Iris path of BLEND is a weighted-blended OIT (WBOIT) over two geometry sub-passes: the first pass adds color * alpha * weight and alpha * weight into an RGBA16F accumulation, the second multiplies 1 - alpha into an R16F revealage. Both passes use the scene depth copied from the main framebuffer, testing depth but not writing it; finally the fullscreen resolve computes color = accumulation.rgb / accumulation.a and alpha = 1 - revealage, then composites back to the main target with straight-alpha source-over. Therefore KasugaLib's BLEND geometry on this path does not depend on the far-to-near submit order.

With an Iris shader pack enabled, the same accumulation/revealage/resolve targets are used, but Iris's entities_translucent shader is kept to produce the straight-alpha color after material, PBR, lighting, and fog. Since Kasuga's depth weight cannot be injected into its fragment shader without modifying the shader pack, the Iris path uses a constant-weight WBOIT with weight 1: RGB accumulates with SRC_ALPHA, ONE, A accumulates with ONE, ONE, and revealage stays ZERO, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA. The translucent entity shader of Iris 1.8.12 carries its own 0.1 alpha test, lower than the 0.5 cutoff usually used by MASK.

Iris binds a shader pack gbuffer and can override the blend state on every ShaderInstance.apply(), so Kasuga rebinds the OIT attachment after apply and before draw, and explicitly restores the blend equation, blend factors, and color/depth mask. The scene depth is copied from Iris's after-translucent default framebuffer, and the resolve writes back to the same framebuffer; only the dedicated OIT composite shader is allowed to bypass the Iris unknown-shader guard, and the compatibility policy for other mod shaders is not relaxed.

WBOIT is an approximation, not an exact source-over for an arbitrary number of layers, and it does not bring vanilla water or the transparent fragments of a shader pack into the same OIT equation; the current stage is still AFTER_TRANSLUCENT_BLOCKS, so its scope is "the KasugaLib BLEND layer composited onto an already finished scene". When a floating-point target is unavailable, the Iris pipeline has no bindable world framebuffer, or a runtime framebuffer operation fails, it falls back safely to the old far-to-near sorting path. Iris OIT resolves the main color only; a shader pack that relies on custom extra gbuffer channels to express transparent materials may still need pack-specific integration.

A material's alphaCutoff for MASK and the near-zero 1/255 working cutoff of BLEND are two independent concepts: the former decides whether depth is written, and the latter only removes OIT work items that are almost invisible.

docs.title: Visual acceptance scene (contentTesting)
docs.text:
In the development client, /ksglib debug oit enables OITVisualTestScene, fixed relative to the camera. The scene splits the screen into six regions A-F:

Region What it verifies A OPAQUE geometry and scene depth; the red BLEND behind it must not pass through the solid blocks B Artificial alpha ramp; alpha < 0.5 must discard, and the retained part must write depth C Red/blue crossing faces whose depth relation is reversed left to right; ordinary object sorting cannot be correct on both sides at once D Two transparent layers in front of and behind an irregular opaque wall, checking depth copy, depth test, and depth write=OFF E 12 colored transparent faces, whose submit order changes by a deterministic permutation F Stage/framebuffer regression for a transparent model composited onto the current scene (you can stand on vanilla water to observe)

Keybinds: F6 toggles between WBOIT and the sorted fallback, F7 toggles the normal/reverse submit order, and F8 cycles FINAL → ACCUM_RGB → ACCUM_WEIGHT → REVEALAGE → COPIED_DEPTH. The HUD shows the actual path; so with Iris, with insufficient capabilities, or when OIT fails, the sorted fallback is not mistaken for WBOIT.

Available commands:

/ksglib debug oit
/ksglib debug oit mode oit|sorted
/ksglib debug oit order auto|normal|reverse|rotate|shuffle
/ksglib debug oit buffer final|accum_rgb|accum_weight|revealage|depth

/ksglib debug oit capture saves oit_normal.png, oit_reverse.png, sorted_normal.png, and sorted_reverse.png in that order to the development client's screenshots/kasuga_oit_visual/, and computes

E_oit = mean(abs(oit_normal - oit_reverse))
E_sorted = mean(abs(sorted_normal - sorted_reverse))

The acceptance condition is E_oit < 1/255 and E_sorted greater than at least 2/255 and significantly higher than E_oit. This does not require WBOIT to equal the exact source-over ground truth; it checks its independence from submit order, and the tiny non-associativity error of floating-point addition should not be treated as a failure.

docs.title: Model render scheduling (Render Scheduling)
docs.text:
Interface, configuration, and call reference. For the principles see render-scheduling.md.

For the public scheduling and buffer/backend contracts see the UML rendering framework. The ModelRenderScheduler in this document is an MC compatibility adapter; the policy and frame marks are managed by uml.framework.schedule; VANILLA_RENDERER corresponds to the public HOST_RENDERER. Multi-camera visibility marks are cleared per view and animation sampling is deduplicated by the shared frame token; see the multi-camera and offscreen output document.

After a UML model is mounted to mc_backend, it is drawn by the phased world pipeline. This document answers "when a model should render and when it should not", and how to integrate with the scheduling mechanism of Minecraft's vanilla renderer.

docs.title: 0. Model handle: the split between the logic side and the render side
docs.text:
Upper-layer code operates on the same model in two halves, following MC's mental model:

upper logic side ────► state machine (FSM / PoseDriver)    decides "what action to perform": state, transition, animation behavior
                     │ writes bone local transforms
                     ▼
              ModelInstance ◄───────────────────── the same instance
                     ▲ writes root transform / scheduling / anchors / physics
upper render side ───► McModelHandle                  decides "where it goes, whether it is visible, which schedule to use"

McModelHandle (mc/api/McModelHandle) is the only entry point on the render side: resource-level outfit uses ofAssembly / switchAssembly, see outfit resources and switching.

// Render side: the handle can be created before resources are published; the pose is stashed and takes effect on mount
McModelHandle handle = McModelHandle.of(modelLoc, null, instanceLoc, new Vec3(x, y, z));
handle.mount();                       // returns false while resources are unpublished; retry next tick
handle.setPos(entity.position());     // vanilla-style verb
handle.scheduleVanillaRenderer();     // visibility is decided by the vanilla renderer
handle.attachToAnchor("hand_r", (name, t) -> placeItem(t));  // held item
handle.enablePhysics(UpdateMode.RENDER_FRAME);
handle.hide() / show() / markRenderedThisFrame();

A state machine is attached through the handle in three forms:

// ① Local data-driven: built from a definition id; the logic side ticks the bound object
var binding = handle.attachLocalStateMachine(Id.of("kasuga_lib", "door"));
if (binding != null) {
    binding.machine().mutableVars().set(OPEN, true);  // the logic side triggers the transition
    binding.tick();                                   // call from the BE/Entity game tick
}

// ② Local programmatic: take over an already built machine directly
var machine = StateMachine.builder(owner)...build();
handle.attachLocalStateMachine(machine);

// ③ Full host with server-authoritative sync (recommended for BE/Entity):
//    create the handle with ofFsm to align the instance identity; it hosts an FsmAnimatedModel
//    internally, the client-bound instance is adopted into the handle automatically,
//    and render scheduling still applies as usual.
McModelHandle handle = McModelHandle.ofFsm(modelLoc, null, pos.asLong(), null);
FsmAnimatedModel fsm = handle.attachSyncedStateMachine(this, pos.asLong(), fsmId);
fsm.tick(level, pos);        // forwarded from the BE ticker (server pushes sync / client drives the puppet)

If the instance was already created by an existing component (such as the FsmAnimatedModel inside an AnimationBlockEntity), the render side adopts it with McModelHandle.ofExisting(modelLoc, modelName, instanceLoc) instead of creating a second instance.

docs.title: 1. The three scheduling modes
docs.text:
ModelRenderScheduler maintains one policy per mounted instance, defaulting to ALWAYS (the historical behavior: unconditional draw every frame). To switch modes:

ModelRenderScheduler.setMode(instance, RenderScheduleMode.VANILLA_RENDERER);
Mode Decision maker Typical host ALWAYS The global pipeline draws every frame Static decoration, effect-type content MANUAL Host code: setVisible(instance, bool) or pipeline.setRendering(model, id, bool) Custom LOD/switch logic VANILLA_RENDERER Whether the vanilla renderer is called Entities (EntityRenderer), block entities (BER)

Beyond the modes there are two orthogonal gates:

  • Render distance: setMaxRenderDistance(instance, blocks) culls by squared camera distance; 0 means unlimited.
  • Frustum: for each instance the pipeline runs a Frustum.isVisible test using "the vertex bounding sphere translated to the root position" (the bounding radius is computed and cached on first use). A culled instance is not sampled for animation and does not upload vertices in that frame — consistent with "the vanilla renderer is not called once a mob is beyond its distance". Physics stepping is independent of visibility (MinecraftRagdollRuntime) and does not freeze because of culling.

Unmounting an instance (stopRendering/removeInstance) automatically cleans up its scheduling state.

docs.title: 2. Integrating with the vanilla Entity renderer
docs.text:
The vanilla flow: EntityRenderer.render is called only after EntityRenderDispatcher.shouldRender (tracking distance + frustum) passes. To make an entity model inherit this scheduling:

  1. Mount the model in VANILLA_RENDERER mode;
  2. Provide a renderer extending UmlModelEntityRenderer<T> and register it for the entity type:
public class MyEntityRenderer extends UmlModelEntityRenderer<MyEntity> {
    public MyEntityRenderer(EntityRendererProvider.Context ctx) { super(ctx); }

    @Override protected ModelInstance resolveModel(MyEntity entity) {
        return entity.getKasugaModel();   // the instance held by the host
    }

    @Override protected ResourceLocation modelTexture(MyEntity entity) {
        return null; // queried only by the vanilla UI overlay; null → white fallback
    }
}

For entities culled by tracking range or outside the frustum, the vanilla code does not call their renderer's render() → no mark → the pipeline skips sampling and drawing for that frame.

docs.title: 3. Integrating with the vanilla BlockEntity renderer
docs.text:
The vanilla flow: BlockEntityRenderDispatcher.render first checks BlockEntityRenderer.shouldRender (view distance, 64 blocks by default), then the section frustum outside it; render() is called only when both pass.

BlockEntityRenderers.register(MY_BE_TYPE,
        context -> new UmlBlockEntityRenderer<>(context,
                be -> be.getKasugaRender().getModelInstance("main")));

Mount in VANILLA_RENDERER mode here as well. getViewDistance can be adjusted at construction time.

docs.title: 4. What about "blocks that go through the chunk dispatcher"
docs.text:
Modern vanilla bakes static block geometry straight into the mesh of a whole chunk section (SectionRenderDispatcher builds in batches) and has no per-block renderer callback — a deliberate batching optimization. The conclusion splits into two cases:

  • Purely static models: they can still be baked into the chunk mesh (or use an ordinary BakedModel) and benefit from the vanilla section-level culling and batching; the price is that they can never move.
  • Dynamic/skeletal models: they cannot be baked into a section mesh (vertices change every frame), so vanilla provides no dispatcher entry point for them. There are two proper paths:
  • Promote to a BlockEntity + the BER adapter above — recommended, it fully reuses vanilla scheduling; this is also how vanilla itself handles "blocks that need to change every frame" (chest open/close animations, banners, etc. are all BEs).
  • Keep the global pipeline mount and use MANUAL mode with your own visibility logic, or rely on the pipeline's built-in frustum/render-distance culling (ALWAYS mode gets these two gates as well).

In short: the chunk baking path carries static content only; any dynamic model that needs scheduling should land in an Entity / BlockEntity renderer or under explicit MANUAL control.

docs.title: 5. Frame timing
docs.text:
vanilla pass: entities + block entities
  └─ EntityRenderer.render / BER.render
       └─ ModelRenderScheduler.markRenderedThisFrame(instance)
kasuga pipelines:
  └─ AFTER_ENTITIES (priority 0 → 1)
       ├─ OPAQUE: no blend + depth write
       └─ MASK: alpha discard + depth write
  └─ AFTER_TRANSLUCENT_BLOCKS
       └─ BLEND: low alpha discard + no depth write + weighted-blended OIT
          (Iris/unsupported-target fallback: far-to-near sort)

  The first pass calls flipFrame() to lock in this frame's marks. The sampled-instance
  cache remains alive until BLEND, so a mixed model is sampled once even
  though its three material classes are submitted independently.

The mark buffer uses a double-buffer swap: marks written by the vanilla pass are locked in at the start of the pipeline, next frame's marks go into the other buffer, and the two stages need no synchronization barrier.

docs.title: Rendering backend integration reference
docs.text: Backend integration and contract reference; for module layering, resource ownership, and synchronization principles see the explanation.

docs.title: Module dependencies
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Host[modelling: Minecraft host adaptation] --> GL[render-opengl: OpenGL / LWJGL]
    Host --> Core[render-core: UML and rendering contracts]
    GL --> Core
    Future[future Vulkan / Metal backend] -. implements the same set of contracts .-> Core

render-core is a plain Java library. It does not apply the ModDev plugin and does not depend on Minecraft, NeoForge, LWJGL, or a specific graphics API. Before compileJava, checkGraphicsApiIsolation runs and checks source imports as well as compile and runtime dependencies, keeping these dependencies out of the core. DataFixerUpper is used for the existing data codecs; it is not Blaze3D or the Minecraft renderer. The dependencies of formula and utils disable transitive resolution and only reuse the existing Java expressions and data structures.

render-opengl likewise does not apply ModDev. It depends on the core and on LWJGL and centrally manages GL buffers, textures, shaders, VAOs, fences, FBOs, readback, and preview windows. The host that runs it is responsible for providing the current GL context, the correct thread, and the LWJGL natives for the platform.

modelling keeps Minecraft's world render events, RenderType, VertexFormat, texture atlases, lighting, Iris/Sodium compatibility, and multi-camera world rendering. These classes are host adapters for the current Minecraft + OpenGL combination and cannot serve as a general interface for other graphics APIs.

docs.title: UML and resource lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as host
    participant P as ModelPipeLine / ModelInstance
    participant B as RenderBackend
    participant C as RenderContext
    participant D as concrete graphics API
    H->>P: load model, create instance, bind PoseDriver
    H->>B: add(key, adapter, instance)
    B->>C: create context and apply()
    C->>D: create backend resources
    loop every view, every render stage
        H->>B: renderAllObjects(hostContext)
        B->>P: schedule, sample pose per frame
        B->>C: beforeRender(hostContext)
        B->>D: upload data, submit draws
    end
    H->>B: remove(key) / close()
    B->>C: close()
    C->>D: release or defer recycling of resources

The core covers model loading, model structures, skeletons, morph, animation, FSM, and pose sampling and scheduling, plus the RenderBackend, RenderContext, ModelGeometryAdapter, RenderableFactory, RenderBuffer, TypedBuffer, and output routing contracts. Its resource type, host frame context, and transform metadata are all generic; it does not require GL objects or Minecraft classes.

Backend / BackendContext provide the default mount and release behavior; a concrete backend implements context creation, data packing, and drawing. A failed mount does not publish a half-built context; removing an instance releases only that mount's backend resources, while the model instance itself is managed by the model pipeline.

The core still contains the Java/JNI physics adaptation of the existing Box3D. Physics is not part of a graphics API; when used standalone, a host that enables Box3D must additionally provide the platform's native library.

docs.title: Upload and output
docs.text:
UploadRing is responsible only for slot rotation, dirty element merging, version tracking, and the resource lifecycle, and performs allocation, writes, and completion-status queries through UploadDevice. GpuUploadRing on the production path is now its OpenGL adapter, keeping the original constructors, statistics types, and FloatBuffer entry points. The macOS TBO orphan policy continues to be provided by MacTboUploadDevice in the OpenGL module.

The integer buffer token and the long completion token of UploadDevice are opaque handles internal to the backend, not cross-API native resource IDs. A new backend can map them into its own resource table. A device must guarantee that reads already submitted remain valid after the storage is replaced; completion queries must not block. A device that cannot meet this contract should use its own upload implementation and reuse the higher-level UploadBuffer / RenderBuffer.

FrameOutputRouter<T>, FrameOutputTarget<T>, OutputFrame<T>, and the camera state belong to the core. T is defined by the backend. FrameTexture is the OpenGL framebuffer/texture carrier and belongs to the OpenGL module; other APIs should provide their own output carrier and target.

docs.title: Integrating another API
docs.text:
1. Create a standalone Java backend module that depends only on render-core and the binding of the target API.
  2. Implement RenderBackend / RenderContext, or extend the default Backend / BackendContext. Model, skeleton, and pose data are read directly from the existing ModelInstance; the adapter is responsible for the target API's vertex layout, skeleton data representation, shader, synchronization, and submission.
  3. Have the host inject the corresponding backend and host frame context. ModelPipeLine.Builder already supports registering a backend; a default implementation can extend Backend, and a standalone RenderBackend implementation can also mount model instances directly.
  4. Implement FrameOutputTarget<YourFrame> and reuse the core output routing and camera lifecycle.
  5. Handle windows, resource reload, render stages, and other platform interop in the host adaptation layer.

Existing public class names are kept to preserve call and serialization name compatibility. Some GL classes therefore still use the historical uml.backend.gpu package name, and the pure math Direction also keeps the historical models.mc.util package name. Whether something belongs to the core is determined by Gradle module dependencies; the core must not import the OpenGL module.

This split did not implement a Vulkan/Metal backend, nor does it let Minecraft's Blaze3D switch APIs at runtime. Minecraft's effect pipeline description still uses its own draw state for now; replacing the whole renderer of that host would additionally require the corresponding host adaptation and shader generation path.

docs.title: Java Shader DSL
docs.text:
• The DSL does not parse a Java AST and does not decompile a lambda. A builder lambda runs immediately in Java and creates typed shader IR.

  • Java conditions and loops control only IR construction. The final shader does not contain these Java structures. Use the shader builder for conditions and loops that must stay dynamic in GLSL.

  • The backend inserts an expression from a Java variable at each use location. The expression does not automatically create a GLSL local variable.

  • A let* call creates an initialized GLSL local variable. For later assignments, use a local* call that returns ShaderVariable.

  • A fullscreen program contains only a fragment module and uses the built-in fullscreen vertex stage.

  • A graphics program contains a vertex module and a fragment module. position(...) writes to gl_Position.

  • Each fragment input must have a vertex output with the same name and type. Otherwise, program construction fails.

  • A uniform or sampler with the same name in both stages must have an identical declaration. An identical declaration occurs only one time in the Minecraft shader JSON.

  • A program ID must use the lowercase namespace:path resource-ID format.

  • The current profile supports float, int, bool, vec2, vec3, vec4, mat2, mat3, mat4, and sampler2D. The profile also supports float uniform arrays and named structs. The profile supports stage inputs and outputs, local variables, structured control flow, common mathematical operations, and texture sampling.

  • The current backend generates GLSL 150 and Minecraft core-shader JSON.

  • During loading, a runtime-generated bundle has priority for its own .vsh, .fsh, and .json files. For a missing resource or import, loading uses the current client ResourceProvider.

  • The DSL checks the stage interface of a graphics program during Java construction. The caller must match the RenderShaderDescriptor vertex format to the attributes.

docs.title: User-Adjustable Shader Parameters
docs.text:
A shader does not expose all uniforms automatically. Register each user-adjustable parameter. Each parameter has a fixed name, description, ShaderParameterType, inclusive range, and defaultValues. The parameter name is also the GLSL uniform name. The name must be a valid, non-reserved GLSL identifier.

public static final ShaderParameter EXPOSURE = ShaderParameter.floatParameter(
        "Exposure",
        "Controls the final output exposure",
        1.0f,  // default
        0.0f,  // minimum
        4.0f   // maximum
);

public static final ShaderParameter TINT = ShaderParameter.builder(
                "Tint",
                "Multiplies the output color",
                ShaderParameterType.COLOR_RGB
        )
        .range(0.0, 1.0)
        .defaultValues(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f)
        .build();

In a generated shader, use the applicable expose* call to declare a uniform and register the parameter specification. A uniform* call keeps the uniform internal. The call does not add the uniform to the public schema.

ShaderProgram program = ShaderProgram.fullscreen("example:adjustable", shader -> {
    FloatExpr exposure = shader.exposeFloat(EXPOSURE);
    Vec3Expr tint = shader.exposeVec3(TINT);
    Vec3Expr color = shader.sampler2D("SceneSampler").sample(shader.texCoord()).rgb();
    shader.fragmentColor(shader.vec4(color.mul(tint).mul(exposure), shader.f32(1.0f)));
});

A resource shader or custom factory cannot use the DSL. Register the same specification on RenderShaderDescriptor. The resource uniform must match the parameter name and basic GLSL type. The first bind fails if the uniform is missing.

RenderShaderDescriptor descriptor = RenderShaderDescriptor.builder(id, format)
        .resource()
        .expose(EXPOSURE)
        .expose(TINT)
        .build();

RenderShaderHandle.parameters() supplies the default runtime parameter block for the registration. ShaderParameterBlock validates each change for component count, numeric type, finite values, and range. A parameter change does not regenerate or compile the shader. reset(name) uses the declared default. resetAll() restores all declared defaults.

RenderShaderHandle handle = registration.handle();
handle.parameters().setFloat(EXPOSURE, 1.35f);
handle.parameters().set(TINT, 1.0, 0.55, 0.2);

When a fullscreen method receives a handle, Kasuga uploads the default parameter block before the draw. The applicable methods are PostProcessContext.fullscreen(...) and PostProcessGraphContext.fullscreen(...). Kasuga cannot infer a registration from a direct ShaderInstance. Use .parameters(block) to bind a parameter block. Use handle.createParameterBlock() for each independent configuration of one shader.

The current ShaderParameterType values include float, integer, boolean, vec2, vec3, vec4, RGB color, and RGBA color. ShaderParameterType also includes mat2, mat3, and mat4. The range applies to all components. Boolean parameters always use [0, 1].

To open the parameter panel:

  1. Enter /kasuga_effects in the client.
  2. Select Parameters.

The schema generates the parameter panel. The panel is not specific to one effect. The panel shows each shader that exposes parameters. A boolean parameter uses a switch. Other parameter types use component sliders.

Vectors, colors, and matrices use the applicable component names. A parameter change applies during the next draw. The change does not regenerate or recompile the shader.

Kasuga saves the default parameter blocks asynchronously in config/kasuga_lib/shader-parameters.json. After a client restart, Kasuga restores values by shader ID and parameter name. An independent block from createParameterBlock() contains effect-instance state. Kasuga does not store this block in the global configuration.

The configuration stores only values that override schema defaults. A reset permits a later schema default to apply. Use isDefault(name) and hasOverrides() to examine the current state.

The following client commands examine, change, and reset exposed shader parameters. Use a command when a slider cannot set a large integer accurately. Also use a command to enter a complete vector or matrix:

/kasuga_effects parameter list <shader-id>
/kasuga_effects parameter set <shader-id> <name> <value...>
/kasuga_effects parameter reset <shader-id> <name>

Spaces or commas separate vector and matrix components. The built-in black-hole example exposes LensingScale, DiskBrightness, and ChromaticScale. The screen, time, and per-effect packed uniforms stay internal.

The following example builds and registers a fullscreen shader from Java expressions:

ShaderProgram program = ShaderProgram.fullscreen("example:screen_tint", shader -> {
    var scene = shader.sampler2D("SceneSampler");
    var tint = shader.uniformVec3("Tint", 1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f);
    var source = scene.sample(shader.texCoord());
    shader.fragmentColor(shader.vec4(source.rgb().mul(tint), source.a()));
});

ShaderRegistration shader = pipelines.shader(
        RenderShaderDescriptor.generated(program)
                .withPreload(ShaderPreloadPolicy.DEFERRED, 50)
);

shader.whenReady().thenAccept(status -> rebuildDependentResources(shader.handle()));

docs.title: Migration from GLSL to the Java Shader DSL
docs.text: A builder lambda represents the body of the GLSL main() function. The lambda does not calculate pixel results. The lambda records declarations, expressions, and statements in call order. The backend then generates GLSL 150.

docs.title: Types and Expressions
docs.text:
The Java DSL uses expression-wrapper types in place of GLSL operators. Use var for an intermediate expression when the expression type is clear. The Java compiler checks the exact type.

GLSL Java DSL float, int, bool FloatExpr, IntExpr, BoolExpr vec2, vec3, vec4 Vec2Expr, Vec3Expr, Vec4Expr mat2, mat3, mat4 Mat2Expr, Mat3Expr, Mat4Expr sampler2D Sampler2DExpr struct Material ShaderStructType, StructExpr 1.0, 1, true shader.f32(1), shader.i32(1), shader.bool(true) vec2(x, y) shader.vec2(x, y) vec4(rgb, alpha) shader.vec4(rgb, alpha) a + b, a - b a.add(b), a.sub(b) a * b, a / b a.mul(b), a.div(b) a < b, a >= b, a == b a.lt(b), a.gte(b), a.equalTo(b) a && b, a || b, !a a.and(b), a.or(b), a.not() texture(image, uv) image.sample(uv) normalize(v), length(v) v.normalize(), v.length() mix(x, y, t) x.mix(y, t) atan(y, x) y.atan2(x) matrix * vector matrix.transform(vector) left * right (matrix) left.mul(right) value.rgb, value.a value.rgb(), value.a() Values[index] values.get(index) float(integer) integer.toFloat()

Only a method from the applicable Expr type can generate code. For example, the current Vec2Expr supplies normalize(). Other vector wrappers do not always supply the same method. If an expression does not accept a Java number, use f32(), i32(), or an applicable primitive overload.

docs.title: Globals, Stage Inputs, and Stage Outputs
docs.text:
• uniformFloat, uniformInt, uniformBool, uniformVec*, and uniformMat* declare GLSL uniforms. Supplied values become defaults in the Minecraft shader JSON. A matrix overload without a default uses an identity matrix.

  • uniformFloatArray is the only current method for uniform arrays. The length must be greater than 1. Use an IntExpr to index an element.

  • sampler2D declares uniform sampler2D.

  • inputFloat, inputInt, and inputVec* declare in values for the current stage.

  • In a vertex stage, outputFloat and outputVec* declare out values. position(...) writes to gl_Position.

  • In a fragment stage, fragmentColor(...) writes to the generated fragColor.

  • A fullscreen fragment can use texCoord() to read the texture coordinates from the built-in vertex stage.

  • A graphics fragment must use a method such as inputVec2 to declare the fragment inputs. A call to texCoord() fails.

  • A vertex program must call position(...) at least one time. A fragment program must call fragmentColor(...) at least one time. Validation only confirms that the IR contains a write. The shader author must write to the required output on all runtime paths.

The two stages in a graphics program represent the .vsh and .fsh files:

ShaderProgram particle = ShaderProgram.graphics(
        "example:particle",
        vertex -> {
            var position = vertex.inputVec3("Position");
            var uv = vertex.inputVec2("UV0");
            var color = vertex.inputVec4("Color");
            var modelView = vertex.uniformMat4("ModelViewMat");
            var projection = vertex.uniformMat4("ProjMat");

            vertex.outputVec2("particleUv", uv);
            vertex.outputVec4("particleColor", color);
            vertex.position(projection.transform(modelView.transform(
                    vertex.vec4(position, vertex.f32(1))
            )));
        },
        fragment -> {
            var uv = fragment.inputVec2("particleUv");
            var color = fragment.inputVec4("particleColor");
            var radial = fragment.f32(1).sub(
                    uv.sub(fragment.vec2(0.5f, 0.5f)).length().mul(2).min(1)
            );
            fragment.fragmentColor(fragment.vec4(
                    color.rgb().mul(radial), color.a().mul(radial)
            ));
        }
);

RenderShaderDescriptor descriptor = RenderShaderDescriptor.generated(
        particle,
        DefaultVertexFormat.POSITION_TEX_COLOR
);

The Position, UV0, and Color input names and types must match the supplied Minecraft VertexFormat. The DSL checks the vertex-to-fragment interface, but it does not check the VertexFormat.

docs.title: Local Variables and Control Flow
docs.text:
A Java variable holds one IR expression. In this example, brightness does not create a GLSL local variable. The backend inserts the brightness expression at the use location:

var brightness = color.rgb().mul(intensity);
shader.fragmentColor(shader.vec4(brightness, color.a()));

letFloat/letVec*, letMat*, and letStruct create GLSL local variables that are read-only in the DSL. For later assignments, use the applicable local* method. get() reads the variable. set() writes the variable.

This GLSL:

float sum = 0.0;
for (int index = 0; index < Count; ++index) {
    if (index >= 8) break;
    if (Values[index] <= 0.0) continue;
    sum = sum + Values[index];
}
fragColor = vec4(sum, sum, sum, 1.0);

The equivalent Java DSL is:

var count = shader.uniformInt("Count", 0);
var values = shader.uniformFloatArray("Values", 8, 0.0f);
var sum = shader.localFloat("sum", shader.f32(0));

shader.forRange("index", shader.i32(0), count, index -> {
    shader.ifThen(index.gte(shader.i32(8)), shader::breakLoop);
    shader.ifThen(values.get(index).lte(shader.f32(0)), shader::continueLoop);
    sum.set(sum.get().add(values.get(index)));
});

shader.fragmentColor(shader.vec4(sum.get(), sum.get(), sum.get(), shader.f32(1)));

  • ifThen and ifThenElse generate shader branches. A Java if runs one time during IR construction.

  • forRange(name, start, end, body) generates an integer loop. The loop increments by 1 and uses < end as the end condition.

  • whileLoop(condition, body) generates while. doWhile(condition, body) generates do while.

  • breakLoop() can exit only the innermost loop. You can use continueLoop() in a loop.

  • A Java for can unroll an expression for constant values. The Java loop does not generate a GLSL loop.

  • If a shader value changes across branches or loops in a Java lambda, use ShaderVariable. Do not rebind a Java local variable to represent a shader assignment.

var cursor = shader.localInt("cursor", shader.i32(0));

shader.whileLoop(cursor.get().lt(count), () -> {
    cursor.set(cursor.get().add(1));
    shader.ifThen(cursor.get().gte(shader.i32(64)), shader::breakLoop);
});

shader.doWhile(cursor.get().gt(shader.i32(0)), () ->
        cursor.set(cursor.get().sub(shader.i32(1)))
);

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
A struct is a named type. The ShaderStructType.Builder that creates a field owns the field key. You cannot use the field key with a different struct. This restriction applies when the other struct has a field with the same name and type.

Declare a dependency struct before you declare the struct that contains the dependency. The current DSL supports structs for typed locals, construction, field reads, and field assignments. The DSL does not support structs for uniforms, stage inputs, or stage outputs.

var materialBuilder = ShaderStructType.builder("Material");
var tint = materialBuilder.vec3Field("tint");
var roughness = materialBuilder.floatField("roughness");
var materialType = materialBuilder.build();

shader.declareStruct(materialType);
var material = shader.localStruct("material", shader.structValue(
        materialType,
        shader.vec3(1.0f, 0.8f, 0.6f),
        shader.f32(0.5f)
));

shader.setStructField(material, roughness, shader.f32(0.25f));
var finalTint = material.get().field(tint);

structValue arguments must follow the order of field declarations. The builder checks the argument count and types during Java construction.

docs.title: Switch Statements
docs.text:
switchOn accepts an IntExpr. caseOf keeps declaration order and does not insert break. Therefore, caseOf permits GLSL fallthrough. Call breakSwitch() to end a case. The generated output puts defaultCase after all cases.

shader.switchOn(mode, cases -> cases
        .caseOf(0, () -> {
            intensity.set(shader.f32(0.25f));
            shader.breakSwitch();
        })
        .caseOf(1, () -> intensity.set(shader.f32(0.75f))) // fallthrough
        .defaultCase(() -> intensity.set(shader.f32(1.0f)))
);

For breakLoop() and breakSwitch(), the applicable structure must be the innermost break target. This rule prevents an invalid bare break. A case in a loop can call breakSwitch(). The case cannot call breakLoop() directly. To exit the outer loop, set a boolean local variable. Test the variable after the switch.

docs.title: Naming and Link Rules
docs.text:
• A shader program ID must use lowercase namespace:path.

  • A shader identifier must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. It must not start with gl_, and it must not be a reserved GLSL word.

  • Globals, locals, and loop indexes in one stage share one name set. A name cannot occur more than one time in the complete stage. Separate code blocks do not create reusable name scopes.

  • A fragment input must have a vertex output with the same name and type. A vertex can have additional outputs that the fragment does not read.

  • If both stages use a uniform or sampler with the same name, its storage, type, array length, and default value must be identical.

  • Names are case-sensitive. The final GLSL and Minecraft JSON use these names without changes.

docs.title: Runtime Uniforms and Samplers
docs.text:
F3+T replaces the current ShaderInstance. For a long-life object:

  1. Store only a RenderShaderHandle.

  2. During each render, access the current generation through the handle or pass context.

  3. On the render thread, update a uniform through currentShader.safeGetUniform(name).set(...).

  4. In a fullscreen pass, use colorSampler, depthSampler, or textureSampler to bind a sampler.

To upload a float array:

  1. Set the float[] capacity to the length in the shader declaration.

  2. Upload the complete float[].

  3. A uniform default in the DSL generates a JSON default. It does not overwrite a current value that Java uploads each frame.

context.fullscreen(PostProcessGraphTarget.main(), shaderHandle)
        .colorSampler("SceneSampler", context.read(scene))
        .uniforms(active -> active.safeGetUniform("Tint").set(red, green, blue))
        .draw(false);

docs.title: Raw GLSL Escape
docs.text:
Use a raw escape for GLSL that the typed API cannot represent. All raw entry points have @DelicateShaderApi. This annotation identifies code for additional review. The annotation does not guarantee API stability. The Java compiler does not validate raw GLSL.

@DelicateShaderApi
static ShaderProgram derivativeShader() {
    return ShaderProgram.fullscreen("example:derivative", shader -> {
        shader.rawPreamble("#extension GL_ARB_gpu_shader5 : enable");
        shader.rawDeclaration("""
                float saturate(float value) {
                    return clamp(value, 0.0, 1.0);
                }
                """);

        var edge = shader.rawFloat("dFdx(texCoord.x)");
        shader.rawStatement("if (edge < 0.0) discard;");
        shader.fragmentColor(shader.vec4(edge, edge, edge, shader.f32(1.0f)));
    });
}

  • rawPreamble inserts text after #version 150. Use it for extensions and macros.

  • rawDeclaration inserts text after globals and before main(). Use it for user functions and backend-specific declarations.

  • rawStatement copies the statement text into the current block. The method does not parse or change the text.

  • rawFloat, rawInt, rawBool, rawVec*, rawMat*, and rawStruct wrap source text in caller-declared expression types.

The raw API rejects only empty strings. The raw API does not parse source text. The raw API does not track types, identifiers, uniforms, stage interfaces, or control flow. The caller is responsible for the declared type of a raw expression. The caller is also responsible for raw-uniform JSON entries and GLSL driver support. Use the typed API when the typed API supports the required feature.

The typed API does not currently supply user functions, struct uniforms, struct stage inputs, or struct stage outputs. The typed API also excludes non-float uniform arrays, arbitrary swizzles, discard, derivatives, and advanced texture sampling. A raw escape can supply these features. A resource shader or custom factory can also supply these features. Extend the typed IR and backend for cross-backend support, link validation, or a long-life public API. Do not use a raw string as a permanent interface.

docs.title: Gradle Shader Generation
docs.text:
plugins {
    id 'builder.kasuga.shader'
}

  • The builder.kasuga.shader plugin creates the shader source set. The plugin reads src/shader/java and src/shader/resources. The plugin also adds the shader DSL dependency.

  • generateKasugaShaders runs before processResources. The task first clears the generated-output directory. The task then runs the shader providers.

  • A provider must be a non-abstract public class that implements ShaderProgramProvider. The provider must have a public no-argument constructor. The generation task fails if the provider does not meet these conditions.

  • The task sorts providers by class name before execution. The task converts each returned program to .vsh, .fsh, and .json resources.

  • If two programs generate the same path, the task fails. The task does not overwrite generated output.

  • The plugin adds the generated directory to the main resources. Therefore, the final JAR contains the generated content.

Other pages of this topic: Custom Rendering Specification and Managed Effects and Post-Processing.
